title: IV. In The Dark
paragraphs: Where was he running? "Where else could she be except at Fyodor Pavlovitch's? She must have run straight there from Samsonov's — that was obvious now. The whole intrigue, the whole deception, was plain." ... It all spun through his mind at once. He didn't run to Marya Kondratyevna's. "No need to go there ... not the slightest need ... I mustn't raise the alarm ... they'd run straight and tell him.... Marya Kondratyevna was clearly in on it, Smerdyakov too, all of them, all bought off!"

He came up with another plan: he ran a long way round Fyodor Pavlovitch's house, crossed the lane, ran down Dmitrovsky Street, then over the little bridge, and came out straight at the deserted alley behind the house — empty, uninhabited, with a neighbor's kitchen-garden fenced off on one side by a hurdle fence, and on the other the tall, sturdy fence running around Fyodor Pavlovitch's garden. Here he picked a spot — apparently the very place where, according to the old story, Lizaveta had once climbed over. "If she could climb it," the thought occurred to him, God knows why, "surely I can." He jumped, and managed at once to catch the top of the fence. Then he hauled himself up hard and sat astride it. Close by, in the garden, stood the bath-house, but from the fence he could also make out the lit windows of the house.

"Yes, the old man's bedroom is lit up. She's there!" And he leapt from the fence into the garden. Though he knew Grigory was ill, and very likely Smerdyakov too, and that there was no one to hear him, he instinctively hid, stood still, and listened. But there was dead silence all around, and, as if by design, total stillness — not the faintest breath of wind.

"And nothing but the whispering silence," the line rose to his mind for some reason. "If only no one heard me jump the fence! I don't think they did." Standing still a minute, he walked softly over the grass in the garden, keeping clear of the trees and bushes. He moved slowly, creeping cautiously at every step, listening to his own footsteps. It took him five minutes to reach the lit window. He remembered that just below it stood several thick, tall bushes of elder and whitebeam. The door from the house into the garden, on the left, was shut — he'd made a point of checking it on his way. At last he reached the bushes and hid behind them, holding his breath. "I have to wait now," he thought, "to reassure them, in case they heard my footsteps and are listening ... just don't let me cough or sneeze."

He waited two minutes. His heart was pounding violently, and at moments he could hardly breathe. "No, this hammering in my chest won't stop," he thought. "I can't wait any longer." He stood behind the bush in the shadow. The light from the window fell on the front of it.

"How red the whitebeam berries are!" he murmured, not knowing why. Softly, noiselessly, step by step, he approached the window and rose on tiptoe. The whole of Fyodor Pavlovitch's bedroom lay open before him. It wasn't a large room, and was split in two by a red screen — "Chinese," Fyodor Pavlovitch called it. The word "Chinese" flashed through Mitya's mind. "And behind the screen is Grushenka," he thought. He began watching Fyodor Pavlovitch, who was wearing a new striped silk dressing-gown Mitya had never seen, with a silk cord and tassels at the waist. A clean, dandified shirt of fine linen with gold studs showed beneath the dressing-gown's collar. On his head Fyodor Pavlovitch still wore the same red bandage Alyosha had seen.
"He's dressed himself up," thought Mitya.

His father stood near the window, apparently lost in thought. Suddenly he jerked his head up, listened a moment, and, hearing nothing, went to the table, poured out half a glass of brandy from a decanter, and drank it down. Then he let out a deep sigh, stood still a moment more, walked carelessly to the looking-glass on the wall, raised the red bandage on his forehead a little with his right hand, and began examining the bruises and scars that hadn't yet faded.
"He's alone," thought Mitya. "In all likelihood, he's alone."
Fyodor Pavlovitch stepped back from the looking-glass, turned suddenly to the window, and looked out. Mitya slipped instantly into the shadow.

"She might be there behind the screen. Maybe she's already asleep," he thought, with a pang. Fyodor Pavlovitch moved away from the window. "He's looking for her out the window, so she's not there. Why else would he stare out into the dark? He's wild with impatience." ... Mitya slipped back at once and fell to watching through the window again. The old man was sitting at the table now, looking disappointed. At last he put his elbow on the table and rested his right cheek in his hand. Mitya watched him eagerly.
"He's alone, he's alone!" he repeated again. "If she were here, his face would look different."

Strangely, an odd, irrational irritation rose in his heart at the thought that she wasn't there. "It's not that she's not here," he explained to himself at once, "it's that I can't say for certain whether she is or not." Mitya remembered afterward that his mind was exceptionally clear at that moment, that he took in everything down to the smallest detail and missed nothing. But a feeling of misery — the misery of uncertainty and indecision — was growing in his heart with every second. "Is she here or not?" The angry doubt filled him, and suddenly, making up his mind, he reached out and softly knocked on the window frame. He knocked the signal the old man had arranged with Smerdyakov — twice, slowly, then three times, quicker — the signal that meant "Grushenka is here!"
The old man started, jerked his head up, and, jumping up quickly, ran to the window. Mitya slipped away into the shadow. Fyodor Pavlovitch threw the window open and thrust his whole head out.
"Grushenka, is that you? Is it you?" he said, in a kind of trembling half-whisper. "Where are you, my angel, where are you?" He was terribly agitated, breathless.
"He's alone," Mitya decided.

"Where are you?" the old man cried again, thrusting his head out farther, right up to the shoulders, peering in every direction, right and left. "Come here, I've got a little present for you. Come, I'll show you...."
"He means the three thousand," thought Mitya.
"But where are you? Are you at the door? I'll open it right away."

And the old man very nearly climbed out of the window, peering to the right, where the door into the garden was, trying to see into the darkness. Another second and he would certainly have run to open the door without waiting for Grushenka's answer.

Mitya watched him from the side without stirring. The old man's profile, which he loathed so much, his sagging Adam's apple, his hooked nose, his lips smiling in greedy anticipation — all of it was lit up sharply by the slanting lamplight from the room on the left. A horrible fury of hatred suddenly surged up in Mitya's heart: "There he is, my rival, the man who's tormented me, who's ruined my life!" It was a rush of that same sudden, furious, vengeful anger he had spoken of, as if foreseeing it, to Alyosha four days before, in the arbor, when, in answer to Alyosha's question, "How can you say you'll kill our father?" he had said, "I don't know, I don't know. Maybe I won't kill him, maybe I will. I'm afraid he'll suddenly seem so loathsome to me in that moment. I hate his double chin, his nose, his eyes, his shameless leer. It's a physical revulsion. That's what I'm afraid of — that it might be more than I can stand." ... That physical revulsion was becoming unbearable now. Mitya was beside himself; he suddenly pulled the brass pestle out of his pocket.

"God was watching over me then," Mitya himself said afterward. At that very moment Grigory woke up on his sickbed. Earlier that evening he had gone through the treatment Smerdyakov had described to Ivan. He had rubbed himself all over with vodka mixed with a secret, very strong decoction, then drunk what was left of the mixture while his wife recited a "certain prayer" over him, after which he'd gone to bed. Marfa Ignatyevna had tasted the stuff too, and, not being used to strong drink, was sleeping like the dead beside her husband.

But Grigory woke suddenly in the night, and after a moment's thought — though he felt a sharp pain in his back at once — he sat up in bed. Then he thought again, got up, and dressed hurriedly. Perhaps his conscience was troubled at the thought of sleeping while the house went unguarded "in such dangerous times." Smerdyakov, worn out by his fit, lay motionless in the next room. Marfa Ignatyevna didn't stir. "That stuff was too much for the woman," Grigory thought, glancing at her, and, groaning, went out onto the steps. He probably only meant to look out from the steps, since he could barely walk — the pain in his back and right leg was unbearable. But he suddenly remembered he hadn't locked the little gate into the garden that evening. He was the most punctual and precise of men, one who kept to an unvarying routine and habits of many years' standing. Limping and wincing with pain, he went down the steps and toward the garden. Sure enough, the gate stood wide open. He stepped into the garden without thinking. Perhaps some notion struck him, or some sound reached him, because, glancing left, he saw his master's window open. No one was looking out of it just then.

"What's it open for? It's not summer now," Grigory thought, and at that very instant he caught sight of something extraordinary ahead of him in the garden. Forty paces off, a man seemed to be running through the dark — a kind of shadow moving very fast.

"Good Lord!" Grigory cried, beside himself, and, forgetting the pain in his back, hurried to cut off the running figure. He took a short cut — he clearly knew the garden better; the fleeing figure was heading for the bath-house, ran behind it, and made for the garden fence. Grigory followed, never losing sight of him, running and forgetting everything. He reached the fence at the very moment the man was climbing over it. Grigory cried out, beside himself, threw himself at him, and clutched his leg with both hands.
Yes, his foreboding hadn't deceived him. He recognized him — it was him, the "monster," the "parricide."
"Parricide!" the old man shouted, loud enough for the whole neighborhood to hear, but he had no time to shout more — he dropped at once, as though struck by lightning.

Mitya jumped back into the garden and bent over the fallen man. In Mitya's hands was the brass pestle, and he flung it away mechanically into the grass. It fell two paces from Grigory, not in the grass but on the path, in the most conspicuous spot possible. For a few seconds he examined the figure lying before him. The old man's head was covered in blood. Mitya reached out and began feeling it. He remembered afterward clearly how anxious he'd been to find out whether he'd cracked the old man's skull or simply stunned him with the pestle. But the blood was flowing horribly, and in a moment Mitya's fingers were drenched in the hot stream. He remembered taking out the clean white handkerchief he'd brought along for his visit to Madame Hohlakov, and pressing it to the old man's head, senselessly trying to wipe the blood from his face and temples. But the handkerchief was soaked through at once.

"Good God, what am I doing this for?" Mitya thought, suddenly pulling himself together. "Even if I've cracked his skull, how could I find that out now? And what difference does it make now?" he added hopelessly. "If I've killed him, I've killed him.... You've come to grief, old man, so there you'll have to lie!" he said aloud. And suddenly, turning to the fence, he vaulted over it into the lane and broke into a run — the blood-soaked handkerchief crushed in his right fist, which, as he ran, he stuffed into the back pocket of his coat. He ran headlong, and the few passers-by who met him in the dark streets remembered afterward that they'd passed a man running that night. He flew back again to the widow Morozov's house.

The moment he'd left the house that evening, Fenya had rushed to the head porter, Nazar Ivanovitch, and begged him, for Christ's sake, "not to let the captain in again today or tomorrow." Nazar Ivanovitch had promised, but then went upstairs, having suddenly been sent for by his mistress, and on the way up met his nephew, a boy of twenty who'd recently come from the country, and told him to take his place — but forgot to mention "the captain." Mitya ran up to the gate and knocked. The boy recognized him at once, since Mitya had tipped him more than once. He opened the gate immediately, let him in, and hastened to tell him, with a good-natured smile, that "Agrafena Alexandrovna isn't home right now, you know."
"Where is she, then, Prohor?" asked Mitya, stopping short.
"She set off this evening, some two hours ago, with Timofey, for Mokroe."
"What for?" Mitya cried.
"That I couldn't say. To see some officer. Someone sent for her and horses were sent to fetch her."
Mitya left him and ran like a madman to Fenya.

title: V. A Sudden Resolution
paragraphs: She was sitting in the kitchen with her grandmother; the two of them were just about to go to bed. Trusting Nazar Ivanovitch, they hadn't locked themselves in. Mitya burst in, pounced on Fenya, and grabbed her by the throat.
"Talk, now! Where is she? Who's she with, at Mokroe?" he roared furiously.
Both women shrieked.
"Aie! I'll tell you. Aie! Dmitri Fyodorovitch, darling, I'll tell you everything right now, I won't hide a thing," Fenya gabbled, scared to death. "She's gone to Mokroe, to her officer."
"What officer?" Mitya roared.
"Her officer, the one she used to know, the one who dropped her five years ago," Fenya rattled off as fast as she could talk.

Mitya let go of her throat, releasing the hands that had been squeezing it. He stood facing her, pale as death, unable to say a word, but his eyes showed he understood everything, all of it, from the very first word — he'd grasped the whole situation. Poor Fenya wasn't in any state, at that moment, to notice whether he understood or not. She stayed sitting on the trunk exactly as she'd been when he burst in, trembling all over, holding her hands out in front of her as if to defend herself. She seemed to have frozen in that position. Her wide, terrified eyes were fixed unmoving on him. And to make it worse, both his hands were smeared with blood. On his way, running, he must have touched his forehead with them, wiping off the sweat, so that patches of blood now marked his forehead and right cheek. Fenya was on the edge of hysterics. The old cook had jumped up and was staring at him like a madwoman, nearly senseless with terror.

Mitya stood there a moment, then sank mechanically onto a chair beside Fenya. He sat there not really thinking, but, as it were, paralyzed with terror, numb. And yet everything was as clear as day: that officer — he knew about him, knew everything perfectly well, had heard it from Grushenka herself, had known a letter had come from him a month before. So this had been going on for a month, a whole month, kept secret from him, right up until this new man's arrival — and he had never once thought of him! But how could that be, how could he not have thought of him? Why had he forgotten this officer like that, forgotten him the moment he'd heard the name? That was the question that loomed before him now like some monstrous thing. And he stared at this monstrous thing in horror, going cold with horror.

But suddenly, as gently and mildly as a gentle, affectionate child, he began speaking to Fenya, as though he had entirely forgotten how he'd just frightened and hurt her. He fell to questioning her with a precision astonishing given his state, and though the girl kept glancing wildly at his blood-stained hands, she too answered every question with remarkable readiness and speed, as if eager to lay the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, before him. Bit by bit, even with a kind of relish, she began explaining every detail — not to torment him, but as though eager to be of the utmost use to him. She described the whole day in great detail: Rakitin and Alyosha's visit, how she, Fenya, had stood watch, how her mistress had set off, and how she'd called out the window to Alyosha to give him, Mitya, her greetings, and tell him "to remember forever how she'd loved him for an hour."
Hearing that message, Mitya suddenly smiled, and color rose in his pale cheeks. At the same moment Fenya said to him, no longer afraid to be curious:
"Look at your hands, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. They're covered in blood!"
"Yes," Mitya answered mechanically. He glanced carelessly at his hands and at once forgot them, and Fenya's question along with them.

He sank into silence again. Twenty minutes had passed since he'd run in. His first shock had passed, but some new, fixed resolve had evidently taken hold of him. He suddenly stood up, smiling dreamily.
"What's happened to you, sir?" said Fenya, pointing at his hands again. She spoke with compassion, as though she now felt very close to him in his grief. Mitya looked at his hands once more.

"That's blood, Fenya," he said, looking at her with a strange expression. "That's human blood, and good God — why was it shed? But ... Fenya ... there's a fence here" (he looked at her as though posing a riddle) "a high fence, and terrible to look at. But at dawn tomorrow, when the sun rises, Mitya will leap over that fence.... You don't understand what fence I mean, Fenya, and never mind that.... You'll hear tomorrow, and you'll understand ... and now, goodbye. I won't stand in her way. I'll step aside — I know how to step aside. Live, my joy.... You loved me for an hour — remember Mityenka Karamazov like that forever.... She always called me Mityenka, remember?"
And with those words he suddenly walked out of the kitchen. Fenya was almost more frightened by this sudden departure than she had been when he'd run in and grabbed her.

Just ten minutes later, Dmitri walked in on Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, the young official with whom he'd pawned his pistols. It was by now half past eight, and Pyotr Ilyitch had finished his evening tea and had just put his coat back on to go to the "Metropolis" to play billiards. Mitya caught him on his way out.
Seeing his face all smeared with blood, the young man cried out in surprise.
"Good God! What's the matter?"
"I've come for my pistols," said Mitya, "and brought your money. And many thanks. I'm in a hurry, Pyotr Ilyitch, please be quick."

Pyotr Ilyitch grew more and more astonished; he suddenly caught sight of a bundle of banknotes in Mitya's hand, and what's more, Mitya had walked in holding the notes the way no one walks in and no one carries money: in his right hand, held out in front of him as if on display. Perhotin's houseboy, who met Mitya in the hallway, said afterward that he'd come in exactly like that, money held straight out in his hand, so he must have been carrying it that way even in the street. They were all rainbow-colored hundred-rouble notes, and the fingers gripping them were covered in blood.

When Pyotr Ilyitch was questioned later about the sum of money, he said it was hard to judge at a glance, but it might have been two thousand, maybe three — in any case a big, "fat" bundle. "Dmitri Fyodorovitch," he testified afterward, "seemed unlike himself too — not drunk, but sort of exalted, oblivious to everything, and at the same time sort of absorbed, as though brooding over something, searching for something, unable to reach a decision. He was in a great hurry, gave abrupt, very strange answers, and at moments seemed not at all downcast but quite cheerful."
"But what IS wrong with you? What's happened?" cried Pyotr Ilyitch, staring wildly at his guest. "Why are you covered in blood? Did you fall? Look at yourself!"
He took him by the elbow and led him to the mirror.
Seeing his own blood-smeared face, Mitya started, and his face darkened with fury.

"Damn it! That's the last straw," he muttered angrily, hurriedly switching the notes from his right hand to his left, and yanking the handkerchief out of his pocket. But the handkerchief turned out to be soaked with blood too (it was the one he'd used to wipe Grigory's face). There was barely a white patch left on it, and it hadn't just started to dry — it had stiffened into a crumpled ball that wouldn't pull apart. Mitya flung it angrily on the floor.
"Oh, damn it!" he said. "Don't you have some rag or other ... to wipe my face?"
"So you're only stained, not wounded? You'd better wash," said Pyotr Ilyitch. "Here's a washstand. I'll pour you some water."
"A washstand? Good ... but where am I supposed to put this?"
With the strangest bewilderment he pointed to his bundle of hundred-rouble notes, looking inquiringly at Pyotr Ilyitch, as if it were up to him to decide what Mitya should do with his own money.
"In your pocket, or here on the table. It won't get lost."

"In my pocket? Yes, in my pocket. Fine.... But listen, this is all nonsense," he cried, as though suddenly snapping out of his daze. "Look here, first let's settle the business of the pistols. Give them back to me. Here's your money ... because I need them badly ... and I haven't a minute, not one minute to spare."
And peeling off the top note from the bundle, he held it out to Pyotr Ilyitch.
"But I won't have enough change. Don't you have something smaller?"
"No," said Mitya, glancing again at the bundle, and, as if not trusting his own words, flipped through two or three of the top notes.
"No, they're all the same," he added, and again looked at Pyotr Ilyitch inquiringly.
"How did you get so rich?" the other asked. "Wait, I'll send my boy over to Plotnikov's — they close late — to see if they'll change it. Here, Misha!" he called into the hallway.

"To Plotnikov's shop — excellent!" cried Mitya, as if struck by an idea. "Misha," he said, turning to the boy as he came in, "listen — run to Plotnikov's and tell them Dmitri Fyodorovitch sends his greetings and will be there directly.... But listen, listen — tell them to have champagne ready, three dozen bottles, before I get there, packed up the way it was for Mokroe. I took four dozen with me that time," he added, suddenly turning to Pyotr Ilyitch. "They know all about it, don't worry, Misha," he turned back to the boy. "Wait, listen — tell them to add cheese, Strasburg pies, smoked fish, ham, caviar, and everything, everything they've got, up to a hundred roubles, or a hundred and twenty like last time.... But wait — don't let them forget dessert, sweets, pears, watermelons, two or three or four — no, one melon's enough — and chocolate, candy, toffee, fondants; in short, everything I took to Mokroe before, three hundred roubles' worth along with the champagne ... let it be exactly the same again. And remember, Misha — if your name is Misha — his name's Misha, isn't it?" he turned back to Pyotr Ilyitch again.
"Wait a minute," Pyotr Ilyitch broke in, watching him uneasily. "You'd better go and tell them yourself. He'll muddle it up."

"He will, I can see he will! Ah, Misha! Why, I was about to kiss you for the errand.... If you don't make a mistake, there's ten roubles for you — run along, hurry.... Champagne's the main thing, tell them to bring up the champagne. And brandy too, and red and white wine, everything I had that time.... They know what I had that time."

"But listen!" Pyotr Ilyitch cut in, a little impatiently. "Let him just run and change the money and tell them not to close, and you go tell them yourself.... Give him your note. Off you go, Misha! Best foot forward!"

Pyotr Ilyitch seemed to hurry Misha off on purpose, because the boy stood there with his mouth and eyes wide open, plainly grasping little of Mitya's orders, staring up in astonishment and fright at his blood-covered face and the trembling, bloodstained fingers holding the notes.
"Well, now come and wash," said Pyotr Ilyitch sternly. "Put the money on the table, or in your pocket.... That's right, come along. But take off your coat."
And as he began helping him out of his coat, he cried out again:
"Look, your coat's covered in blood too!"

"That's ... it's not the coat. It's only a little, here on the sleeve.... And that's just where the handkerchief was lying. It must have soaked through. I must have sat on the handkerchief at Fenya's, and the blood came through," Mitya explained at once, with a childlike unawareness that was astonishing. Pyotr Ilyitch listened, frowning.
"Well, you must have gotten up to something — you must have been in a fight with someone," he muttered.

They started washing. Pyotr Ilyitch held the jug and poured the water. Mitya, in a desperate hurry, barely soaped his hands (they were trembling, as Pyotr Ilyitch remembered afterward). But the young official insisted he soap them thoroughly and rub harder. He seemed to gain more and more command over Mitya as time went on. It's worth noting, in passing, that he was a young man of sturdy character.

"Look, your nails aren't clean. Now rub your face — here, on your temples, by your ear.... Are you going in that shirt? Where are you going, anyway? Look, the whole cuff of your right sleeve is covered in blood."
"Yes, it's all bloody," Mitya observed, glancing at his shirt cuff.
"Then change your shirt."

"I don't have time. Look, I'll..." Mitya went on with the same trusting simplicity, drying his face and hands with the towel and putting on his coat. "I'll turn it up at the wrist. It won't show under the coat.... See!"

"Tell me now, what have you been up to? Been fighting with someone? At the tavern again, like before? Have you gone and beaten that captain again?" Pyotr Ilyitch asked reproachfully. "Who have you been beating this time ... or killing, maybe?"
"Nonsense!" said Mitya.
"Why 'nonsense'?"
"Don't worry about it," said Mitya, and suddenly laughed. "I smashed an old woman in the marketplace just now."
"Smashed? An old woman?"
"An old man!" cried Mitya, staring Pyotr Ilyitch straight in the face, laughing, and shouting at him as if he were deaf.
"Damn it! An old woman, an old man.... Have you killed someone?"

"We made up. We had a row — and made up. At a place I know. We parted friends. A fool.... He's forgiven me.... He's sure to have forgiven me by now ... if he got up, he wouldn't have forgiven me" — Mitya suddenly winked — "but damn him anyway, you know, I say, Pyotr Ilyitch, damn him! Don't worry about him! I don't want to right now!" Mitya snapped, decisively.

"What's the point of picking quarrels with everyone? ... Just like you did with that captain over some nonsense.... You've been fighting and now you're off on a spree — that's you all over! Three dozen champagne — what do you need all that for?"

"Bravo! Now give me the pistols. On my honor, I've no time now. I'd like to have a chat with you, dear boy, but there's no time. And there's no need — it's too late for talk. Where's my money? Where did I put it?" he cried, thrusting his hands into his pockets.

"You put it on the table yourself.... Here it is. Had you forgotten? Money's like dirt or water to you, it seems. Here are your pistols. Odd thing — at six o'clock you pawned them for ten roubles, and now you've got thousands. Two or three, I'd say."
"Three, you can bet," Mitya laughed, stuffing the notes into his trouser side-pocket.
"You'll lose it that way. Found a gold mine, have you?"

"The mines? The gold mines?" Mitya shouted at the top of his voice and burst into a roar of laughter. "Would you like to go to the mines, Perhotin? There's a lady here who'd cough up three thousand for you, just for going. She did it for me — she's so awfully fond of gold mines. Do you know Madame Hohlakov?"
"I don't know her, but I've heard of her and seen her. Did she really give you three thousand? Did she really?" said Pyotr Ilyitch, eyeing him doubtfully.

"As soon as the sun rises tomorrow, as soon as ever-young Phoebus flies upward, praising and glorifying God, you go to her, this Madame Hohlakov, and ask her whether she coughed up that three thousand or not. Go and find out."

"I don't know what terms you're on with her ... but since you say it so flatly, I suppose she did give it to you. You've got the money in your hand, but instead of heading to Siberia you're spending it all.... Where are you really off to now, eh?"
"To Mokroe."
"To Mokroe? But it's night!"
"Once the lad had all, now the lad has naught," Mitya suddenly cried.
"What do you mean, 'naught'? You're saying that with all those thousands!"
"I'm not talking about thousands. Damn the thousands! I'm talking about the female character.
Fickle is the heart of woman, treacherous and full of vice —
I agree with Ulysses. That's what he says."
"I don't understand you!"
"Am I drunk?"
"Not drunk, but worse."
"I'm drunk in spirit, Pyotr Ilyitch, drunk in spirit! But enough of that!"
"What are you doing, loading the pistol?"
"I'm loading the pistol."

Unfastening the pistol case, Mitya actually opened the powder horn and carefully poured and rammed in the charge. Then he took the bullet and, before loading it, held it up between two fingers in front of the candle.
"Why are you looking at the bullet?" asked Pyotr Ilyitch, watching him with uneasy curiosity.
"Oh, just a fancy. Look — if you meant to put that bullet through your own brain, would you look at it first, or not?"
"Why would you look at it?"

"It's going into my brain, so it's interesting to have a look and see what it's like. But that's foolishness — a moment's foolishness. There, done," he added, inserting the bullet and driving it home with the ramrod. "Pyotr Ilyitch, my dear fellow, that's nonsense, all nonsense, and if only you knew what kind of nonsense! Give me a scrap of paper, will you."
"Here's some paper."
"No, a clean new sheet, writing paper. That's right."

And taking a pen from the table, Mitya quickly wrote two lines, folded the paper in four, and stuffed it into his waistcoat pocket. He put the pistols back in the case, locked it, and kept it in his hand. Then he looked at Pyotr Ilyitch with a slow, thoughtful smile.
"Now, let's go."
"Go where? No, wait a minute.... You're not thinking of putting that bullet through your brain, are you?" Pyotr Ilyitch asked uneasily.
"I was only fooling about the bullet! I want to live. I love life! You can be sure of that. I love golden-haired Phoebus and his warm light.... Dear Pyotr Ilyitch, do you know how to step aside?"
"What do you mean by 'stepping aside'?"

"Making way. Making way for a dear creature, and for one I hate. And letting the one I hate become dear — that's what making way means! And saying to them: God bless you, go your way, pass on, while I—"
"While you—?"
"Enough of that, let's go."
"Honestly. I'll get someone to stop you going there," said Pyotr Ilyitch, looking at him. "What are you going to Mokroe for, now, of all times?"
"There's a woman there, a woman. That's enough for you. Now hush."
"Listen, savage as you are, I've always liked you.... I'm worried."
"Thanks, old fellow. A savage, you say. Savages, savages! That's what I'm always saying. Savages! Ah, here's Misha! I was forgetting him."

Misha ran in at full tilt, a handful of change in his hand, and reported that everyone at Plotnikov's was in a bustle — "They're carrying down the bottles, and the fish, and the tea, it'll all be ready right away." Mitya grabbed ten roubles and handed it to Pyotr Ilyitch, then tossed another ten-rouble note to Misha.

"Don't you dare do such a thing!" cried Pyotr Ilyitch. "I won't have it in my house, it's a bad, corrupting habit. Put your money away. Here, put it here — why waste it? It'll come in handy tomorrow, and I dare say you'll be coming to me to borrow ten roubles again. Why do you keep shoving the notes into your side pocket? Ah, you'll lose them!"
"I say, dear fellow, let's go to Mokroe together."
"What would I go for?"
"I say, let's open a bottle right now, and drink to life! I want to drink, and especially to drink with you. I've never had a drink with you, have I?"
"All right, we can go to the 'Metropolis.' I was just heading there."
"No time for that. Let's drink at Plotnikov's, in the back room. Shall I ask you a riddle?"
"Ask away."
Mitya took the scrap of paper out of his waistcoat pocket, unfolded it, and showed it to him. In a large, clear hand was written: "I punish myself for my whole life, my whole life I punish!"
"I'm certainly going to speak to someone, I'll go right now," said Pyotr Ilyitch, after reading the paper.
"You won't have time, dear boy — come and have a drink. March!"

Plotnikov's shop stood at the corner of the street, two doors down from Pyotr Ilyitch's. It was the biggest grocery in our town, and by no means a poor one, owned by some wealthy merchants. It carried everything you'd find in a Petersburg shop — every kind of grocery, wines "bottled by the Eliseyev brothers," fruit, cigars, tea, coffee, sugar, and so on. Three shop assistants and two errand boys were always kept on. Though our part of the country had grown poorer, the landowners had moved away, and trade had gotten worse, the grocery stores still flourished as before, growing more prosperous every year — there was no shortage of buyers for their goods.

They were waiting for Mitya at the shop with real impatience. They remembered vividly how, three or four weeks earlier, he'd bought wine and goods of every kind worth several hundred roubles, paid for in cash (they'd never have given him anything on credit, of course). They remembered that then, as now, he'd had a bundle of hundred-rouble notes in his hand and had scattered them about carelessly, without haggling, without a thought for what he might actually want with so much wine and food. The story had gone round the whole town that, driving off then with Grushenka to Mokroe, he had "spent three thousand in a single night and the day after, and come back from the spree without a penny." He'd rounded up a whole band of gypsies (camped in our district at the time), who for two days had wrung money out of him without limit while he was drunk, and had drunk expensive wine without limit themselves. People liked to tell, laughing at Mitya, how he'd handed out champagne to grimy-handed peasants and treated the village women and girls to sweets and Strasburg pies. Though laughing at Mitya to his face was a risky business, there was plenty of laughter behind his back, especially at the tavern, over his own guileless public confession that all he'd gotten out of Grushenka for that whole "escapade" was "permission to kiss her foot, and that was the most she'd allowed him."

By the time Mitya and Pyotr Ilyitch reached the shop, they found a cart with three horses harnessed abreast, bells jingling, and Andrey the driver waiting at the entrance for Mitya. Inside the shop they'd nearly finished packing one crate of provisions, and were only waiting for Mitya to arrive before nailing it shut and loading it onto the cart. Pyotr Ilyitch was astounded.
"Where did this cart spring from so quickly?" he asked Mitya.

"I ran into Andrey on my way to you, and told him to drive straight here to the shop. No time to lose. Last time I drove with Timofey, but Timofey's already gone on ahead of me with the witch. Will we be very late, Andrey?"

"They'll get there an hour ahead of us at most, maybe not even that. I saw Timofey off myself. I know how he drives. His pace won't be ours, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. How could it be? They won't beat us by an hour!" Andrey, a lanky, red-haired, middle-aged driver in a full-skirted coat with a kaftan over his arm, answered warmly.
"Fifty roubles for vodka if we're only an hour behind them."
"I'll stake my word on the time, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. Eh, they won't be half an hour ahead of us, let alone a full one."

Though Mitya bustled about seeing to things, he gave his orders strangely, in a disjointed, disconnected way. He'd start a sentence and forget how it was supposed to end. Pyotr Ilyitch found himself having to step in and help.
"Four hundred roubles' worth, not a kopeck less, exactly as it was that time," Mitya commanded. "Four dozen champagne, not a bottle less."
"What do you want with so much? What's it for? Wait!" cried Pyotr Ilyitch. "What's in this box? Surely there isn't four hundred roubles' worth in there?"

The obliging shop clerks began explaining, with oily politeness, that the first box held only half a dozen bottles of champagne, along with "the most essential items" — savories, sweets, toffee, and so on. The main part of the order would be packed and sent on, as it had been the last time, in a separate cart, also with three horses traveling at full speed, so that it would arrive no more than an hour behind Dmitri Fyodorovitch himself.
"No more than an hour! No more than an hour! And add more toffee and fondants. The girls there are so fond of them," Mitya insisted hotly.

"The fondants are fine. But what do you want with four dozen champagne? One dozen would be plenty," said Pyotr Ilyitch, nearly angry now. He began haggling, demanded an itemized bill, and wouldn't be satisfied. But he only managed to save a hundred roubles. In the end it was agreed that only three hundred roubles' worth would be sent.
"Well, go to the devil, then!" cried Pyotr Ilyitch, on second thought. "What business is it of mine? Throw your money away, seeing as it costs you nothing."

"This way, my economist, this way, don't be angry." Mitya pulled him into a room at the back of the shop. "They'll bring us a bottle here in a moment. We'll taste it. Ah, Pyotr Ilyitch, come along with me — you're a good fellow, just the sort I like."

Mitya sat down in a wicker chair, at a little table covered with a grimy dinner napkin. Pyotr Ilyitch sat across from him, and the champagne soon arrived, with oysters offered to the gentlemen — "first-class oysters, the last shipment."
"To hell with the oysters. I don't eat them. And we don't need anything," cried Pyotr Ilyitch, nearly angrily.
"No time for oysters," said Mitya. "And I'm not hungry. You know, friend," he said suddenly, with feeling, "I've never liked all this disorder."
"Who does like it? Three dozen champagne for peasants, upon my word, that's enough to make anyone angry!"

"That's not what I mean. I'm talking about a higher order. There's no order in me — no higher order. But ... that's over now. No use grieving over it. Too late, damn it! My whole life has been disorder, and it's time to set it in order. Was that a pun?"
"You're raving, not making puns!"
"Glory to God in Heaven, glory to God in me....
"That line came from my heart once — it's not a verse, it's a tear.... I made it up myself ... not while I was pulling the captain's beard, though...."
"Why bring him up all of a sudden?"
"Why do I bring him up? Foolishness! Everything comes to an end; everything's made equal in the end. That's the long and short of it."
"You know, I keep thinking about your pistols."

"That's foolishness too! Drink, and don't get fanciful. I love life. I've loved life too much, shamefully much. Enough! Let's drink to life, dear boy, I propose the toast. Why am I pleased with myself? I'm a scoundrel, but I'm satisfied with myself. And yet it torments me that I'm a scoundrel and satisfied with myself all at once. I bless creation. I'm ready to bless God and all He's made, right now, but ... I have to kill one noxious insect first, so it doesn't crawl around spoiling life for everyone else.... Let's drink to life, dear brother. What could be more precious than life? Nothing! To life — and to one queen among queens!"
"Let's drink to life, and to your queen too, if you like."
They each drank a glass. Excited and expansive as Mitya was, he was also melancholy. It was as though some heavy, crushing anxiety weighed on him.
"Misha ... here's your Misha! Misha, come here, my boy, drink this glass to golden-haired Phoebus, to tomorrow morning...."
"What are you giving it to him for?" cried Pyotr Ilyitch irritably.
"Yes, yes, yes, let me! I want to!"
"E-ech!"
Misha drained the glass, bowed, and ran off.

"He'll remember this later," Mitya remarked. "Woman — I love woman! What is woman? The queen of creation! My heart is sad, my heart is sad, Pyotr Ilyitch. Do you remember Hamlet? 'I am very sorry, good Horatio! Alas, poor Yorick!' Maybe that's me — Yorick? Yes, I'm Yorick now, and a skull afterward."
Pyotr Ilyitch listened in silence. Mitya, too, fell silent for a while.
"What kind of dog is that you've got here?" he asked the shopman, offhandedly, noticing a pretty little lap-dog with dark eyes sitting in the corner.
"It belongs to Varvara Alexyevna, the mistress," the clerk answered. "She brought it and forgot it here. It'll have to be taken back to her."

"I saw one like it once ... in the regiment ..." Mitya murmured dreamily, "only that one had a broken hind leg.... By the way, Pyotr Ilyitch, I wanted to ask you — have you ever stolen anything in your life?"
"What a question!"
"Oh, I didn't mean anything by it. Out of someone's pocket, you know. I don't mean government money — everyone steals that, no doubt you do too...."
"Go to the devil."
"I mean other people's money. Stealing straight out of a pocket. Out of a purse, eh?"
"I stole twenty kopecks from my mother when I was nine. Took it off the table on the sly and held it tight in my fist."
"Well, and what happened?"
"Oh, nothing. I kept it three days, then felt ashamed, confessed, and gave it back."
"And then?"
"Naturally I was whipped. But why do you ask? Have you stolen something?"
"I have," said Mitya, winking slyly.
"What did you steal?" Pyotr Ilyitch asked, curious.
"I stole twenty kopecks from my mother when I was nine, and gave it back three days later."
As he said this, Mitya suddenly got to his feet.
"Dmitri Fyodorovitch, aren't you coming now?" Andrey called from the shop door.

"Are you ready? We're coming!" Mitya started. "A few last words and — Andrey, a glass of vodka before we start. Give him some brandy too! That box" (the one with the pistols) "put under my seat. Goodbye, Pyotr Ilyitch, don't think ill of me."
"But you're coming back tomorrow?"
"Of course."
"Will you settle the bill now?" cried the clerk, springing forward.
"Oh, yes, the bill. Of course."

He pulled the bundle of notes back out of his pocket, peeled off three hundred roubles, threw them on the counter, and hurried out of the shop. Everyone followed him out, bowing and wishing him luck. Andrey, coughing from the brandy he'd just downed, jumped up onto the box. But Mitya had barely taken his seat when, to his surprise, he saw Fenya standing before him. She ran up panting, clasped her hands together with a cry, and dropped at his feet.

"Dmitri Fyodorovitch, dear, good Dmitri Fyodorovitch, don't harm my mistress. And it was me who told you all about it.... And don't murder him, he came first, he's hers! He'll marry Agrafena Alexandrovna now. That's why he's come back from Siberia. Dmitri Fyodorovitch, dear, don't take a fellow creature's life!"

"Tut-tut-tut! So that's it, is it! Off there to stir up trouble!" muttered Pyotr Ilyitch. "Now it's all clear, clear as day. Dmitri Fyodorovitch, hand over your pistols this instant if you mean to act like a decent man," he shouted at Mitya. "Do you hear me, Dmitri?"

"The pistols? Wait a bit, brother, I'll toss them in the pond along the road," Mitya answered. "Fenya, get up, don't kneel to me. Mitya won't hurt anyone, the foolish fool won't hurt anyone again. But listen, Fenya," he called out, once he'd taken his seat, "I hurt you just now, so forgive me, take pity on me, forgive a scoundrel.... But it doesn't matter if you don't. Nothing matters now. Now then, Andrey, look alive, fly like the wind!"
Andrey whipped up the horses, and the bells began to ring.
"Goodbye, Pyotr Ilyitch! My last tear is for you!..."

"He's not drunk, but he's babbling like a lunatic," Pyotr Ilyitch thought, watching him go. He half considered staying to see the cart loaded with the rest of the wine and provisions, knowing they'd cheat and shortchange Mitya. But, suddenly annoyed with himself, he turned away with a curse and went off to the tavern to play billiards.

"He's a fool, though he's a good fellow," he muttered as he went. "I've heard about that officer, Grushenka's old flame. Well, if he's turned up.... Ah, those pistols! Damn it all! I'm not his nursemaid! Let them do as they please! Besides, it'll all come to nothing. They're a bunch of brawlers, that's all. They'll drink and fight, fight and make up again. They're not the sort who actually do anything. What does he mean, 'I'm stepping aside, I'm punishing myself'? It'll come to nothing! He's shouted phrases like that a thousand times, drunk, in taverns. But he's not drunk now. 'Drunk in spirit' — they do love their fine phrases, the rascals. Am I his nursemaid? He must have been in a fight, his face was all bloody. With whom? I'll find out at the 'Metropolis.' And his handkerchief was soaked in blood.... It's still lying on my floor.... Damn it all!"

He reached the tavern in a foul mood and at once joined a game. The game cheered him up. He played a second, and suddenly found himself telling one of his partners that Dmitri Karamazov had come into money again — something like three thousand roubles — and had gone off to Mokroe again to spend it with Grushenka.... The news roused strange interest among his listeners. Everyone started talking about it, not laughing, but with a peculiar gravity. They stopped playing.
"Three thousand? Where could he have gotten three thousand?"
Questions flew. The story of Madame Hohlakov's gift was met with skepticism.
"Hasn't he robbed his own father — that's the question."
"Three thousand! There's something odd about it."
"He boasted out loud that he'd kill his father; we all heard him, right here. And it was three thousand he was talking about ..."
Pyotr Ilyitch listened. All at once his answers grew short and clipped. He said not a word about the blood on Mitya's face and hands, though he'd meant to mention it at first.

They started a third game, and gradually the talk about Mitya died down. But by the end of the third game, Pyotr Ilyitch no longer felt like playing billiards; he put down his cue, and, without having supper as he'd planned, walked out of the tavern. When he reached the marketplace he stood still, puzzled at himself. He realized what he wanted was to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch's and find out if anything had happened there. "Over some stupid nonsense — which is surely all it'll turn out to be — am I going to wake up the whole household and cause a scandal? Ugh, damn it, is it my business to look after them?"

In a thoroughly bad mood he headed straight home, and suddenly remembered Fenya. "Damn it all! I should have questioned her just now," he thought, annoyed with himself. "I'd have heard everything." And the urge to talk to her, to find out, became so pressing and insistent that, halfway home, he turned abruptly and headed toward the house where Grushenka lodged. Reaching the gate, he knocked. The sound of the knock in the night's silence sobered him and left him irritated. No one answered; the whole household was asleep.
"And here I am, making a fuss!" he thought, with genuine discomfort. But instead of leaving altogether, he fell to knocking again with all his might, filling the street with noise.
"Not answering? Well, I'll rouse them, I will!" he muttered at each knock, fuming at himself, but redoubling his knocks on the gate all the same.

title: VI. “I Am Coming, Too!”
paragraphs: But Dmitri Fyodorovitch was flying down the road. It was a little more than twenty versts to Mokroe, but Andrey's three horses galloped at such a pace that the distance could be covered in an hour and a quarter. The swift motion revived Mitya. The air was fresh and cool, and big stars shone in the sky. It was the very night, and perhaps the very hour, in which Alyosha had fallen to the earth and sworn, in rapture, to love it forever and ever.

Everything was confusion in Mitya's soul, sheer confusion, and though many things were goading his heart, at that moment his whole being yearned for her, his queen, to whom he was flying to look on for the last time. One thing I can say for certain: his heart never wavered for an instant. I'll perhaps not be believed when I say that this jealous lover felt not the slightest jealousy toward this new rival, who seemed to have sprung out of the earth. Had anyone else appeared on the scene, he'd have been jealous at once, and might well have stained his fierce hands with blood again. But as he flew through the night, he felt no envy, not even hostility, toward the man who had been her first love.... True, he hadn't yet laid eyes on him.

"There's no room for argument here: it's her right, and his; this was her first love, which, after five years, she still hadn't forgotten; so she'd loved only him for those five years, and where do I come into it? What right do I have? Step aside, Mitya, and make way! What am I now? Now everything's over, officer or no officer — even if he'd never shown up, everything would still be over ..."

That, roughly, is what his feelings would have said, had he been capable of reasoning. But he couldn't reason at that moment. His present course of action had arisen without any reasoning at all. At Fenya's first words it had sprung from pure feeling, and been seized on in a flash, consequences and all. And yet, for all his resolve, there was confusion in his soul, an agonizing confusion: his resolution brought him no peace. Too much lay behind him, tormenting him. And it struck him, at moments, as strange that he'd already written his own death sentence in pen and ink — "I punish myself" — and that the paper was sitting there in his pocket, ready; the pistol was loaded; he'd already decided how, come morning, he'd meet the first warm ray of "golden-haired Phoebus."

And yet he couldn't be free of the past, of everything he'd left behind that tormented him. He felt that wretchedly, and the thought of it sank into his heart with despair. There was one moment when he felt the urge to stop Andrey, jump from the cart, pull out his loaded pistol, and put an end to everything without waiting for dawn. But the moment flashed by like a spark. The horses galloped on, "devouring space," and as he drew nearer his goal, the thought of her, of her alone, took hold of his soul more and more completely, chasing off the terrible images that had been haunting him. Oh, how he longed to look at her, if only for a moment, if only from a distance!

"She's with him now," he thought, "now I'll see what she looks like with him, her first love, and that's all I want." Never had this woman, who'd been such a fateful force in his life, stirred such love in his breast — such a new, unfamiliar feeling, surprising even to himself, a feeling tender to the point of devotion, of self-effacement before her! "I'll efface myself!" he said, in a rush of almost hysterical rapture.

They'd been galloping nearly an hour. Mitya was silent, and though Andrey was as a rule a talkative peasant, he too said not a word. He seemed afraid to speak, and only whipped his three lean but spirited bay horses on smartly. Suddenly Mitya cried out in terrible anxiety:
"Andrey! What if they're asleep?"
The thought struck him like a blow. It hadn't occurred to him before.
"It could well be they've gone to bed by now, Dmitri Fyodorovitch."

Mitya frowned as though in pain. Yes, indeed ... here he was, racing there ... with such feelings ... while they slept ... and she, perhaps, was asleep too, right there.... A rush of anger surged in his heart.
"Drive on, Andrey! Whip them up! Look alive!" he cried, beside himself.
"But maybe they're not in bed!" Andrey went on after a pause. "Timofey said there were a lot of them there—"
"At the station?"
"Not the posting station — at Plastunov's, the inn, where they hire out horses too."
"I know it. So you say there are a lot of them? How's that? Who are they?" cried Mitya, badly rattled by this unexpected news.

"Well, Timofey said they're all gentlefolk. Two from our town — who exactly, I couldn't say — and two others, strangers, maybe more besides. I didn't ask closely. They'd sat down to cards, Timofey said."
"Cards?"
"So maybe they're not in bed, if they're at cards. It's most likely not past eleven."
"Faster, Andrey! Faster!" Mitya cried again, nervously.
"May I ask you something, sir?" said Andrey, after a pause. "Only I'm afraid of angering you, sir."
"What is it?"

"Well, Fenya threw herself at your feet just now, begging you not to harm her mistress, and someone else too ... so you see, sir — here I am driving you there ... forgive me, sir, it's my conscience troubling me ... maybe it's foolish of me to say anything—"
Mitya suddenly seized him by the shoulders from behind.
"Are you a driver?" he asked frantically.
"Yes, sir."

"Then you know one has to make way. What would you say to a driver who wouldn't make way for anyone, but just drove on and crushed people? No, a driver mustn't run people down. You can't run a man over. You can't ruin people's lives. And if you have ruined a life — punish yourself.... If you've only spoiled it, only ruined someone's life — punish yourself and go away."
These phrases burst out of Mitya almost hysterically. Though Andrey was startled, he kept up the conversation.

"That's right, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, you're quite right — a man shouldn't be crushed or tormented, nor any creature, for every creature is made by God. Take a horse, for instance — some folks, even among us drivers, drive it any old way. Nothing holds them back, they just force it on."

"Straight to hell?" Mitya broke in, bursting into his short, abrupt laugh. "Andrey, simple soul," he seized him by the shoulders again, "tell me — will Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov go to hell, or not? What do you think?"

"I don't know, my dear fellow, it's up to you, for you are ... you see, sir, when the Son of God was nailed to the Cross and died, He went straight down to hell from the Cross, and set free all the sinners who were in torment there. And the devil groaned, because he thought he'd get no more sinners into hell. And God said to him then, 'Don't groan, for you'll have all the mighty of the earth — the rulers, the chief judges, the rich men — and you'll be filled up as you have been through all the ages, until I come again.' Those were His very words ..."
"A peasant legend! Splendid! Whip up the left one, Andrey!"

"So you see, sir, who hell is for," said Andrey, whipping up the left horse, "but you're like a little child ... that's how we look at you ... and though you're hot-tempered, sir, God will forgive you for your good heart."
"And you, Andrey — do you forgive me?"
"What would I forgive you for, sir? You've never done me any harm."
"No, for everyone, for everyone — you here alone, on this road, will you forgive me for everyone? Speak, simple peasant heart!"
"Oh, sir! I'm afraid to drive you, your talk is so strange."
But Mitya didn't hear him. He was praying frantically, muttering to himself.

"Lord, receive me, with all my lawlessness, and do not condemn me. Let me pass by Thy judgment ... do not condemn me, for I have condemned myself; do not condemn me, for I love Thee, O Lord. I am a wretch, but I love Thee. If Thou sendest me to hell, I'll love Thee there too, and from there I'll cry out that I love Thee forever and ever.... But let me love to the end.... Here and now, for just five hours ... until the first light of Thy day ... for I love the queen of my soul ... I love her and I cannot help loving her. Thou seest my whole heart.... I'll gallop up, I'll fall before her and say, 'You're right to pass on and leave me. Farewell, and forget your victim ... never trouble yourself over me!'"
"Mokroe!" cried Andrey, pointing ahead with his whip.

Through the pale darkness of the night loomed a solid black mass of buildings, flung down, as it were, across the vast plain. The village of Mokroe numbered two thousand souls, but at that hour all were asleep, and only here and there a light still flickered.
"Drive on, Andrey, I'm coming!" Mitya exclaimed feverishly.
"They're not asleep," Andrey said again, pointing with his whip to the Plastunovs' inn, at the entrance to the village. Its six windows facing the street were all brightly lit.
"They're not asleep," Mitya repeated joyfully. "Faster, Andrey! Gallop! Drive up with a dash! Set the bells ringing! Let them all know I've come. I'm coming! I'm coming too!"
Andrey lashed his exhausted team into a gallop, drove up with a flourish, and pulled his steaming, panting horses up short at the top of the steps.
Mitya jumped out of the cart just as the innkeeper, on his way to bed, peered out from the steps, curious who had arrived.
"Trifon Borissovitch, is that you?"
The innkeeper bent forward, peered closely, ran down the steps, and rushed to greet his guest with obsequious delight.
"Dmitri Fyodorovitch, your honor! Do my eyes see you again?"

Trifon Borissovitch was a thick-set, sturdy peasant of middling height, with a rather fleshy face. His expression was stern and unyielding, especially toward the peasants of Mokroe, but he had a gift for putting on the most obsequious face imaginable whenever he sensed it was to his advantage. He dressed in the Russian style, with a shirt buttoning down on one side and a full-skirted coat. He'd saved up a good deal of money, but was forever dreaming of improving his position further. More than half the local peasants were in his clutches; everyone in the district owed him money. From the neighboring landowners he bought and rented land, which the peasants worked off in payment of debts they could never shake free of. He was a widower with four grown daughters. One was already a widow and lived at the inn with her two children — his grandchildren — working for him like a hired charwoman. Another daughter was married to a minor official, and in one of the inn's rooms, among the family photographs on the wall, you could see a little portrait of this official in uniform and official epaulettes. The two younger daughters liked to wear fashionable blue or green dresses, fitted tight at the back with trains a yard long, on church holidays or when paying calls. But the next morning they'd be up at dawn as usual, sweeping the rooms with a birch broom, emptying the slops, and clearing up after the lodgers.

Despite the thousands of roubles he'd saved, Trifon Borissovitch was very fond of emptying a drunken guest's pockets, and, recalling that not a month before he'd made two, if not three, hundred roubles off Dmitri in a single twenty-four hours during his escapade with Grushenka, he now greeted him with eager welcome, scenting his prey the instant Mitya pulled up at the steps.
"Dmitri Fyodorovitch, dear sir, we see you again!"
"Wait, Trifon Borissovitch," Mitya began, "first and foremost — where is she?"
"Agrafena Alexandrovna?" The innkeeper understood at once, peering sharply into Mitya's face. "She's here too ..."
"With whom? With whom?"

"Some strangers. One's an official gentleman, a Pole, judging by his speech. He sent the horses for her from here; and there's another with him, a friend, or maybe a fellow traveler, hard to say. They're dressed like civilians."
"Well, are they feasting? Do they have money?"
"A poor sort of feast! Nothing to boast of, Dmitri Fyodorovitch."
"Nothing to boast of? And who are the others?"

"Two gentlemen from town.... They've come back from Tcherny and are putting up here. One's quite a young gentleman, a relative of Mr. Miüsov's, I believe, but I've forgotten his name ... and I expect you know the other one too, a gentleman called Maximov. He's been on a pilgrimage, so he says, to the monastery in town. He's traveling with that young relation of Mr. Miüsov's."
"Is that all?"
"Yes."
"Wait, listen, Trifon Borissovitch. Tell me the main thing: what about her? How is she?"
"Oh, she's only just arrived. She's sitting with them."
"Is she cheerful? Is she laughing?"
"No, I don't think she's laughing much. She's sitting there quite dull. She's combing the young gentleman's hair."
"The Pole — the officer?"
"He's not young, and he's no officer either. Not him, sir. It's the young gentleman, Mr. Miüsov's relation ... I've forgotten his name."
"Kalganov."
"That's it, Kalganov!"
"All right. I'll see for myself. Are they playing cards?"
"They were playing, but they've stopped. They've been drinking tea; the official gentleman asked for liqueurs."
"Wait, Trifon Borissovitch, wait, my good man, I'll see for myself. Now answer one more question: are the gypsies here?"

"You can't have the gypsies now, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. The authorities sent them packing. But we've got Jews here in the village who play the cymbals and the fiddle, so we could send for them. They'd come."
"Send for them. Certainly, send for them!" cried Mitya. "And you can round up the girls the way you did before — Marya especially, and Stepanida too, and Arina. Two hundred roubles for a chorus!"

"Oh, for a sum like that I could gather the whole village, though by now they're asleep. Are the peasants worth such generosity, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, or the girls either? To spend a sum like that on such coarse, rude folk! What's the good of giving a peasant a cigar to smoke, the stinking rascal! And the girls are all lousy. Besides, I'll get my own daughters up for nothing, let alone a sum like that. They've only just gone to bed — I'll give them a kick and set them singing for you. You had the peasants drinking champagne the other day, e-ech!"

For all his pretended pity for Mitya, Trifon Borissovitch had squirreled away half a dozen bottles of champagne on that last occasion, and had picked up a hundred-rouble note off the floor, which had stayed firmly in his grip.
"Trifon Borissovitch, I sent more than a thousand roubles flying last time I was here. Remember?"
"You did send it flying. I remember well enough. You must have left three thousand behind you."
"Well, I've come to do the same again, do you see?"
And he pulled out his roll of notes and held it up in front of the innkeeper's nose.

"Now, listen and remember. In an hour the wine will arrive, savories, pies, and sweets — bring it all up at once. That box Andrey's got is to be brought up right away too. Open it and hand out the champagne immediately. And the girls — we must have the girls, Marya especially."
He turned to the cart and pulled out the pistol case.
"Here, Andrey, let's settle up. Here's fifteen roubles for the drive, and fifty for vodka ... for your readiness, for your kindness.... Remember Karamazov!"
"I'm afraid to take it, sir," Andrey faltered. "Give me five extra, but no more than that, I won't take it. Trifon Borissovitch, bear witness. Forgive my foolish talk ..."

"What are you afraid of?" asked Mitya, looking him over. "Well, go to the devil, then, if that's how it is!" he cried, flinging him five roubles. "Now, Trifon Borissovitch, take me up quietly and let me get a look at them first, so they don't see me. Where are they? In the blue room?"

Trifon Borissovitch glanced at Mitya apprehensively, but obeyed at once. Leading him through the passage, he went ahead into the first large room, adjoining the one where the visitors were sitting, and took the light away with him. Then he crept Mitya in and stationed him in a dark corner, from where he could watch the company freely without being seen himself. But Mitya didn't look long, and in fact couldn't really see them — he saw only her; his heart pounded violently, and everything went dark before his eyes.

She was sitting sideways to the table, in a low chair, and beside her, on the sofa, was the handsome young Kalganov. She was holding his hand and seemed to be laughing, while he, looking vexed and not looking at her, was saying something loudly to Maximov, who sat on the other side of the table, facing Grushenka. Maximov was laughing violently at something. On the sofa sat the man himself, and on a chair beside the sofa sat another stranger. The one on the sofa was lolling back, smoking a pipe, and Mitya had the impression of a stoutish, broad-faced, short little man, apparently annoyed about something. His companion, the other stranger, struck Mitya as extraordinarily tall, but he couldn't make out anything more. He caught his breath. He couldn't bear it another minute; he set the pistol case down on a chest, and, heart pounding, feeling cold all over, walked straight into the blue room to face them all.
"Aie!" Grushenka shrieked, the first to notice him.

title: VII. The First And Rightful Lover
paragraphs: With his long, quick strides, Mitya walked straight up to the table.

"Gentlemen," he said, in a loud voice, almost shouting, yet stammering at every word, "I ... I'm all right! Don't be afraid!" he exclaimed. "I — there's nothing wrong," he said, turning suddenly to Grushenka, who had shrunk back in her chair toward Kalganov and gripped his hand tight. "I ... I'm coming too. I'm here till morning. Gentlemen, may I stay with you till morning? Just till morning, for the last time, in this same room?"
That's how he finished, turning to the fat little man with the pipe, seated on the sofa. The man removed his pipe from his lips with dignity and observed severely:
"Panie, this is a private gathering. There are other rooms."
"Why, it's you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch! What do you mean by this?" Kalganov answered suddenly. "Sit down with us. How are you?"
"Delighted to see you, my dear ... precious fellow, I've always thought highly of you," Mitya responded, joyfully and eagerly, at once reaching his hand across the table.
"Aie! What a grip! You've nearly broken my fingers," laughed Kalganov.

"He always squeezes like that, always," Grushenka put in cheerfully, with a timid smile, seeming suddenly convinced from Mitya's face that he wasn't going to make a scene. She was watching him with intense curiosity and still some unease. Something about him struck her, and indeed the last thing she'd expected was for him to walk in and speak like this, at a moment like this.
"Good evening," Maximov ventured mildly, on the left. Mitya rushed over to him too.

"Good evening. You're here too! How glad I am to find you here as well! Gentlemen, gentlemen, I—" (he addressed the Polish gentleman with the pipe again, clearly taking him for the most important person present) "—I flew here.... I wanted to spend my last day, my last hour, in this room, this very room ... where I too once worshipped ... my queen.... Forgive me, panie," he cried wildly, "I flew here and swore an oath — Oh, don't be afraid, it's my last night! Let's drink to our good understanding. They'll bring the wine directly.... I brought this with me." (Something made him pull out his bundle of notes.) "Allow me, panie! I want music, singing, a proper revel, like we had before. But the worm, the unneeded worm, will crawl off, and there'll be no more of him. I'll mark my day of joy on my last night."

He was nearly choking. There was so much, so much he wanted to say, but only strange exclamations made it out of his mouth. The Pole stared fixedly at him, at the bundle of notes in his hand, glanced at Grushenka, and was plainly puzzled.
"If my sovereign lady will permit—" he began.

"What does 'sovereign' mean? I suppose it means 'sovereign'?" Grushenka broke in. "I can't help laughing at you, the way you talk. Sit down, Mitya, what are you going on about? Don't frighten us, please. You won't frighten us, will you? If you won't, I'm glad to see you ..."
"Me, frighten you?" cried Mitya, flinging up his hands. "Oh, pass me by, go your way, I won't stand in it!..."

And suddenly he surprised everyone, and no doubt himself as well, by dropping into a chair and bursting into tears, turning his head away toward the far wall, his arms clasped tight around the chair back as though embracing it.

"Now, now, what a fellow you are!" Grushenka cried, reproachfully. "That's exactly how he comes to see me — he starts talking, and I can't make out a word of it. He cried like that once before, and now he's crying again! It's shameful! Why are you crying? As if you had anything to cry about!" she added, cryptically, stressing each word with a touch of irritation.
"I ... I'm not crying.... Well, good evening!" He spun round in his chair at once, and suddenly laughed — not his abrupt, wooden laugh, but a long, quivering, near-silent, nervous laugh.

"Well, there you go again.... Come, cheer up, cheer up!" Grushenka coaxed him. "I'm very glad you've come, very glad, Mitya, do you hear — very glad! I want him to stay here with us," she said, peremptorily, addressing the whole company, though her words were plainly meant for the man on the sofa. "I want it, I want it! And if he goes, I go too!" she added, her eyes flashing.
"Whatever my queen commands is law!" the Pole pronounced, gallantly kissing Grushenka's hand. "I invite you, panie, to join our company," he added politely, to Mitya.
Mitya was on his feet, clearly meaning to launch into another speech, but the words wouldn't come.
"Let's drink, panie," he blurted instead of making a speech. Everyone laughed.

"Good heavens! I thought he was about to start up again!" Grushenka exclaimed, nervously. "Do you hear, Mitya," she went on, insistently, "don't go prancing about, but it's nice you brought the champagne. I want some myself, I can't stand liqueurs. And best of all, you've come yourself. We were terribly bored here.... You've come for another spree, I suppose? But put your money away. Where did you get so much?"

All this while Mitya had been holding the crumpled bundle of notes in his hand, and every eye in the room, especially the Poles', was fixed on it. Embarrassed, he shoved it hastily into his pocket. He flushed. At that moment the innkeeper brought in an uncorked bottle of champagne and glasses on a tray. Mitya grabbed the bottle, but was so flustered he had no idea what to do with it. Kalganov took it from him and poured the champagne.

"Another! Another bottle!" Mitya called to the innkeeper, and, forgetting to clink glasses with the Pole he'd so solemnly invited to drink to their good understanding, drank off his glass without waiting for anyone else. His whole face suddenly changed. The solemn, tragic look he'd walked in with vanished completely, replaced by something childlike. He seemed to have turned gentle and subdued all at once. He looked around at everyone shyly and happily, with a constant nervous little laugh, wearing the blissful look of a dog who's misbehaved, been punished, and been forgiven. He seemed to have forgotten everything, gazing round at everyone with a childlike, delighted smile. He looked at Grushenka, laughing continually, and pulled his chair close to hers. By degrees he formed some impression of the two Poles, though nothing definite yet.

The Pole on the sofa struck him with his dignified manner and his Polish accent, and above all with his pipe. "Well, what of it? It's good that he smokes a pipe," he mused. The Pole's puffy, middle-aged face, with its tiny nose and two very thin, pointed, dyed, insolent-looking mustaches, hadn't yet raised the faintest doubt in Mitya's mind. He wasn't even particularly struck by the Pole's absurd Siberian-made wig, with its foolish little curls combed forward at the temples. "I suppose it's all fine, since he wears a wig," he went on, musing blissfully. The other, younger Pole, staring insolently and defiantly at the company and listening to the conversation with silent contempt, impressed Mitya only by his great height, so strikingly different from the Pole on the sofa. "If he stood up, he'd be six foot three." The thought flitted through Mitya's mind. It occurred to him too that this Pole must be the other one's friend, a kind of "bodyguard," and no doubt the big Pole was at the disposal of the little one with the pipe. But all this seemed to Mitya perfectly natural and not worth questioning. In his dog-like mood of submission, every trace of rivalry had died away.

Grushenka's mood, and the cryptic tone of some of her remarks, he utterly failed to grasp. All he understood, with a thrill in his heart, was that she was being kind to him, that she'd forgiven him, and had made him sit beside her. He was beside himself with delight, watching her sip her glass of champagne. The silence of the company seemed to strike him somehow, though, and he glanced round at everyone with expectant eyes.
"Why are we just sitting here, gentlemen? Why don't we get on with something?" his smiling eyes seemed to ask.
"He keeps talking nonsense, and we were all laughing," Kalganov said suddenly, as though reading his mind, pointing at Maximov.
Mitya at once stared at Kalganov, and then at Maximov.
"He's talking nonsense?" he laughed, his short, wooden laugh, seeming suddenly delighted at something — "ha ha!"
"Yes. Would you believe it, he insists that in the eighteen-twenties all our cavalry officers married Polish women. That's absolute rot, isn't it?"
"Polish women?" Mitya repeated, in perfect ecstasy.

Kalganov was well aware of Mitya's feelings for Grushenka, and had guessed about the Pole too, but that interested him only slightly, perhaps not at all; what interested him was Maximov. He'd come here with Maximov by chance, and had met the Poles at the inn for the first time in his life just now. He'd known Grushenka before, and had once called on her with someone; but she hadn't taken to him. Yet tonight she looked at him very warmly: before Mitya's arrival she'd been making much of him, though he seemed somehow unmoved by it. He was a boy, not yet twenty, dressed like a dandy, with a charming, fair-skinned face and splendid thick fair hair. From that fair face looked out beautiful pale blue eyes, with an intelligent, sometimes even deep expression, well beyond his years — though the young man sometimes looked and talked quite like a child, and wasn't at all ashamed of it, even when he noticed it himself. As a rule he was very willful, even capricious, though always friendly. Sometimes there was something fixed, obstinate, in his expression. He'd look at you and listen, seeming all the while to be lost in some private daydream. Often he was listless and lazy; at other times he'd grow excited, sometimes, it seemed, over the most trivial things.

"Just imagine, I've been dragging him around with me for the last four days," he went on, drawling his words lazily, though quite naturally, without the slightest affectation. "Ever since your brother — remember? — shoved him off the carriage and sent him flying. That's what got me interested in him at the time, and I took him out to the country, but he keeps talking such rot I'm ashamed to be seen with him. I'm taking him back."
"The gentleman has never seen Polish ladies, and says what's impossible," the Pole with the pipe observed to Maximov.
He spoke Russian fairly well, at any rate far better than he let on. Whenever he used a Russian word, he always twisted it into a Polish shape.
"But I was married to a Polish lady myself," Maximov tittered.
"But did you serve in the cavalry? You were talking about the cavalry. Were you a cavalry officer?" Kalganov put in at once.
"Was he a cavalry officer, indeed! Ha ha!" cried Mitya, listening eagerly, turning his inquiring eyes from one to another as though there were no telling what he might hear from each.

"No, you see," Maximov turned to him. "What I mean is, those pretty Polish ladies ... when they danced the mazurka with our Uhlans ... when one of them dances a mazurka with a Uhlan, she jumps onto his knee like a kitten ... a little white one ... and the pan-father and pan-mother look on and allow it.... They allow it ... and the next day the Uhlan comes and offers her his hand.... That's how it is ... offers her his hand, he he!" Maximov finished, tittering.

"The pan is a lajdak!" the tall Pole on the chair suddenly growled, crossing one leg over the other. Mitya's eye caught his huge, greased boot with its thick, dirty sole. Both Poles' clothing looked rather greasy.
"Now it's 'lajdak'! What's he scolding about?" said Grushenka, suddenly vexed.
"Pani Agrippina, what the gentleman saw in Poland were servant girls, not ladies of good family," the Pole with the pipe observed to Grushenka.
"You may depend on that," the tall Pole snapped, contemptuously.
"What next! Let him talk! People talk — why stop them? It makes things livelier," Grushenka said, crossly.
"I'm not stopping anyone, pani," said the Pole in the wig, with a long look at Grushenka, and, lapsing back into dignified silence, sucked at his pipe again.

"No, no. The Polish gentleman is telling the truth." Kalganov grew excited again, as though it were a matter of vast importance. "He's never been to Poland, so how can he talk about it? You weren't married in Poland, were you?"

"No, in the province of Smolensk. Only, a Uhlan had brought her to Russia before that — my future wife — along with her mother, her aunt, and another female relation with a grown son. He brought her straight from Poland and handed her over to me. He was a lieutenant in our regiment, a very nice young man. At first he meant to marry her himself. But he didn't, because it turned out she was lame."
"So you married a lame woman?" cried Kalganov.
"Yes. They both deceived me a little at the time, and hid it from me. I thought she was hopping; she kept hopping.... I thought it was for fun."
"So pleased she was, to be marrying you!" Kalganov shrieked, in a ringing, childish voice.

"Yes, so pleased. But it turned out to be for quite a different reason. Later, once we were married, that very evening after the wedding, she confessed, and very touchingly asked my forgiveness. 'I jumped over a puddle once, as a child,' she said, 'and hurt my leg.' He he!"
Kalganov burst into the most childish laughter, nearly falling onto the sofa. Grushenka laughed too. Mitya was at the height of happiness.

"You know, that's actually true — he's not lying this time," Kalganov exclaimed, turning to Mitya. "And you know, he's been married twice — that's his first wife he's talking about. But his second wife, you know, ran off, and she's still alive."
"Is that possible?" said Mitya, turning quickly to Maximov with an expression of utter astonishment.

"Yes. She ran off, all right. I've had that unpleasant experience," Maximov admitted modestly, "with a monsieur. And worse still, she'd had all my little property signed over to her beforehand. 'You're an educated man,' she told me. 'You can always earn a living.' That's how she settled the matter. A venerable bishop once told me: 'One of your wives was lame, but the other was too light on her feet.' He he!"

"Listen, listen!" cried Kalganov, bubbling over. "If he's lying — and he often is — he's only doing it to entertain us all. There's no harm in that, is there? You know, I actually like him sometimes. He's awfully low, but it's natural to him, isn't it? Don't you think so? Some people are low out of self-interest, but he's simply low by nature. Just imagine, he claims — he was arguing about it the whole way yesterday — that Gogol wrote Dead Souls about him. You remember, there's a landowner named Maximov in it, whom Nozdryov thrashes. He was charged, remember, 'with inflicting bodily injury by rods on the landowner Maximov while in a state of intoxication.' Would you believe it, he claims he was that Maximov, and that he was the one beaten! Now, can that be so? Tchitchikov made his journey, at the very latest, in the early eighteen-twenties, so the dates don't add up. He couldn't have been beaten then — could he?"
