It was hard to say what exactly had Kalganov so worked up, but his excitement was genuine. Mitya followed his lead without objection.
"Well, but what if they did thrash him!" he cried, laughing.
"It's not exactly that they thrashed me, but what I mean is—" Maximov put in.
"What do you mean? Either they thrashed you or they didn't."
"What time is it, panie?" the Pole with the pipe asked his tall friend, with a bored air. The other shrugged in reply. Neither of them owned a watch.

"Why shouldn't he talk? Let other people talk. Must other people go quiet just because you're bored?" Grushenka flew at him, plainly out to pick a fight. For the first time something seemed to flash across Mitya's mind. This time the Pole answered with unmistakable irritation.
"Pani, I raised no objection. I said nothing."
"All right, then. Come, tell us your story," Grushenka called to Maximov. "Why's everyone gone silent?"

"There's nothing to tell, it's all so foolish," Maximov answered at once, with evident satisfaction, mincing a little. "Besides, it's all allegory in Gogol, since he gave every name a hidden meaning. Nozdryov's real name was Nosov, and Kuvshinikov had an entirely different name — he was called Shkvornev. Fenardi really was called Fenardi, only he wasn't Italian, he was Russian, and Mamzelle Fenardi was a pretty girl with pretty little legs in tights, and a little short skirt with spangles, and she'd spin round and round, only not for four hours, just four minutes, and she bewitched everyone..."
"But what were you beaten for?" cried Kalganov.
"For Piron!" Maximov answered.
"What Piron?" cried Mitya.

"The famous French writer, Piron. We were all drinking then, a big party of us, at a tavern at that very fair. They'd invited me, and I started off by quoting epigrams. 'Is that you, Boileau? What a ridiculous get-up!' And Boileau answers that he's off to a masquerade — that is, to the baths, he he! And they took it as aimed at them, so I hurried to recite another, a very biting one, known to every educated person:
Yes, Sappho and Phaon are we! But one grief weighs upon me. You don't know your way to the sea!

They took even more offense, and began abusing me in the most unseemly way for it. And, wouldn't you know it, trying to set things right, I launched into a very refined anecdote about Piron — how he wasn't accepted into the French Academy, and, to get his revenge, wrote his own epitaph:
Ci-gît Piron qui ne fut rien, Pas même académicien.
They grabbed me and thrashed me."
"But what for? What for?"
"For my education. People can thrash a man for anything," Maximov concluded, briefly and sententiously.
"Eh, that's enough! It's all stupid, I don't want to hear it. I thought it would be amusing," Grushenka cut them off, suddenly.

Mitya started, and at once stopped laughing. The tall Pole rose to his feet and, with the haughty air of a man bored and out of his element, began pacing from corner to corner of the room, his hands behind his back.
"Ah, he can't sit still," said Grushenka, eyeing him with contempt. Mitya began to feel uneasy. He noticed, besides, that the Pole on the sofa was watching him with an irritated expression.
"Panie!" cried Mitya, "let's drink! And the other pan too! Let's drink."
In a flash he'd pulled three glasses toward him and filled them with champagne.
"To Poland, panovie, I drink to your Poland!" cried Mitya.
"I shall be delighted, panie," said the Pole on the sofa, with dignity and gracious condescension, and took his glass.
"And the other pan, what's his name? Drink, most illustrious, take your glass!" Mitya urged.
"Pan Vrublevsky," the Pole on the sofa supplied.
Pan Vrublevsky came up to the table, swaying as he walked.
"To Poland, panovie!" cried Mitya, raising his glass. "Hurrah!"
All three drank. Mitya seized the bottle and poured three more glasses.
"Now to Russia, panovie, and let's be brothers!"
"Pour some for us," said Grushenka. "I'll drink to Russia too!"
"So will I," said Kalganov.
"And I would too ... to Russia, the old grandmother!" Maximov tittered.
"All of you! All of you!" cried Mitya. "Trifon Borissovitch, more bottles!"
The other three bottles Mitya had brought were set on the table. Mitya filled the glasses.
"To Russia! Hurrah!" he shouted again. Everyone drank the toast except the Poles, and Grushenka drained her whole glass at once. The Poles didn't touch theirs.
"How's this, panovie?" cried Mitya. "Won't you drink it?"
Pan Vrublevsky took his glass, raised it, and said in a resonant voice:
"To Russia, as she was before 1772."
"There, that's better!" cried the other Pole, and both drained their glasses at once.
"You're fools, you panovie," burst out of Mitya suddenly.
"Panie!" both Poles shouted menacingly, squaring up at Mitya like a pair of fighting cocks. Pan Vrublevsky was especially furious.
"Can a man help loving his own country?" he shouted.

"Quiet! No quarreling! I won't have any quarreling!" Grushenka cried imperiously, stamping her foot on the floor. Her face glowed, her eyes shone. The effects of the glass she'd just drunk were plain to see. Mitya was terribly alarmed.
"Panovie, forgive me! It was my fault, I'm sorry. Vrublevsky, panie Vrublevsky, I'm sorry."
"Hold your tongue, you, at least! Sit down, you fool!" Grushenka scolded, in angry annoyance.
Everyone sat down. All fell silent, looking at one another.
"Gentlemen, it was all my fault," Mitya began again, unable to make sense of Grushenka's words. "Come, why are we just sitting here? What shall we do ... to amuse ourselves again?"
"Ach, it's certainly anything but amusing!" Kalganov mumbled lazily.
"Let's play faro again, like we were doing before," Maximov suddenly tittered.
"Faro? Splendid!" cried Mitya. "If only the panovie—"
"It's lite, panovie," the Pole on the sofa responded, as if reluctantly.
"That's true," Pan Vrublevsky agreed.
"Lite? What do you mean, 'lite'?" asked Grushenka.
"Late, pani! I mean, 'a late hour,'" the Pole on the sofa explained.

"It's always late with them. They can never manage anything!" Grushenka nearly shrieked in her anger. "They're bored themselves, so they want everyone else bored too. Before you came, Mitya, they were sitting just as silent, turning up their noses at me."
"My goddess!" cried the Pole on the sofa. "I see you're not well-disposed toward me — that's why I'm gloomy. I'm ready, panie," he added, addressing Mitya.
"Begin, panie," Mitya agreed, pulling his notes from his pocket and laying two hundred-rouble notes on the table. "I want to lose a lot to you. Take the cards. Bank it."
"We'll get cards from the landlord, panie," said the little Pole, gravely and firmly.
"That's much the best way," Pan Vrublevsky chimed in.
"From the landlord? Very good, I understand, let's get them from him. Cards!" Mitya shouted at the landlord.

The landlord brought in a new, unopened pack, and informed Mitya that the girls were getting ready, and that the Jews with the cymbals would very likely be along soon, but the cart with the provisions hadn't arrived yet. Mitya jumped up from the table and ran into the next room to give orders, but only three girls had arrived so far, and Marya wasn't among them yet. He didn't quite know himself what orders to give, or why he'd run out at all. He only told them to take the presents for the girls out of the box — the sweets, the toffee, the fondants. "And vodka for Andrey, vodka for Andrey!" he cried hurriedly. "I was rude to Andrey!"
Suddenly Maximov, who'd followed him out, touched him on the shoulder.
"Give me five roubles," he whispered to Mitya. "I'll stake something at faro too, he he!"
"Splendid! Capital! Take ten, here!"
Again he pulled all the notes out of his pocket and picked out a ten-rouble one. "And if you lose that, come back, come back again."

"Very good," Maximov whispered joyfully, and ran back inside. Mitya returned too, apologizing for keeping them waiting. The Poles had already sat down and opened the pack. They looked much more amiable now, almost cordial. The Pole on the sofa had lit another pipe and was preparing to deal. He wore an air of solemnity.
"To your places, gentlemen," cried Pan Vrublevsky.
"No, I'm not playing anymore," Kalganov remarked. "I've already lost fifty roubles to them just now."
"The pan had no luck — perhaps he'll be lucky this time," the Pole on the sofa observed, in his direction.
"How much in the bank? To match?" asked Mitya.
"That depends, panie — maybe a hundred, maybe two hundred, as much as you care to stake."
"A million!" laughed Mitya.
"Has the Pan Captain perhaps heard of Pan Podvysotsky?"
"What Podvysotsky?"

"In Warsaw there was a bank, and anyone could come stake against it. Podvysotsky comes, sees a thousand gold pieces, stakes against the bank. The banker says, 'Panie Podvysotsky, are you laying down the gold, or must we trust to your honor?' 'To my honor, panie,' says Podvysotsky. 'So much the better.' The banker throws the dice. Podvysotsky wins. 'Take it, panie,' says the banker, and, pulling out the drawer, hands him a million. 'Take it, panie, it's your winnings.' There was a million in the bank. 'I didn't know that,' says Podvysotsky. 'Panie Podvysotsky,' says the banker, 'you pledged your honor, and we pledged ours.' Podvysotsky took the million."
"That's not true," said Kalganov.
"Panie Kalganov, in gentlemanly company one doesn't say such things."

"As if a Polish gambler would ever give away a million!" cried Mitya, but checked himself at once. "Forgive me, panie, my fault again — he would, he would give away a million, for honor, for Polish honor. See how I speak Polish, ha ha! Here, I stake ten roubles, the jack leads."

"And I'll put a rouble on the queen, the queen of hearts, the pretty little panienotchka, he he!" laughed Maximov, drawing out his queen, and, as though trying to hide it from everyone, leaned in close and hurriedly crossed himself under the table. Mitya won. The rouble won too.
"A corner!" cried Mitya.
"I'll bet another rouble, a 'single' stake," Maximov muttered gleefully, thoroughly delighted at having won a rouble.
"Lost!" shouted Mitya. "A 'double' on the seven!"
The seven was trumped too.
"Stop!" Kalganov cried suddenly.
"Double! Double!" Mitya doubled his stakes, and every time he doubled, the Poles trumped the card he'd doubled. The rouble stakes kept winning.
"On the double!" Mitya shouted furiously.
"You've lost two hundred, panie. Will you stake another hundred?" the Pole on the sofa asked.
"What? Lost two hundred already? Then another two hundred! All doubles!"
And pulling his money out of his pocket, Mitya was about to throw two hundred roubles on the queen, but Kalganov covered it with his hand.
"That's enough!" he shouted, in his ringing voice.
"What's the matter?" Mitya stared at him.
"That's enough! I don't want you playing anymore. Don't!"
"Why not?"
"Because I don't want you to. Hang it, come away. That's why. I won't let you keep playing."
Mitya gazed at him in astonishment.
"Give it up, Mitya. He may be right. You've lost a lot as it is," said Grushenka, with a strange note in her voice. Both Poles rose from their seats, looking deeply offended.
"Are you joking, panie?" said the short one, staring severely at Kalganov.
"How dare you!" Pan Vrublevsky growled at Kalganov too.
"Don't you dare shout like that," cried Grushenka. "Ah, you turkey-cocks!"
Mitya looked at each of them in turn. But something in Grushenka's face suddenly struck him, and in that same instant something new flashed into his mind — a strange, new thought!
"Pani Agrippina," the little Pole was beginning, crimson with anger, when Mitya suddenly walked up to him and slapped him on the shoulder.
"Most illustrious, a word with you."
"What do you want?"
"In the next room — I have two words to say to you, something pleasant, very pleasant. You'll be glad to hear it."
The little pan was taken aback, and eyed Mitya apprehensively. He agreed at once, all the same, on condition that Pan Vrublevsky came along too.
"The bodyguard? Let him come — I want him along too. I need him!" cried Mitya. "March, panovie!"
"Where are you going?" Grushenka asked anxiously.
"We'll be back in a moment," Mitya answered.
There was a kind of boldness, a sudden confidence, shining in his eyes now. His face had looked very different an hour before, when he'd first walked into the room.

He led the Poles not into the large room where the girls' chorus was gathering and the table was being laid, but into the bedroom on the right, where the trunks and bundles were kept, with two large beds and pyramids of cotton pillows on each. A lit candle stood on a small deal table in the corner. The little man and Mitya sat down at this table, facing each other, while the huge Vrublevsky stood beside them, hands behind his back. The Poles looked severe but were plainly curious.
"What can I do for you, panie?" the little Pole lisped.
"Well, look here, panie, I won't keep you long. There's money here for you," he pulled out his notes. "Would you like three thousand? Take it and be on your way."
The Pole stared wide-eyed at Mitya, searchingly.
"Three thousand, panie?" He exchanged glances with Vrublevsky.

"Three, panovie, three! Listen, panie, I can see you're a sensible man. Take three thousand and go to the devil, and Vrublevsky with you — d'you hear? But at once, this very minute, and forever. You understand me, panie — forever. There's the door, you go through it. What have you got there, a greatcoat, a fur coat? I'll bring it out to you. They'll have the horses out directly, and then — goodbye, panie!"
Mitya waited for an answer with confidence. He had no doubts. A look of extraordinary resolve crossed the Pole's face.
"And the money, panie?"

"The money, panie? Five hundred roubles I'll give you this instant, for the journey and as a first installment, and two thousand five hundred tomorrow, in town — I swear on my honor, I'll get it, I'll get it whatever it costs!" cried Mitya.
The Poles exchanged glances again. The short man's face darkened further.

"Seven hundred, seven hundred, not five hundred, right now, this minute, cash in hand!" Mitya added, sensing something was wrong. "What's the matter, panie? Don't you trust me? I can't hand over the full three thousand straight off. If I did, you might just come back to her tomorrow.... Besides, I don't have the three thousand on me. It's at home, in town," Mitya faltered, his spirits sinking with every word. "On my word, the money's there, hidden away."
Instantly, an extraordinary air of personal dignity came over the little man's face.
"What next?" he asked, ironically. "For shame!" And he spat on the floor. Pan Vrublevsky spat too.
"You do that, panie," said Mitya, realizing with despair that it was all over, "because you're hoping to squeeze more out of Grushenka? A pair of capons, that's what you are!"

"This is a mortal insult!" The little Pole flushed crab-red, and strode out of the room, briskly, as if unwilling to hear another word. Vrublevsky swung out after him, and Mitya followed, embarrassed and crestfallen. He was afraid of Grushenka, afraid the pan would immediately raise an outcry. And that's exactly what he did. The Pole walked into the room and flung himself before Grushenka in a theatrical pose.
"Pani Agrippina, I have received a mortal insult!" he exclaimed. But Grushenka suddenly lost all patience, as though they'd wounded her in the most tender spot.
"Speak Russian! Speak Russian!" she cried. "Not another word of Polish! You used to speak Russian. You can't have forgotten it in five years."
She was red with fury.
"Pani Agrippina—"
"My name's Agrafena, Grushenka — speak Russian, or I won't listen!"
The Pole gasped with offended dignity, and delivered himself, quickly and pompously, in broken Russian:
"Pani Agrafena, I came here to forget the past and forgive it, to forget everything that's happened up till today—"
"Forgive? Came here to forgive me?" Grushenka cut him off, jumping up from her seat.
"Just so, pani, I'm no coward, I'm magnanimous. But I was astounded when I saw your lovers. Pan Mitya offered me three thousand, in the other room, to leave. I spat in the pan's face."
"What? He offered you money for me?" cried Grushenka, hysterically. "Is that true, Mitya? How dare you? Am I for sale?"
"Panie, panie!" Mitya shouted, "she's pure and radiant, and I've never been her lover! That's a lie...."

"How dare you defend me to him?" Grushenka shrieked. "It wasn't virtue that kept me pure, and it wasn't that I was afraid of Kuzma — it was so that I could hold my head up when I met him and tell him he's a scoundrel. And did he really turn down the money?"
"He took it! He took it!" cried Mitya. "Only he wanted the full three thousand at once, and I could only give him seven hundred outright."
"I see — he heard I had money, and came here to marry me!"
"Pani Agrippina!" cried the little Pole. "I'm — a knight, I'm — a nobleman, not a lajdak. I came here to make you my wife, and I find you a different woman — perverse and shameless."

"Oh, go back where you came from! I'll have them throw you out, and out you'll go," cried Grushenka, furiously. "I've been a fool, a fool, to have made myself miserable these five years! And it wasn't for his sake — it was my own anger that made me miserable. And this isn't even him at all! Was he like this? He could be his own father! Where did you get that wig? He was a falcon, and this is a gander. He used to laugh and sing to me.... And I've been crying for five years — a damned fool, abject, shameless I was!"
She sank back into her low chair and buried her face in her hands. At that instant the Mokroe chorus struck up in the room to the left — a rollicking dance song.
"A regular Sodom!" Vrublevsky suddenly roared. "Landlord, send the shameless hussies away!"
The landlord, who'd been peeping curiously in at the door for some time, hearing the shouting and guessing his guests were quarreling, stepped in at once.
"What are you shouting for? Trying to split your throat?" he said to Vrublevsky, with startling rudeness.
"Animal!" bellowed Pan Vrublevsky.

"Animal, is it? And what sort of cards were you playing with just now? I gave you a fresh pack and you hid it. You were playing with marked cards! I could send you to Siberia for playing with false cards, d'you know that — it's the same as forging banknotes...."
And going up to the sofa, he thrust his fingers between the sofa back and the cushion, and pulled out an unopened pack of cards.
"Here's my pack, still unopened!"
He held it up for the whole room to see. "From where I was standing I saw him slip my pack away and put his own in its place — you're a cheat, not a gentleman!"
"And I saw the pan switch a card, twice!" cried Kalganov.
"How shameful! How shameful!" Grushenka exclaimed, clasping her hands, blushing with genuine shame. "Good Lord, has he come to this?"
"I thought as much myself!" said Mitya. But before he'd finished saying it, Vrublevsky, his face confused and furious, shook his fist at Grushenka, shouting:
"You low harlot!"
Mitya flew at him at once, seized him with both hands, lifted him bodily into the air, and in an instant had carried him into the room on the right, the one they'd just come from.
"I've laid him out on the floor in there," he announced, coming back at once, gasping with excitement. "He's struggling, the scoundrel! But he won't be coming back, no fear of that!..."
He closed one half of the folding doors, and, holding the other ajar, called out to the little Pole:
"Most illustrious, will you kindly withdraw as well?"
"My dear Dmitri Fyodorovitch," said Trifon Borissovitch, "make them give you back what you lost. It's as good as stolen from you."
"I don't want my fifty roubles back," Kalganov declared suddenly.
"I don't want my two hundred either," cried Mitya, "I wouldn't take it for anything! Let him keep it as a consolation."
"Bravo, Mitya! You're a trump, Mitya!" cried Grushenka, and there was a note of fierce anger in the exclamation.
The little pan, crimson with rage but still mindful of his dignity, was heading for the door, but stopped short and turned suddenly to Grushenka:
"Pani, if you want to come with me, come. If not, farewell."

And swelling with indignation and self-importance, he went to the door. Here was a man of real character: he thought so well of himself that even after all that had happened, he still expected she would marry him. Mitya slammed the door behind him.
"Lock it," said Kalganov. But the key clicked from the other side — they'd already locked it from within.
"That's perfect!" Grushenka exclaimed, without mercy. "Serves them right!"

title: VIII. Delirium
paragraphs: What followed was almost an orgy, a feast open to all comers. Grushenka was the first to call for wine.
"I want to drink. I want to get thoroughly drunk, like we did before. Remember, Mitya, remember how we made friends here last time!"
Mitya himself was nearly delirious, feeling his happiness within reach. But Grushenka kept sending him away from her.

"Go and enjoy yourself. Tell them to dance, to make merry — 'let the stove and the cottage dance,' like we had it last time," she kept exclaiming. She was tremendously excited. And Mitya hurried to obey. The chorus was in the next room. The room they'd been sitting in until now was too small, and was split in two by cotton curtains, behind which stood a huge bed with a puffy feather mattress and a pyramid of cotton pillows. All four guest rooms had beds. Grushenka settled herself right by the door. Mitya set an easy chair out for her. She'd sat in that same spot to watch the dancing and singing "the time before," when they'd made merry there. All the girls who'd come tonight had been there then too; the Jewish band with fiddles and zithers had come as well, and at last the long-awaited cart had arrived with the wine and provisions.

Mitya bustled about. All sorts of people started coming into the room to look on — peasants and their wives, roused from sleep and drawn by the hope of another marvelous entertainment like the one they'd enjoyed a month before. Mitya remembered their faces, greeting and embracing everyone he knew. He uncorked bottles and poured wine for anyone who showed up. Only the girls were really eager for champagne. The men preferred rum, brandy, and, above all, hot punch. Mitya had chocolate made for all the girls, and ordered three samovars kept boiling all night, so tea and punch would be there for the taking.

An absurd, chaotic confusion followed, but Mitya was in his element, and the more foolish it grew, the higher his spirits climbed. Had the peasants asked him for money at that moment, he'd have pulled out his notes and handed them out right and left. That was probably why the landlord, Trifon Borissovitch, kept hovering near Mitya to look after his interests. He seemed to have given up all thought of going to bed that night, but drank little — only one glass of punch — and kept a sharp watch over Mitya's money, in his own fashion. He'd step in at just the right moment, politely and obsequiously talking Mitya out of handing over "cigars and Rhine wine," and above all money, to the peasants, as he had before. He was also very put out that the peasant girls were drinking liqueur and eating sweets.
"They're a lousy lot, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," he said. "I'd give them a kick, every one of them, and they'd take it as an honor — that's all they're worth!"

Mitya remembered Andrey again, and ordered punch sent out to him. "I was rude to him just now," he repeated, his voice sinking, softened. Kalganov didn't want to drink, and at first cared nothing for the girls' singing; but after a couple of glasses of champagne he grew remarkably lively, wandering the room, laughing, praising the music and songs, admiring everyone and everything. Maximov, blissfully drunk, never left his side. Grushenka, too, was starting to get drunk. Pointing at Kalganov, she said to Mitya:
"What a dear, charming boy he is!"

And Mitya, delighted, ran off to kiss Kalganov and Maximov. Oh, how great his hopes were! She'd said nothing yet, and seemed, in fact, to be deliberately holding back. But every so often she looked at him with caressing, passionate eyes. At last she suddenly gripped his hand and pulled him hard toward her. She was sitting, at that moment, in the low chair by the door.
"How is it you came just now, eh? Just walked right in!... I was frightened. So you meant to hand me over to him, did you? Did you really mean to?"
"I didn't want to spoil your happiness!" Mitya faltered, blissfully. But she didn't need an answer from him.
"Well, go and enjoy yourself ..." she sent him off again. "Don't cry, I'll call you back."
He'd run off, and she'd listen to the singing and watch the dancing, though her eyes followed him wherever he went. But within another quarter hour she'd call him back, and again he'd run to her.
"Come, sit by me, tell me — how did you hear about me, about my coming here yesterday? Who did you hear it from first?"
And Mitya began telling her the whole thing, disjointedly, incoherently, feverishly. He spoke strangely, often frowning, breaking off abruptly.
"What are you frowning about?" she asked.
"Nothing.... I left a man back there, badly hurt. I'd give ten years of my life for him to get well, just to know he's all right!"

"Well, never mind him, if he's hurt. So you meant to shoot yourself tomorrow! What a silly boy! Whatever for? I like reckless fellows like you," she said, her tongue a little thick. "So you'd go to any length for me, eh? Did you really mean to shoot yourself tomorrow, you fool? No, wait a while. Tomorrow I may have something to tell you.... I won't say it today, but tomorrow. You'd like it to be today? No, I don't want it today. Go on now, go and enjoy yourself."
Once, though, she called him over looking puzzled and uneasy.

"Why are you sad? I can see you're sad.... Yes, I see it," she added, looking hard into his eyes. "Even with all your kissing the peasants and shouting, I can see something. No, be cheerful. I'm cheerful; you be cheerful too.... I love somebody here. Guess who it is. Ah, look, my boy's fallen asleep, poor dear, he's drunk."

She meant Kalganov. He was, in fact, drunk, and had dropped off for a moment, sitting on the sofa. But it wasn't just drowsiness from drink; he'd suddenly grown dejected, or, as he put it, "bored." He was thoroughly depressed by the girls' songs, which, as the drinking wore on, grew steadily coarser and wilder. The dances were no better. Two girls dressed up as bears, and a lively girl named Stepanida, stick in hand, played the bear-keeper, and began "putting them through their paces."
"Look alive, Marya, or you'll get the stick!"
The bears ended up rolling on the ground in the most unseemly fashion, to roars of laughter from the tightly packed crowd of men and women.
"Well, let them! Let them!" said Grushenka, weightily, an ecstatic look on her face. "When they do get a day to enjoy themselves, why shouldn't folks be happy?"
Kalganov looked as though he'd been smeared with dirt.
"It's swinish, all this peasant foolery," he muttered, moving away. "It's the sort of game they play on the long light nights of summer."
He particularly disliked one "new" song set to a jaunty dance tune. It told how a gentleman came along to try his luck with the girls, to see whether they'd love him:
The master came to try the girls: Would they love him, would they not?
But the girls couldn't love the master:
He would beat me cruelly And such love won't do for me.
Then a gypsy comes along, and tries his luck too:
The gypsy came to try the girls: Would they love him, would they not?
But they couldn't love the gypsy either:
He would be a thief, I fear, And would cause me many a tear.
And many more men come to try their luck, a soldier among them:
The soldier came to try the girls: Would they love him, would they not?
But the soldier is turned down with contempt, in two indecent lines, sung with total frankness, to the crowd's uproarious delight. The song ends with a merchant:
The merchant came to try the girls: Would they love him, would they not?
And it turns out he wins their love, because:
The merchant will make gold for me And his queen I'll gladly be.
Kalganov was thoroughly indignant.

"That's just a song made up yesterday," he said, aloud. "Who writes this stuff for them? They might as well have had a railway man or a Jew come try his luck with the girls; he'd have swept the field."

And, as though it were a personal insult, he announced, then and there, that he was bored, sat down on the sofa, and fell asleep almost at once. His pretty face looked rather pale as it dropped back against the sofa cushion.
"Look how pretty he is," said Grushenka, drawing Mitya over to look. "I was combing his hair just now; his hair's like flax, and so thick...."
And, bending tenderly over him, she kissed his forehead. Kalganov's eyes opened at once; he looked at her, stood up, and asked, with the most anxious air, where Maximov had got to.
"So that's who you want." Grushenka laughed. "Stay with me a minute. Mitya, go find his Maximov."

Maximov, it turned out, couldn't tear himself away from the girls, only breaking off now and then to pour himself another glass of liqueur. He'd had two cups of chocolate. His face was red, his nose crimson; his eyes were moist and sickly-sweet. He ran up to announce he was about to dance the "sabotière."
"They taught me all those refined, aristocratic dances when I was a boy...."
"Go with him, Mitya, and I'll watch from here how he dances," said Grushenka.

"No, no, I'm coming to watch too," exclaimed Kalganov, brushing off, with perfect naivety, Grushenka's offer to sit with him. They all went to watch. Maximov danced his dance. But it stirred no great admiration in anyone but Mitya. It consisted of nothing but skipping and hopping and kicking up the feet, and with every skip Maximov slapped the upturned sole of his foot. Kalganov didn't care for it at all, but Mitya kissed the dancer.
"Thanks. Tired, maybe? What are you after here? Want some sweets? A cigar, perhaps?"
"A cigarette."
"Don't you want a drink?"
"I'll just have a liqueur.... Do you have any chocolates?"
"Yes, there's a whole heap of them on the table there. Take your pick, my dear soul!"
"I like the vanilla kind ... for old folks. He he!"
"No, brother, we've none of that special kind."
"I say," the old man leaned in to whisper in Mitya's ear. "That girl there, little Marya, he he! What if you were to help me make friends with her?"
"So that's what you're after! No, brother, that won't do!"
"I wouldn't do anyone any harm," Maximov muttered, disconsolately.
"Oh, all right, all right. They only come here to dance and sing, you know, brother. But damn it all, wait a bit!... Eat and drink and be merry, meanwhile. Don't you want some money?"
"Later on, perhaps," Maximov smiled.
"All right, all right...."

Mitya's head was on fire. He went out onto the wooden balcony that ran around the whole building on the inner side, overlooking the courtyard. The fresh air revived him. He stood alone in a dark corner, and suddenly clutched his head in both hands. His scattered thoughts drew together; his sensations fused into a whole and threw a sudden light across his mind. A fearful, terrible light! "If I'm going to shoot myself, why not now?" flashed through his mind. "Why not go get the pistols, bring them here, and here, in this dark, filthy corner, make an end of it?" He stood almost a full minute, undecided. A few hours earlier, when he'd been racing here, he'd been pursued by disgrace, by the theft he'd committed, and that blood, that blood!... And yet it had been easier for him then. Then everything was over: he'd lost her, given her up. She was gone, for him — oh, his death sentence had been easier then; it had at least seemed necessary, inevitable, for what had he left to stay on earth for?

But now? Was it the same as then? Now at least one phantom, one terror, had come to an end: that first, rightful lover, that fateful figure, had vanished without a trace. The terrible phantom had turned into something so small, so absurd; it had been carried off to the bedroom and locked in. It would never come back. She was ashamed, and from her eyes he could now see whom she loved. Now he had everything to make his life happy ... but he couldn't go on living, he couldn't; oh, damnation! "O God! Bring the man I struck down by the fence back to life! Let this terrible cup pass from me! Lord, Thou hast worked miracles for sinners like me before! But what, what if the old man's alive? Oh, then I'd wipe away the shame of the other disgrace. I'd give back the stolen money. I'd return it; I'd get it somehow.... No trace of that shame would remain, except in my own heart forever! But no, no; oh, impossible, cowardly dreams! Oh, damnation!"

And yet there was a ray of light and hope in his darkness. He jumped up and ran back into the room — to her, to her, his queen forever! Wasn't one moment of her love worth the whole rest of life, even amid the agonies of disgrace? This wild question gripped his heart. "To her, to her alone — to see her, to hear her, to think of nothing, to forget everything, if only for that night, for an hour, for a moment!" Just as he turned from the balcony into the passage, he ran into the landlord, Trifon Borissovitch. He thought the man looked gloomy and troubled, and guessed he'd come looking for him.
"What is it, Trifon Borissovitch? Looking for me?"
"No, sir." The landlord seemed thrown off. "Why would I be looking for you? Where have you been?"
"Why do you look so glum? You're not angry, are you? Wait a bit, you'll soon get to bed.... What's the time?"
"Must be three o'clock. Past three, more like."
"We'll leave off soon. We'll leave off."
"Don't mention it; it doesn't matter. Keep it up as long as you like...."

"What's the matter with him?" Mitya wondered for a moment, and ran back to the room where the girls were dancing. But she wasn't there. Nor was she in the blue room; no one there but Kalganov, asleep on the sofa. Mitya peered behind the curtain — there she was. She was sitting in the corner, on a trunk. Bent forward, her head and arms resting on the bed beside her, she was crying bitterly, doing everything she could to stifle her sobs so no one would hear. Seeing Mitya, she beckoned him over, and when he ran to her, she gripped his hand tight.

"Mitya, Mitya, I loved him, you know. How I've loved him these five years, the whole time! Did I love him, or only my own anger? No, him, him! It's a lie to say it was my anger I loved and not him. Mitya, I was only seventeen then; he was so kind to me, so cheerful; he used to sing to me.... Or so it seemed to a silly girl like me.... And now, O Lord, he's not the same man. Even his face isn't the same; he's changed entirely. I wouldn't have known him. I rode here with Timofey, and the whole way I kept thinking about how I'd meet him, what I'd say to him, how we'd look at each other. My soul was faint, and all of a sudden it was as though he'd dumped a pail of dirty water over me. He talked to me like a schoolmaster, so grave and learned; he greeted me so solemnly I was struck dumb. I couldn't get a word in. At first I thought he was embarrassed to talk in front of his great big Pole. I sat there staring at him, wondering why I suddenly couldn't say a word to him. It must have been his wife who ruined him; you know, he threw me over to get married. She must have changed him like that. Mitya, how shameful it all is! Oh, Mitya, I'm ashamed, I'll be ashamed my whole life. Curse it, curse it, curse those five years!"
And again she burst into tears, but clung tight to Mitya's hand and wouldn't let it go.

"Mitya, darling, stay, don't go away. I want to say one thing to you," she whispered, and suddenly raised her face to him. "Listen, tell me who it is I love. I love one man here. Who is that man? That's what you have to tell me."
A smile lit up her tear-swollen face, and her eyes shone in the half-darkness.

"A falcon flew in, and my heart sank. 'Fool! That's the man you love!' That's what my heart whispered to me right away. You walked in and everything grew bright. What's he afraid of? I wondered. Because you were frightened; you couldn't speak. It's not them he's afraid of — could you be afraid of anyone? It's me he's afraid of, I thought, only me. So Fenya told you, you little fool, how I called out the window to Alyosha that I'd loved Mityenka for one hour, and that now I was going to love ... someone else. Mitya, Mitya, how could I be such a fool as to think I could love anyone after you? Do you forgive me, Mitya? Do you forgive me, or not? Do you love me? Do you love me?" She jumped up and gripped his shoulders with both hands. Mitya, speechless with rapture, gazed into her eyes, at her face, her smile, and suddenly clasped her tightly in his arms and kissed her passionately.

"You'll forgive me for having tormented you? It was out of spite that I tormented all of you. It was out of spite that I drove the old man out of his mind.... Remember the time you drank at my place and broke a wine glass? I remembered that, and today I broke a glass and drank 'to my vile heart.' Mitya, my falcon, why don't you kiss me? He kissed me once, and now he draws back and just looks and listens. Why listen to me? Kiss me, kiss me hard, that's right. If you love me, then love me! I'll be your slave now, your slave for the rest of my life. It's sweet to be a slave. Kiss me! Beat me, mistreat me, do whatever you want with me.... And I deserve to suffer. Wait, stop, that's for later, I won't have it now...." she suddenly pushed him away. "Go on, Mitya, I'll come and have some wine, I want to get drunk, I'm going to get drunk and dance; I must, I must!" She tore herself away from him and vanished behind the curtain. Mitya followed like a drunken man.

"Yes, come what may — whatever happens now, I'd give the whole world for one minute of it," he thought. Grushenka, in fact, downed a whole glass of champagne in one gulp, and grew tipsy at once. She sat back down in the same chair as before, a blissful smile on her face. Her cheeks glowed, her lips burned, her flashing eyes were moist; there was a passionate appeal in them. Even Kalganov felt something stir in his chest, and went over to her.

"Did you feel me kiss you, just now, while you were asleep?" she said, thickly. "I'm drunk now, that's what it is.... And aren't you drunk? And why isn't Mitya drinking? Why don't you drink, Mitya? I'm drunk, and you're not drinking...."
"I am drunk! I'm drunk as it is ... drunk on you ... and now I'll get drunk on wine too."

He drained another glass, and — strange as it seemed even to him — that glass left him completely drunk. He was suddenly drunk, though up to that very moment he'd been perfectly sober; he remembered that clearly. From that moment on, everything spun around him, as if he were delirious. He walked, laughed, talked to everyone, without knowing what he was doing. Only one persistent, burning sensation kept making itself felt, "like a red-hot coal in his heart," as he said afterward. He went up to her, sat beside her, looked at her, listened to her.... She grew very talkative, kept calling everyone over to her, beckoning different girls out of the chorus. When a girl came up, she'd either kiss her or make the sign of the cross over her. Another minute and she might have burst into tears. She was greatly amused by the "little old man," as she called Maximov. He kept running up to kiss her hands, "each little finger," and finally danced another dance to an old song he sang himself. He danced with special vigor to the refrain:

The little pig says — umph! umph! umph! The little calf says — moo, moo, moo, The little duck says — quack, quack, quack, The little goose says — ga, ga, ga. The hen goes strutting through the porch; Troo-roo-roo-roo-roo, she'll say, Troo-roo-roo-roo-roo, she'll say!

"Give him something, Mitya," said Grushenka. "Give him a present, he's poor, you know. Ah, the poor, the insulted!... Do you know, Mitya, I'm going to enter a convent. No, I really will, one day, Alyosha said something to me today that I'll remember my whole life.... Yes.... But today, let's dance. Tomorrow the convent, but today we dance. I want to be wild today, good people, and what of it? God will forgive us. If I were God, I'd forgive everyone: 'My dear sinners, from this day forward I forgive you.' I'm going to go beg forgiveness: 'Forgive me, good people, a foolish girl.' I'm a beast, that's what I am. But I want to pray. I gave away a little onion once. Wicked as I've been, I want to pray. Mitya, let them dance, don't stop them. Everyone in the world is good. Everyone — even the worst of them. The world's a good place. Even though we're bad, the world's all right. We're good and bad, good and bad.... Come, tell me, I've got something to ask you: come here, everyone, and I'll ask you — why am I so good? You know I'm good. I'm very good.... Come, why am I so good?"

So Grushenka rambled on, getting drunker and drunker. At last she announced she was going to dance too. She got up from her chair, staggering. "Mitya, don't give me any more wine — if I ask for it, don't give it to me. Wine doesn't bring peace. Everything's spinning, the stove, everything. I want to dance. Let everyone see how I dance ... let them see how beautifully I dance...."

She really meant it. She pulled a white cambric handkerchief from her pocket and took it by one corner in her right hand, to wave as she danced. Mitya ran back and forth; the girls went quiet, ready to break into a dance-song at the first signal. Maximov, hearing that Grushenka meant to dance, squealed with delight and skipped along in front of her, humming:
With legs so slim and sides so trim And its little tail curled tight.
But Grushenka waved her handkerchief at him and drove him off.
"Sh-h! Mitya, why aren't they coming? Let everyone come ... to watch. Call in the ones that were locked in too.... Why did you lock them in? Tell them I'm going to dance. Let them watch too...."
Mitya walked with drunken swagger to the locked door and began pounding on it with his fist, calling to the Poles.
"Hi, you ... Podvysotskys! Come on, she's going to dance. She's calling you."
"Lajdak!" one of the Poles shouted back.
"You're the lajdak! You're a little scoundrel, that's what you are."
"Stop mocking Poland," Kalganov said, weightily. He was drunk too.
"Quiet, boy! If I call one man a scoundrel, that doesn't mean I called all Poland one. One lajdak doesn't make a Poland. Quiet, my pretty boy, eat a sweet."

"Ach, what fellows! As though they weren't human. Why won't they make friends?" said Grushenka, and stepped forward to dance. The chorus broke into "Ah, my porch, my new porch!" Grushenka tossed her head back, parted her lips a little, smiled, waved her handkerchief, and suddenly, with a violent lurch, stopped dead in the middle of the room, looking bewildered.
"I'm weak...." she said, in an exhausted voice. "Forgive me.... I'm weak, I can't.... I'm sorry."
She bowed to the chorus, then began bowing in every direction.
"I'm sorry.... Forgive me...."
"The lady's had too much to drink. The pretty lady's had a drop too many," voices could be heard saying.
"The lady's had a drop too much," Maximov explained to the girls, giggling.
"Mitya, take me away ... take me," said Grushenka, helplessly. Mitya pounced on her, swept her up into his arms, and carried his precious burden through the curtains.

"Well, now I'll be going," thought Kalganov, and, walking out of the blue room, he pulled the two halves of the door shut behind him. But the revelry in the larger room went on, growing louder and louder. Mitya laid Grushenka on the bed and kissed her on the lips.

"Don't touch me...." she faltered, in a pleading voice. "Don't touch me, until I'm yours.... I've told you I'm yours, but don't touch me ... spare me.... With them here, so close, you mustn't. He's here. It's ugly here...."
"I'll obey you! I won't even think of it ... I worship you!" Mitya muttered. "Yes, it's ugly here, it's disgraceful."
And still holding her in his arms, he sank to his knees by the bedside.

"I know, brute as you are, you're generous," Grushenka got out, with difficulty. "It has to be honorable ... it will be honorable from now on ... and let's be honest, let's be good, not brutes, but good ... take me away, take me far away, do you hear? I don't want it to be here, but far, far away...."
"Oh, yes, yes, it must be!" said Mitya, pressing her to him. "I'll take you and we'll fly away.... Oh, I'd give my whole life for just one year, only to know about that blood!"
"What blood?" asked Grushenka, bewildered.
"Nothing," Mitya muttered through his teeth. "Grusha, you wanted to be honest, but I'm a thief. But I've stolen money from Katya.... Disgrace, a disgrace!"

"From Katya, from that young lady? No, you didn't steal it. Give it back to her, take it from me.... Why make a fuss? Now everything of mine is yours. What does money matter? We'll waste it anyway.... People like us are bound to waste money. But we'd do better to go work the land. I want to dig the earth with my own hands. We have to work, do you hear? Alyosha said so. I won't be your mistress, I'll be faithful to you, I'll be your slave, I'll work for you. We'll go to the young lady and bow down to her together, so she'll forgive us, and then we'll go away. And if she won't forgive us, we'll go anyway. Take her her money and love me.... Don't love her.... Don't love her anymore. If you love her, I'll strangle her.... I'll put out both her eyes with a needle...."
"I love you. I love only you. I'll love you in Siberia...."

"Why Siberia? Never mind, Siberia, if you like. I don't care ... we'll work ... there's snow in Siberia.... I love riding through the snow ... and there have to be bells.... Do you hear, there's a bell ringing? Where's that bell ringing from? There are people coming.... Now it's stopped."

She closed her eyes, worn out, and suddenly dropped off to sleep for an instant. There had, in fact, been the sound of a bell in the distance, but the ringing had stopped. Mitya let his head sink onto her breast. He didn't notice that the bell had gone quiet, nor did he notice that the singing had stopped, and that instead of song and drunken uproar there was total stillness in the house. Grushenka opened her eyes.

"What's the matter? Was I asleep? Yes ... a bell ... I fell asleep and dreamed I was riding over the snow with bells ringing, and I dozed off. I was with someone I loved — with you. And far, far away. I was holding you and kissing you, nestling close to you. I was cold, and the snow sparkled.... You know how the snow sparkles at night, under the moon. It was as though I wasn't on this earth. I woke up, and my dear one is right beside me. How sweet that is!..."

"Right beside you," murmured Mitya, kissing her dress, her breast, her hands. And suddenly he had a strange fancy: it seemed to him she was staring straight ahead, not at him, not into his face, but over his head, with an intent, almost uncanny fixity. A look of wonder, almost of alarm, came suddenly over her face.
"Mitya, who's that looking at us?" she whispered.
Mitya turned, and saw that someone had in fact parted the curtains and seemed to be watching them. And not just one person, it seemed.
He jumped up and walked quickly toward the intruder.
"Here, come to us, come here," said a voice — not loud, but firm and commanding.

Mitya stepped past the curtain and froze on the spot. The room was full of people, but not the ones who'd been there before. A sudden shiver ran down his back, and he shuddered. He recognized every one of them at once. That tall, stout old man in the overcoat and forage cap with a cockade — that was the police captain, Mihail Makarovitch. And that trim, "consumptive-looking" dandy "who always has such polished boots" — that was the deputy prosecutor. "He's got a chronometer worth four hundred roubles; he showed it to me." And that small young man in spectacles.... Mitya had forgotten his surname, though he knew him, had seen him before: he was the "investigating lawyer," from the "school of jurisprudence," who'd only recently arrived in town. And this man — the police inspector, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, whom he knew well. And those men with the brass plates — why were they here? And those other two ... peasants.... And there at the door, Kalganov with Trifon Borissovitch....
"Gentlemen! What's this about, gentlemen?" Mitya began, but suddenly, as though beside himself, not knowing what he was doing, he cried out at the top of his voice:
"I un — der — stand!"
The young man in spectacles stepped forward suddenly, and, coming up to Mitya, began with dignity, though hurriedly:
"We have to ... in short, I ask you to come this way, this way to the sofa.... It's absolutely essential that you give an explanation."
"The old man!" Mitya cried, frantically. "The old man and his blood!... I understand."
And he sank, almost fell, onto a chair nearby, as if cut down by a scythe.
"You understand? He understands it! Monster, and parricide! Your father's blood cries out against you!" the old police captain suddenly roared, stepping up to Mitya.
He was beside himself, crimson in the face, and quivering all over.
"This is impossible!" cried the small young man. "Mihail Makarovitch, Mihail Makarovitch, this won't do!... I beg you to let me speak. I would never have expected such behavior from you...."

"This is delirium, gentlemen, raving delirium," the police captain cried. "Look at him — drunk, at this hour of the night, in the company of a disreputable woman, with his father's blood on his hands.... It's delirium!..."
"I beg you most earnestly, dear Mihail Makarovitch, to restrain yourself," the prosecutor said, in a rapid whisper, to the old police captain, "or I'll be forced to resort to—"
But the little lawyer didn't let him finish. He turned to Mitya, and delivered himself in a loud, firm, dignified voice:
"Ex-Lieutenant Karamazov, it's my duty to inform you that you stand charged with the murder of your father, Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, committed this night...."
He said something more, and the prosecutor too put in a word, but though Mitya heard them, he didn't take it in. He stared at them all with wild eyes.

title: I. The Beginning Of Perhotin’s Official Career
paragraphs: Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, whom we left knocking at the stoutly locked gates of the widow Morozov's house, ended, naturally enough, by making himself heard. Fenya, still shaken from the fright she'd had two hours earlier and too "upset" to go to bed, was nearly startled into hysterics by the furious knocking at the gate. Though she'd watched Mitya drive off herself, she imagined it must be Dmitri Fyodorovitch knocking again — no one else could knock so savagely. She ran to the house porter, who'd already woken and gone out to the gate, and begged him not to open it. But after questioning Pyotr Ilyitch and learning that he wanted to see Fenya on very "important business," the man finally decided to let him in. Pyotr Ilyitch was shown into Fenya's kitchen, though the girl asked him to let the porter stay, "on account of her misgivings." He began questioning her and immediately learned the crucial fact: that when Dmitri Fyodorovitch had run out to look for Grushenka, he'd snatched up a pestle from the mortar, and that when he came back, the pestle wasn't with him, and his hands were smeared with blood.

"And the blood was just flowing off him, dripping, dripping!" Fenya kept exclaiming. This horrifying detail was purely the product of her overwrought imagination. But though it hadn't been "dripping," Pyotr Ilyitch had seen the blood-stained hands himself, and had even helped wash them. Besides, the question he had to settle wasn't how quickly the blood had dried, but where Dmitri Fyodorovitch had run off to with the pestle — or rather, whether it really had been to Fyodor Pavlovitch's, and how he might confirm it for certain. Pyotr Ilyitch kept circling back to this point, and though he turned up nothing conclusive, he came away convinced that Dmitri Fyodorovitch could have gone nowhere else but his father's house, and that something must have happened there.

"And when he came back," Fenya added, agitated, "I told him the whole story, and then I started asking him, 'Why is there blood on your hands, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?' and he told me it was human blood, and that he'd just killed someone. He confessed it all to me, and then suddenly ran off like a madman. I sat down and started thinking — where's he run off to now, like a madman? He'll go to Mokroe, I thought, and kill my mistress there. I ran out to beg him not to kill her. I was running toward his lodgings, but I glanced at Plotnikov's shop and saw him just setting off, and there was no blood on his hands then." (Fenya had noticed this, and remembered it.) Fenya's old grandmother backed up her account as far as she was able. After a few more questions, Pyotr Ilyitch left the house even more unsettled and uneasy than when he'd arrived.

The most direct and simplest thing for him to do would have been to go straight to Fyodor Pavlovitch's, to find out whether anything had happened there, and if so, what — and only go to the police captain, as Pyotr Ilyitch firmly intended to, once he'd confirmed the facts. But the night was dark, Fyodor Pavlovitch's gates were sturdy, and he'd have to knock again. He barely knew Fyodor Pavlovitch, and what if, after all that knocking, they let him in and nothing had happened at all? Then Fyodor Pavlovitch, in his mocking way, would tell the story all over town — how some stranger named Perhotin had burst in on him at midnight to ask whether anyone had killed him. It would make a scandal. And scandal was what Pyotr Ilyitch dreaded more than anything in the world.

And yet the feeling gripping him was so strong that, though he stamped his foot angrily and cursed himself, he set off again — not to Fyodor Pavlovitch's, but to Madame Hohlakov's. He decided that if she denied having just given Dmitri Fyodorovitch three thousand roubles, he'd go straight to the police captain; but if she admitted giving him the money, he'd go home and let the matter rest until morning.

It's plain enough, of course, that going to a fashionable lady, a complete stranger, at eleven at night, and perhaps rousing her from bed to ask her a startling question, was even more likely to cause a scandal than going to Fyodor Pavlovitch. But that's just how it goes, sometimes, especially in cases like this one, with even the most precise and even-tempered people's decisions. Pyotr Ilyitch was anything but even-tempered at that moment. He remembered all his life how a haunting unease had gradually taken hold of him, growing more and more painful, driving him on against his own will. Yet, of course, he kept cursing himself the whole way for going to this lady, but "I'll get to the bottom of it, I will!" he repeated for the tenth time, grinding his teeth, and carried out his plan.

It was exactly eleven o'clock when he entered Madame Hohlakov's house. He was let into the yard readily enough, but when he asked whether the lady was still up, the porter had no answer to give him, beyond saying she was usually in bed by that hour.
"Ask upstairs. If the lady wants to see you, she'll see you. If she won't, she won't."

Pyotr Ilyitch went up, but found things not so simple here. The footman was reluctant to take in his name, but finally called for a maid. Pyotr Ilyitch, politely but insistently, asked her to tell her mistress that an official living in town, named Perhotin, had come on particular business, and that if it weren't of the greatest importance he wouldn't have dared to come. "Tell her exactly that, word for word," he asked the girl.

She went off. He waited in the entry. Madame Hohlakov herself was already in her bedroom, though not yet asleep. She'd been unsettled ever since Mitya's visit, and had a feeling she wouldn't get through the night without the sick headache that always followed such upsets, for her. She was startled to hear the maid's announcement. She irritably refused to see him at first, though the unexpected visit at such an hour, from an "official living in town" who was a total stranger, sharply piqued her feminine curiosity. But this time Pyotr Ilyitch was as stubborn as a mule. He earnestly begged the maid to carry another message back, in these exact words:
"That he had come on business of the greatest importance, and that Madame Hohlakov might have cause to regret it later, if she refused to see him now."
"I threw myself in headlong," he described it afterward.

The maid, staring at him in astonishment, went to deliver the message again. Madame Hohlakov was impressed. She thought it over a moment, asked what he looked like, and learned that he was "very well dressed, young, and so polite." We might note, in passing, that Pyotr Ilyitch was a rather good-looking young man, and well aware of it. Madame Hohlakov made up her mind to see him. She was in her dressing gown and slippers, but she threw a black shawl over her shoulders. "The official" was shown into the drawing room — the very same room Mitya had been received in shortly before. The lady came to meet her visitor with a sternly questioning look, and, without asking him to sit, began at once:
"What do you want?"
"I've taken the liberty of disturbing you, madam, on a matter concerning our mutual acquaintance, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov," Perhotin began.
But he'd barely gotten the name out when the lady's face showed signs of intense irritation. She very nearly shrieked, cutting him off in a fury:

"How much longer am I to be tormented by that dreadful man?" she cried, hysterically. "How dare you, sir, how could you possibly presume to disturb a lady who is a complete stranger to you, in her own home, at such an hour!... And to force yourself on her to talk about a man who came here, to this very drawing room, only three hours ago, to murder me, and stormed out of the room the way no one would leave a decent house. Let me tell you, sir, I intend to lodge a complaint against you, I won't let this pass. Kindly leave at once.... I am a mother.... I ... I—"
"Murder! Then he tried to murder you too?"
"Why, has he killed someone else?" Madame Hohlakov asked, impulsively.

"If you'll kindly listen for half a moment, madam, I'll explain everything in a couple of words," Perhotin answered, firmly. "At five o'clock this afternoon Dmitri Fyodorovitch borrowed ten roubles from me, and I know for a fact he had no money. Yet at nine o'clock he came to see me with a bundle of hundred-rouble notes in his hand — some two or three thousand roubles. His hands and face were covered in blood, and he looked like a madman. When I asked where he'd gotten so much money, he told me he'd just received it from you, that you'd given him three thousand to go to the gold mines...."
Madame Hohlakov's face took on an expression of intense, agonized excitement.

"Good God! He must have killed his own father!" she cried, clasping her hands. "I never gave him money, never! Oh, go, run!... Don't say another word! Save the old man ... run to his father's ... run!"
"Excuse me, madam — so you didn't give him money? You're certain, as a matter of fact, that you gave him nothing?"

"No, I didn't, I didn't! I refused to give it to him, because he couldn't appreciate it. He ran out furious, stamping his feet. He lunged at me, but I slipped away.... And let me tell you, since I mean to hide nothing from you now, that he actually spat at me. Can you imagine! But why are we standing here? Ah, do sit down."
"Excuse me, I...."
"Or better yet, run, run, you must run and save that poor old man from a horrible death!"
"But what if he's already killed him?"
"Ah, good heavens, yes! Then what are we to do now? What do you think we should do?"

Meanwhile she'd gotten Pyotr Ilyitch to sit, and sat down herself, facing him. Briefly but fairly clearly, Pyotr Ilyitch told her the whole story — at least the part of it he'd witnessed himself. He described, too, his visit to Fenya, and told her about the pestle. All these details produced an overwhelming effect on the distraught lady, who kept letting out shrieks and covering her face with her hands....

"Would you believe it, I foresaw all of this! I have that particular gift — whatever I imagine comes to pass. And how many times have I looked at that dreadful man and thought, that man will end up murdering me. And now it's happened ... that is, if he hasn't murdered me, only his own father, it's only because the finger of God preserved me, and what's more, he was ashamed to murder me, because right here, in this very spot, I placed the holy icon holding relics of the holy martyr Saint Varvara around his neck.... And to think how close I came to death at that instant, I walked right up to him and he stretched his neck out to me!... Do you know, Pyotr Ilyitch — I believe you said your name was Pyotr Ilyitch — I don't believe in miracles, but that icon, and this unmistakable miracle just now, that shakes me, I'm ready to believe anything you like. Have you heard of Father Zossima?... But I don't know what I'm saying ... and just imagine, with the icon around his neck he spat at me.... He only spat, it's true, he didn't murder me, and ... he dashed off! But what are we to do, what must we do now? What do you think?"
Pyotr Ilyitch got up and announced that he was going straight to the police captain, to tell him everything and leave him to decide what to do.

"Oh, he's an excellent man, excellent! Mihail Makarovitch, I know him. Of course, he's the man to go to. How practical you are, Pyotr Ilyitch! How well you've thought this all through! I'd never have thought of it, in your place!"

"Especially since I know the police captain quite well myself," Pyotr Ilyitch observed, still standing, visibly anxious to get away from this impulsive lady as quickly as possible — she wouldn't even let him say goodbye and leave.

"And mind, mind," she prattled on, "come back and tell me what you find there, what you learn ... what comes out ... how they'll try him ... what he's sentenced to.... Tell me, we don't have capital punishment, do we? But be sure to come, even if it's three in the morning, or four, or half past four.... Tell them to wake me, to shake me awake if I'm not up.... But, good heavens, I shan't sleep a wink! But wait — hadn't I better come with you?"
"N—no. But if you'd write three lines in your own hand, stating that you didn't give Dmitri Fyodorovitch any money, it might be useful ... in case it's needed...."

"Of course!" Madame Hohlakov skipped over to her writing desk, delighted. "And you know, I'm simply astonished, amazed, at your resourcefulness, your good sense in matters like this. Are you in government service here? I'm delighted to think you're in service here!"
And still talking, she scribbled the following lines on half a sheet of notepaper:

I have never in my life lent that unhappy man, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov (for, whatever else, he is unhappy), three thousand roubles, today or any day. I have never given him money, never: this I swear by all that is holy!
K. HOHLAKOV.
"Here's the note!" she turned quickly to Pyotr Ilyitch. "Go, save him. It's a noble thing you're doing!"
And she made the sign of the cross over him three times. She ran out to see him off to the passage.

"How grateful I am to you! You can't imagine how grateful I am that you came to me first. How is it we've never met before? I shall be flattered to see you at my house from now on. How delightful that you live here!... Such precision! Such practical ability!... People ought to appreciate you, they ought to understand you. If there's ever anything I can do, believe me ... oh, I love young people! I'm in love with young people! The younger generation is the one support of our suffering country. Her one hope.... Oh, go, go!..."

But Pyotr Ilyitch had already fled — or she'd never have let him go so soon. Still, Madame Hohlakov had left him a rather pleasant impression, one that softened somewhat his uneasiness at being dragged into such an unpleasant affair. Tastes differ, as we all know. "She's really not so old," he thought, pleased, "quite the opposite, I'd have taken her for her own daughter."

As for Madame Hohlakov, she was simply enchanted by the young man. "Such sense! Such precision! In so young a man! In this day and age! And with such manners, such looks besides! People say the young people of today are good for nothing, but here's living proof otherwise!" and so on. So she simply forgot the whole "dreadful affair," and it was only as she was climbing into bed, suddenly recalling "how close to death she'd come," that she exclaimed: "Ah, it's awful, awful!"
But she dropped at once into a sound, sweet sleep.

I wouldn't, however, have lingered over such trivial and beside-the-point details, if this odd meeting between the young official and the not-at-all-elderly widow hadn't later turned out to lay the foundation for that practical, precise young man's entire career. His story is still remembered with astonishment in our town to this day, and I may perhaps have something to say about it once I've finished this long history of the Brothers Karamazov.

title: II. The Alarm
paragraphs: Our police captain, Mihail Makarovitch Makarov, a retired lieutenant colonel, was a widower and an excellent man. He'd come to us only three years before, but had won everyone's esteem, chiefly because he "knew how to keep society together." He was never without visitors, and couldn't have gotten on without them. Someone or other was always dining with him; he never sat down to a meal without guests. He also held regular dinners for all sorts of occasions, sometimes rather surprising ones. The fare wasn't exquisite, but there was plenty of it. The fish pies were excellent, and the wine made up in quantity what it lacked in quality.

The first room guests entered was a well-appointed billiard room, hung with pictures of English racehorses in black frames — an essential decoration, as we all know, for a bachelor's billiard room. There was card-playing at his house every evening, even if only at one table. But at frequent intervals, all of our town's society, mothers and young ladies included, gathered there to dance. Though Mihail Makarovitch was a widower, he didn't live alone. His widowed daughter lived with him, along with her two unmarried daughters, grown girls who'd finished their schooling. They were pleasant to look at and lively in temperament, and though everyone knew they'd have no dowry, they drew all the fashionable young men of the town to their grandfather's house.

Mihail Makarovitch was by no means highly capable at his work, though he performed his duties no worse than most others. To put it plainly, he was a man of rather limited education. His grasp of the boundaries of his own administrative authority couldn't always be relied on. It wasn't so much that he failed to understand certain reforms enacted under the present reign, as that he made conspicuous blunders interpreting them. This wasn't from any particular lack of intelligence, but from carelessness — he was always in too much of a hurry to go into things properly.

"I have the heart of a soldier, not a civilian," he liked to say of himself. He'd never even formed a clear idea of the basic principles behind the reforms tied to the emancipation of the serfs, and had only picked it up, so to speak, year by year, building his knowledge unintentionally through practice. And yet he was himself a landowner. Pyotr Ilyitch knew for certain he'd find some of Mihail Makarovitch's regular visitors there that evening, though he didn't know which ones. As it happened, at that moment the prosecutor, and Varvinsky, our district doctor — a young man who'd only just arrived from Petersburg after taking a brilliant degree at the Academy of Medicine — were playing whist at the police captain's. Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor (he was really the deputy prosecutor, but we always called him the prosecutor), was a rather peculiar man of about thirty-five, prone to consumption, married to a stout, childless woman. He was vain and irritable, though he had a sharp mind and even a kind heart. It seemed the only real trouble with him was that he thought more highly of himself than his abilities warranted. And that kept him in a state of near-constant unease. He also had certain loftier, even artistic, inclinations — toward psychology, say, a particular interest in the human heart, a particular grasp of the criminal and his crime. He nursed a grievance on this score, believing he'd been passed over in his career, and was firmly convinced that in higher circles he wasn't properly appreciated, and that he had enemies. In his gloomier moods he even threatened to resign his post and take up criminal law as a barrister. The unexpected Karamazov case stirred him profoundly: "It was a case that might well be talked about across all of Russia." But I'm getting ahead of myself.

Nikolay Parfenovitch Nelyudov, the young investigating lawyer, who'd arrived from Petersburg only two months before, was sitting in the next room with the young ladies. People talked about it afterward, marveling that all the gentlemen should, as if on purpose, have been gathered that evening — the evening of "the crime" — at the house of the local authority. And yet it was perfectly simple, and had come about quite naturally.

Ippolit Kirillovitch's wife had had a toothache for the past two days, and he'd had to get out of the house to escape her groaning. The doctor, by his very nature, couldn't spend an evening any other way than at cards. Nikolay Parfenovitch Nelyudov had been planning for three days to drop in that evening at Mihail Makarovitch's, as if by chance, in order to slyly startle the eldest granddaughter, Olga Mihailovna, by letting her know he'd found out her secret — that it was her birthday, and that she was trying to hide it on purpose so as not to have to host a dance. He looked forward to plenty of merriment: playful jokes about her age and her fear of revealing it, about his knowing her secret and telling everyone, and so on. The charming young man was a great hand at that kind of teasing; the ladies had nicknamed him "the naughty man," and he seemed rather pleased with it. He was, however, extremely well-bred, of good family, good education, good feeling, and, though he lived a life of pleasure, his jokes were always innocent and in good taste. He was short and delicate-looking. On his slender white little fingers he always wore a number of large, glittering rings. When engaged in his official duties, he turned extraordinarily grave, as though fully conscious of his position and the sanctity of the obligations resting on him. He had a special knack for confusing murderers and other criminals from the peasant class during questioning, and if he didn't manage to win their respect, he certainly managed to leave them in awe.

Pyotr Ilyitch was simply dumbfounded when he walked into the police captain's. He saw at once that everyone already knew. They'd actually thrown down their cards; everyone was on their feet, talking. Even Nikolay Parfenovitch had left the young ladies and hurried in, looking tense and ready for action. Pyotr Ilyitch was met with the stunning news that old Fyodor Pavlovitch really had been murdered that evening, in his own house — murdered and robbed. The news had only just reached them, in the following way.

Marfa Ignatyevna, wife of old Grigory, who'd been knocked senseless near the fence, was sleeping soundly in bed and might well have slept until morning, given the draught she'd taken. But all at once she woke up, no doubt roused by a terrible epileptic scream from Smerdyakov, lying unconscious in the next room. That scream always preceded his fits, and always terrified and unsettled Marfa Ignatyevna. She could never get used to it. She jumped up and ran, half-awake, to Smerdyakov's room. But it was dark in there, and all she could hear was the sick man beginning to gasp and thrash. Marfa Ignatyevna herself let out a scream then, and was about to call her husband, but suddenly realized that when she'd gotten up, he hadn't been beside her in bed. She ran back to the bedstead and groped around with her hands, but the bed was truly empty. Then he must have gone out — but where? She ran to the steps and timidly called for him. No answer came, of course, but she caught the sound of groaning somewhere off in the dark garden. She listened. The groans came again, clearly from the garden.
"Good Lord! Just like it was with Lizaveta Smerdyastchaya!" she thought, distractedly. She crept timidly down the steps and saw that the garden gate stood open.
"He must be out there, poor dear," she thought. She went up to the gate, and all at once clearly heard Grigory calling her name — "Marfa! Marfa!" — in a weak, moaning, dreadful voice.

"Lord, keep us from harm!" Marfa Ignatyevna murmured, and ran toward the voice, and that's how she found Grigory. But she found him not by the fence where he'd been struck down, but about twenty paces off. It turned out later that he'd crawled that far after coming to, and had probably taken a long time getting there, losing consciousness several times along the way. She noticed at once that he was covered in blood, and screamed at the top of her lungs. Grigory was muttering incoherently:
"He's murdered ... murdered his father.... Why are you screaming, fool ... run ... fetch someone...."

But Marfa went on screaming, and, seeing that her master's window was open with a candle lit inside, she ran to it and began calling for Fyodor Pavlovitch. But peering in through the window, she saw a horrifying sight. Her master lay motionless on his back on the floor. His light-colored dressing gown and white shirt were soaked in blood. The candle on the table lit up, brightly, the blood and the still, dead face of Fyodor Pavlovitch. Terror-struck, Marfa fled the window, ran out of the garden, drew the bolt on the main gate, and ran headlong, by the back way, to the neighbor, Marya Kondratyevna. Both mother and daughter were asleep, but woke at Marfa's desperate, unrelenting screaming and pounding on the shutter. Marfa, shrieking and gabbling incoherently, managed to get the main fact across, and to beg for help. As it happened, Foma had returned from his travels and was staying the night with them. They roused him at once, and all three ran to the scene. On the way, Marya Kondratyevna remembered that around eight o'clock she'd heard a terrible scream from their garden — no doubt Grigory's scream of "Parricide!" when he'd grabbed Mitya's leg.

"Someone screamed out once, and then went quiet," Marya Kondratyevna explained as she ran. Reaching the spot where Grigory lay, the two women, with Foma's help, carried him to the lodge. They lit a candle and saw that Smerdyakov was no better — writhing in convulsions, his eyes fixed in a squint, foam flowing from his lips. They wet Grigory's forehead with water mixed with vinegar, and it revived him at once. He asked immediately:
"Is the master murdered?"

Then Foma and both women ran to the house, and this time saw that not just the window but the garden door too stood wide open, even though Fyodor Pavlovitch had, for the past week, locked himself in every night and wouldn't let even Grigory in on any pretext. Seeing the door open, they were afraid to go in to Fyodor Pavlovitch, "in case something happened to them afterward." And when they got back to Grigory, the old man told them to go straight to the police captain. Marya Kondratyevna ran there and raised the alarm with the whole party at the police captain's house. She arrived only five minutes ahead of Pyotr Ilyitch, so his own account came through not as mere guesswork and theory on his part, but as direct confirmation, by a witness, of the theory everyone already held about the identity of the criminal — a theory he himself had, deep down, refused to believe until that very moment.

It was decided to act at once, and decisively. The deputy police inspector of the town was directed to take four witnesses, enter Fyodor Pavlovitch's house, and open an inquiry on the spot, following the proper procedures, which I won't go into here. The district doctor, a zealous man new to his work, all but insisted on accompanying the police captain, the prosecutor, and the investigating lawyer.

I'll note briefly that Fyodor Pavlovitch was found quite dead, his skull crushed in. But with what? Most likely with the very same weapon used on Grigory. And that weapon was found almost immediately: Grigory, who was given every possible medical attention at once, described, in a weak, faltering voice, how he'd been struck down. They searched by lantern along the fence and found the brass pestle, dropped in the most conspicuous spot right on the garden path. There were no signs of disturbance in the room where Fyodor Pavlovitch lay. But by the bed, behind the screen, they picked up off the floor a large, thick envelope, inscribed: "A gift of three thousand roubles for my angel Grushenka, if she's willing to come." And below that, Fyodor Pavlovitch had added, "For my little chick." The envelope bore three seals of red sealing wax, but it had been torn open and was empty — the money was gone. They also found on the floor a strip of narrow pink ribbon, which had been used to tie the envelope shut.

One piece of Pyotr Ilyitch's testimony made a strong impression on the prosecutor and the investigating magistrate — his account of Dmitri Fyodorovitch's plan to shoot himself before daybreak, that he'd resolved on it, had spoken of it to Pyotr Ilyitch, had taken the pistols, loaded them right in front of him, written a note, put it in his pocket, and so on. When Pyotr Ilyitch, still not quite believing it, had threatened to tell someone in order to stop the suicide, Mitya had answered, grinning: "You'll be too late." So they had to hurry to Mokroe to catch the criminal before he actually shot himself.

"That's clear, that's perfectly clear!" the prosecutor repeated, in great excitement. "That's exactly the way it goes with madmen like that: 'I'll kill myself tomorrow, so I'll make merry till I die!'"
The story of how he'd bought the wine and provisions worked the prosecutor up even more.

"Do you remember the fellow who murdered a merchant named Olsufyev, gentlemen? Stole fifteen hundred, went straight off to have his hair curled, and then, without even hiding the money, carrying it almost right out in his hand the same way, went off to see the girls."

Everyone was held up, though, by the inquiry, the search, and the various formalities at Fyodor Pavlovitch's house. It all took time, so, two hours before setting off, they sent ahead to Mokroe the district police officer, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch Schmertsov, who'd arrived in town the morning before to collect his pay. He was instructed to avoid raising any alarm once he reached Mokroe, but to keep the "criminal" under steady watch until the proper authorities arrived, and also to line up witnesses for the arrest, constables, and so on. Mavriky Mavrikyevitch did exactly as told, keeping his presence secret, giving no hint of his business to anyone but his old acquaintance Trifon Borissovitch. He'd spoken to him just before Mitya, searching for the landlord in the dark, met him on the balcony, and noticed at once a change in Trifon Borissovitch's face and voice.
