So neither Mitya nor anyone else knew he was being watched. The pistol case had been carried off by Trifon Borissovitch and stowed somewhere fitting. It was only after four o'clock, nearly at sunrise, that all the officials — the police captain, the prosecutor, the investigating lawyer — arrived in two carriages, each drawn by three horses. The doctor stayed behind at Fyodor Pavlovitch's to perform a post-mortem the next day. But he was especially interested in the condition of the servant, Smerdyakov.

"Such violent, prolonged epileptic fits, recurring continuously for twenty-four hours, are rarely seen, and are of real scientific interest," he declared enthusiastically to his companions, who laughingly congratulated him, as they left, on his find. The prosecutor and the investigating lawyer both clearly remembered the doctor saying that Smerdyakov wouldn't survive the night.
After these lengthy, but I think necessary, explanations, we'll go back to the moment in our story where we left off.

title: III. The Sufferings Of A Soul, The First Ordeal
paragraphs: And so Mitya sat there, staring wildly at the people around him, not understanding what was being said to him. Suddenly he got to his feet, flung his hands up, and shouted at the top of his voice:
"I'm not guilty! I'm not guilty of that blood! I'm not guilty of my father's blood.... I meant to kill him. But I'm not guilty. Not me."
But he'd barely said this when Grushenka rushed out from behind the curtain and threw herself at the police captain's feet.

"It was my fault! Mine! My wickedness!" she cried, in a heartbreaking voice, drenched in tears, stretching her clasped hands out toward them. "He did it because of me. I tortured him and drove him to it. I tortured that poor old man too, the one who's dead now, with my wickedness, and I drove him to this! It's my fault, mine first, mine most of all, my fault!"

"Yes, it's your fault! You're the chief criminal here! You fury! You harlot! You're the one most to blame!" the police captain shouted, shaking his hand at her. But he was quickly and firmly shut down. The prosecutor practically grabbed hold of him.
"This is thoroughly irregular, Mihail Makarovitch!" he cried. "You're actively obstructing the inquiry.... You're ruining the case...." he nearly gasped.
"Follow proper procedure! Follow proper procedure!" cried Nikolay Parfenovitch, badly rattled too. "Otherwise it's simply impossible!..."
"Try us together!" Grushenka cried, frantic, still on her knees. "Punish us together. I'll go with him now, even if it's to death!"

"Grusha, my life, my blood, my holy one!" Mitya dropped to his knees beside her and held her tight in his arms. "Don't believe her," he cried, "she's not guilty of anything, of any blood, of anything at all!"

He remembered afterward that several men had to drag him bodily away from her, and that she was led out, and that when he came to himself he was sitting at the table. Beside him and behind him stood the men with the metal plates. Across the table from him sat Nikolay Parfenovitch, the investigating lawyer, urging him to drink a little water from a glass on the table.

"That will refresh you, that will calm you down. Stay calm, don't be frightened," he added, with extreme politeness. Mitya (he remembered this afterward) suddenly grew intensely fascinated by the man's big rings — one set with an amethyst, another with a bright, transparent yellow stone of great brilliance. And long afterward he remembered, with wonder, how those rings had held his attention through all those terrible hours of questioning, so that he simply couldn't tear his eyes away and dismiss them as things that had nothing whatever to do with his situation. On Mitya's left, in the seat where Maximov had been sitting earlier that evening, the prosecutor now sat, and on Mitya's right, where Grushenka had been, sat a rosy-cheeked young man in a somewhat shabby hunting jacket, with ink and paper laid out before him. This was the secretary the investigating lawyer had brought along. The police captain now stood by the window at the far end of the room, beside Kalganov, who was seated there.
"Drink some water," the investigating lawyer said softly, for the tenth time.
"I have drunk it, gentlemen, I have ... but ... come, gentlemen, crush me, punish me, decide my fate!" cried Mitya, staring at the investigating lawyer with terribly fixed, wide-open eyes.
"So you flatly deny that you are guilty of your father Fyodor Pavlovitch's death?" the investigating lawyer asked, softly but insistently.

"I am not guilty. I'm guilty of another old man's blood, but not my father's. And for that I weep! I struck the old man down, I struck him.... But it's hard to have to answer for that killing with another one too — a terrible murder I had no part in.... It's a terrible accusation, gentlemen, it knocks a man flat. But who killed my father, who killed him? Who could have killed him, if not me? It's astonishing, extraordinary, impossible."
"Yes, who could have killed him?" the investigating lawyer began, but Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor, glancing at him, turned to Mitya instead.

"You needn't trouble yourself over the old servant, Grigory Vassilyevitch. He's alive, he's recovered, and despite the terrible blows he took — by his own account and yours — there seems little doubt he'll live, or so the doctor says, at least."

"Alive? He's alive?" cried Mitya, throwing up his hands. His face lit up. "Lord, I thank Thee for the miracle Thou hast worked for me, a sinner and evildoer. That's an answer to my prayer. I've been praying all night." And he crossed himself three times. He could barely catch his breath.
"So, from this Grigory, we've received evidence about you significant enough that—" the prosecutor was going to continue, but Mitya suddenly leapt up from his chair.
"One moment, gentlemen, for God's sake, one moment; I'll run to her—"

"Excuse me, but at this moment that's quite impossible," Nikolay Parfenovitch nearly shrieked, leaping to his feet as well. Mitya was seized by the men with the metal plates, but sat back down of his own accord....

"Gentlemen, what a pity! I only wanted to see her for one minute; I wanted to tell her it's washed away, it's gone — that blood that had been weighing on my heart all night — and that I'm not a murderer anymore! Gentlemen, she's my betrothed!" he said, ecstatic and reverent, glancing round at them all. "Oh, thank you, gentlemen! Oh, in one minute you've given me a new life, a new heart!... That old man used to carry me in his arms, gentlemen. He bathed me in the tub when I was a baby of three, abandoned by everyone — he was like a father to me!..."
"And so you—" the investigating lawyer began.

"Allow me, gentlemen, allow me one moment more," Mitya cut in, resting his elbows on the table and covering his face with his hands. "Give me a moment to think, let me breathe, gentlemen. All of this is horribly upsetting, horribly. A man's not a drum, gentlemen!"
"Drink a little more water," Nikolay Parfenovitch murmured.

Mitya took his hands from his face and laughed. His eyes were confident now. He seemed completely transformed in an instant. His whole manner had changed; he was once more the equal of these men, all of whom he knew, as though they'd all just met the day before, at some social gathering, with nothing having happened. We might note, in passing, that when he'd first arrived in town, Mitya had been made very welcome at the police captain's, but lately — especially over the past month — he'd hardly called at all, and when the captain ran into him, in the street, say, Mitya had noticed that he frowned and only bowed out of politeness. His acquaintance with the prosecutor was less close, though he sometimes paid polite visits to the man's wife, a nervous, fanciful lady, without quite knowing why, and she always received him graciously and had, for some reason, taken an interest in him right up to the end. He hadn't had time to get to know the investigating lawyer, though he'd met him and spoken with him twice, each time about the fair sex.

"You're a highly skilled lawyer, I can see, Nikolay Parfenovitch," Mitya cried, laughing merrily, "but I can help you now. Oh, gentlemen, I feel like a new man, and don't take offense at my speaking to you so plainly and directly. I'm rather drunk too, I'll admit that frankly. I believe I've had the honor and pleasure of meeting you, Nikolay Parfenovitch, at my kinsman Miüsov's. Gentlemen, gentlemen, I don't pretend to be your equal. I understand perfectly well in what capacity I'm sitting before you. Oh, of course, there's a terrible suspicion ... hanging over me ... if Grigory has given evidence.... A terrible suspicion! It's awful, awful, I understand that! But to business, gentlemen, I'm ready, and we'll get it over with in a moment; because, listen, listen, gentlemen! Since I know I'm innocent, we can settle this in a minute. Can't we? Can't we?"
Mitya spoke a great deal, quickly, nervously, effusively, as though he genuinely took his listeners for his closest friends.
"So, for now, we'll record that you flatly deny the charge brought against you," Nikolay Parfenovitch said, impressively, and, leaning down to the secretary, dictated in an undertone what to write.

"Write it down? You want that written down? Well, write it; I consent, I give my full consent, gentlemen, only ... do you see?... Wait, wait, write this. Of disorderly conduct I am guilty, of violence against a poor old man I am guilty. And there's something else at the bottom of my heart I'm guilty of too — but that you needn't write down" (he turned suddenly to the secretary); "that's my private life, gentlemen, that's none of your concern, the bottom of my heart, I mean.... But of my old father's murder I am not guilty. That's a wild notion. A perfectly wild notion!... I'll prove it to you, and you'll be convinced in no time.... You'll laugh, gentlemen. You'll laugh at your own suspicion!..."

"Calm yourself, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," said the investigating lawyer, clearly trying to soothe Mitya's agitation with his own composure. "Before we go further with our inquiry, I'd like, if you'll consent to answer, to hear you confirm that you disliked your father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, that you were caught up in constant disputes with him. Just a quarter of an hour ago you exclaimed that you wanted to kill him: 'I didn't kill him,' you said, 'but I wanted to.'"
"Did I say that? Ach, that may well be, gentlemen! Yes, unhappily, I did want to kill him ... many times I wanted to ... unhappily, unhappily!"
"You wanted to. Would you be willing to explain precisely what led you to such a feeling of hatred for your parent?"

"What is there to explain, gentlemen?" Mitya shrugged sullenly, looking down. "I've never hidden my feelings. The whole town knows about it — everyone in the tavern knows. Only recently I declared them in Father Zossima's very cell.... And that same evening I beat my father. I nearly killed him, and I swore, before witnesses, that I'd come back and kill him.... Oh, a thousand witnesses! I've been shouting it aloud for the last month, anyone can tell you that!... The fact stares you in the face, speaks for itself, cries out — but feelings, gentlemen, feelings are another matter entirely. You see, gentlemen" — Mitya frowned — "it seems to me you've no right to question me about feelings. I understand you're bound by your office, I understand that perfectly, but that's my own affair, my private, intimate affair — yet ... since I've never hidden my feelings before ... in the tavern, for instance, I've talked to everyone about it, so ... so I won't make a secret of it now either. You see, I understand, gentlemen, that the facts stand terribly against me in this matter. I told everyone I'd kill him, and now, suddenly, he's been killed. So it must have been me! Ha ha! I can make allowances for you, gentlemen, I can quite make allowances. I'm floored myself, because who else could have murdered him, if not me? That's what it comes down to, isn't it? If not me, who, who? Gentlemen, I want to know, I insist on knowing!" he exclaimed suddenly. "Where was he killed? How was he killed? How, and with what? Tell me," he asked quickly, looking at the two lawyers.
"We found him in his study, lying on his back on the floor, his head crushed in," said the prosecutor.
"That's horrible!" Mitya shuddered, and, resting his elbows on the table, buried his face in his right hand.
"Let's go on," Nikolay Parfenovitch put in. "So what drove you to this feeling of hatred? You've stated in public, I believe, that it was rooted in jealousy?"
"Well, yes, jealousy. And not only jealousy."
"Disputes over money?"
"Yes, over money too."
"There was a dispute, I believe, over three thousand roubles, which you claimed as part of your inheritance?"

"Three thousand! More, more," Mitya cried, heatedly, "more than six thousand, more than ten, perhaps. I told everyone so, shouted it at them. But I made up my mind to settle for three thousand. I was desperate for that three thousand ... so the bundle of notes for three thousand that I knew he kept under his pillow, ready for Grushenka, I considered simply stolen from me. Yes, gentlemen, I looked on it as mine, my own property...."
The prosecutor gave the investigating lawyer a meaningful look, and managed a sly wink at him.
"We'll come back to that subject later," the lawyer said promptly. "You'll allow us to note this point and write it down — that you regarded that money as your own property?"

"Write it down, by all means. I know that's another fact against me, but I'm not afraid of facts, and I'll bring them out against myself. Do you hear me? Do you know, gentlemen, you take me for a different kind of man than I am," he added, suddenly gloomy, dejected. "You're dealing with a man of honor, a man of the highest honor — above all, don't lose sight of that — a man who's done plenty of vile things, but who's always been, and still is, honorable at bottom, in his inner being. I don't know how to put it. That's exactly what's made my whole life wretched, that I longed to be honorable, that I was, so to speak, a martyr to a sense of honor, hunting for it with a lantern, Diogenes' lantern, and yet all my life I've been doing filthy things, like all of us, gentlemen ... that is, like me alone. That was the mistake — like me alone, me alone!... Gentlemen, my head aches..." His brows knit in pain. "You see, gentlemen, I couldn't bear the sight of him — there was something in him base, insolent, trampling on everything sacred, something mocking and irreverent, loathsome, loathsome. But now that he's dead, I feel differently."
"How do you mean?"
"I don't feel differently, exactly, but I wish I hadn't hated him so much."
"You feel penitent?"
"No, not penitent, don't write that down. I'm not much good myself, I'm nothing beautiful to look at, so I had no right to find him repulsive. That's what I mean. Write that down, if you like."
Saying this, Mitya grew very mournful. He'd been growing gloomier and gloomier as the inquiry went on.

At that moment another unexpected scene unfolded. Though Grushenka had been removed, she hadn't been taken far — only to the room two doors down from the blue room where the examination was underway. It was a small room with one window, just beyond the large room where they'd danced and feasted so lavishly. She sat there with no one but Maximov beside her, terribly downcast, terribly frightened, clinging to her side as though for safety. At their door stood one of the peasants with a metal plate on his chest. Grushenka was crying, and suddenly her grief overwhelmed her — she jumped up, flung her arms out, and, with a loud wail of sorrow, rushed out of the room toward him, toward her Mitya, so suddenly that no one had time to stop her. Mitya, hearing her cry, trembled, sprang up, and with a shout rushed headlong to meet her, not knowing what he was doing. But they weren't allowed to reach each other, though they saw one another. He was seized by the arms. He struggled, tried to tear himself free. It took three or four men to hold him. She was seized too, and he saw her stretching her arms out to him, crying aloud as they carried her away. When it was over, he came back to himself, sitting in the same spot as before, across from the investigating lawyer, and crying out to them:
"What do you want with her? Why are you tormenting her? She's done nothing, nothing!..."
The lawyers tried to calm him down. About ten minutes passed like this. At last Mihail Makarovitch, who'd been out of the room, hurried back in and said, loudly and excitedly, to the prosecutor:
"She's been taken away, she's downstairs. Will you allow me, gentlemen, to say one word to this unhappy man? In your presence, gentlemen, in your presence."
"By all means, Mihail Makarovitch," the investigating lawyer answered. "In this case, we have no objection."

"Listen, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, my dear fellow," the police captain began, his excited face showing warm, almost fatherly, feeling toward the unlucky prisoner. "I took your Agrafena Alexandrovna downstairs myself, and left her in the care of the landlord's daughters, and that old fellow Maximov's staying with her the whole time. And I comforted her, do you hear? I comforted her and calmed her down. I made it clear to her that you need to clear your name, so she mustn't get in your way, mustn't weigh you down, or you might lose your head and say the wrong thing in your testimony. I talked it all through with her, and she understood. She's a sensible girl, my boy, a good-hearted girl — she'd have kissed my old hands, begging me to help you. She sent me herself to tell you not to worry about her. And now I must go, my dear fellow, I must go and tell her that you're calm and at peace about her. So you must be calm, do you understand? I was unfair to her; she's a Christian soul, gentlemen, yes, I tell you, she's a gentle soul, not to blame for anything. So what shall I tell her, Dmitri Fyodorovitch? Will you sit quietly, or not?"

The good-natured police captain said a great deal that was highly irregular, but Grushenka's suffering — a fellow creature's suffering — touched his kindly heart, and tears stood in his eyes. Mitya jumped up and rushed toward him.

"Forgive me, gentlemen, oh, allow me, allow me!" he cried. "You have the heart of an angel, an angel, Mihail Makarovitch, I thank you for her sake. I will, I will be calm, cheerful even. Tell her, out of the kindness of your heart, that I'm cheerful, quite cheerful, that I'll be laughing in a moment, knowing she has a guardian angel like you. I'll be done with all this soon, and the moment I'm free, I'll go to her, she'll see, let her wait. Gentlemen," he said, turning to the two lawyers, "now I'll open my whole soul to you; I'll pour it all out. We'll finish this off directly, finish it off cheerfully. We'll laugh about it in the end, won't we? But, gentlemen, that woman is the queen of my heart. Oh, let me tell you that. That much I'll tell you right now.... I can see I'm among honorable men. She is my light, she is my holy one, and if only you knew! Did you hear her cry, 'I'll go to death with you'? And what have I, a penniless beggar, ever done for her? Why such love for me? How can a clumsy, ugly brute like me, with this ugly face of mine, deserve love like that, love that would send her into exile with me? And how she threw herself at your feet for my sake, just now!... and yet she's proud, and she's done nothing wrong! How can I help adoring her, how can I help crying out and rushing to her, the way I did just now? Gentlemen, forgive me! But now, now I'm comforted."

And he sank back into his chair and, covering his face with his hands, burst into tears. But they were happy tears. He recovered himself at once. The old police captain looked well pleased, and so did the lawyers. They sensed the examination had moved into a new phase. When the police captain left the room, Mitya was positively cheerful.

"Now, gentlemen, I'm at your disposal, entirely at your disposal. And if it weren't for all these trivial details, we'd understand one another in a minute. There I go again, on about details. I'm at your disposal, gentlemen, but I'll say this: we must trust one another, you in me and I in you, or there'll be no end to it. I say this for your own good. To business, gentlemen, to business, and don't go digging around in my soul; don't badger me over trifles, just ask me about the facts, about what matters, and I'll satisfy you at once. And damn the details!"
So spoke Mitya. The interrogation began again.

title: IV. The Second Ordeal
paragraphs: "You have no idea how much you encourage us, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, with your readiness to answer," said Nikolay Parfenovitch, looking animated, obvious satisfaction shining in his prominent, near-sighted, light-gray eyes, from which he'd removed his spectacles a moment before. "And your remark about mutual confidence is a very fair one — without it, it's sometimes downright impossible to get anywhere in cases of such importance, when the accused genuinely hopes and wants to defend himself and is in a position to do so. For our part, we'll do everything in our power, and you can see for yourself how we're conducting the case. You approve, Ippolit Kirillovitch?" He turned to the prosecutor.
"Oh, undoubtedly," the prosecutor replied. His tone was rather cool, compared to Nikolay Parfenovitch's enthusiasm.

I'll note, once and for all, that Nikolay Parfenovitch, who'd arrived among us only recently, had felt marked respect for Ippolit Kirillovitch, our prosecutor, from the very start, and had become almost his closest friend. He was nearly the only person who put unquestioning faith in Ippolit Kirillovitch's extraordinary gifts as a psychologist and orator, and in the justice of his grievances. He'd heard of him back in Petersburg. And, for his part, young Nikolay Parfenovitch was the one person in the whole world our "unappreciated" prosecutor genuinely liked. On the road to Mokroe they'd had time to reach an understanding about the present case. And now, sitting at the table, the sharp-witted junior man caught and read every signal from his senior colleague's face — a half-word, a glance, a wink.
"Gentlemen, just let me tell my own story and don't break in with trivial questions, and I'll tell you everything in no time," Mitya said, excitedly.

"Excellent! Thank you. But before we go on to hear your account, will you allow me to ask about one more small fact of considerable interest to us? I mean the ten roubles you borrowed yesterday, around five o'clock, against your pistols, from your friend Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin."
"I pawned them, gentlemen. Pawned them for ten roubles. What else is there to say? That's all there is to it. As soon as I got back to town, I pawned them."
"You got back to town? So you'd been out of town?"
"Yes, I went off forty versts into the countryside. Didn't you know that?"
The prosecutor and Nikolay Parfenovitch exchanged glances.

"Well, how would it be if you began your account with a systematic description of everything you did yesterday, starting from the morning? Allow us, for instance, to ask why you were out of town, and exactly when you left and when you returned — all those facts."

"You should have asked me that way from the start," cried Mitya, laughing aloud, "and, if you like, let's not even start from yesterday, but from the morning of the day before; then you'll understand how, why, and where I went. Two days ago, gentlemen, I went to see a merchant here in town, a man named Samsonov, to borrow three thousand roubles from him against solid security. It was urgent, gentlemen, a sudden necessity."
"Allow me to interrupt," the prosecutor put in, politely. "Why were you in such urgent need of exactly that sum — three thousand?"

"Oh, gentlemen, you don't need to go into the how, the when, the why, and why exactly that much money and not some other amount, and all that rigmarole. Why, it would run to three volumes, and then you'd need an epilogue on top of it!"
Mitya said all this with the good-natured but impatient familiarity of a man eager to tell the whole truth and full of the best intentions.

"Gentlemen!" — he corrected himself hastily — "don't be annoyed at my restlessness, I ask you again. Believe me once more, I hold you in the greatest respect and understand the actual state of affairs. Don't think I'm drunk. I'm quite sober now. And besides, being drunk wouldn't be any obstacle. With me, you know, it's like the saying goes: 'Sober, he's a fool; drunk, he's a wise man.' Ha ha! But I see, gentlemen, it's not really proper to make jokes with you before we've had our talk out, I mean. And I've got my own dignity to maintain, too. I understand the difference between us perfectly well, for the moment. I am, after all, in the position of a criminal, and so, far from being your equal. And it's your job to keep an eye on me. I can't expect you to pat me on the head for what I did to Grigory, since one can't go cracking old men's skulls without consequences. I suppose you'll lock me away for that — six months, maybe a year, in a house of correction. I don't know what the sentence is — but it won't cost me my rank, my title, will it? So you see, gentlemen, I understand the distinction between us.... But you have to admit, you could confound God Himself with questions like this. 'How did you step? Where did you step? When did you step? And on what did you step?' I'll get all muddled if you keep on like this, and you'll hold it all against me. And what will that lead to? Nothing! And even if what I'm saying now is nonsense, let me finish, and you, gentlemen, being men of honor and refinement, will forgive me! Let me finish by asking you, gentlemen, to drop that standard method of questioning — I mean, starting off with some miserable trifle, how I got up, what I had for breakfast, how I spat, and where I spat, distracting the criminal's attention that way, and then suddenly hitting him with a crushing question: 'Whom did you murder? Whom did you rob?' Ha ha! That's your regulation trick, that's where all your cunning comes in. You can catch peasants off guard that way, but not me. I know the tricks. I've been in the service myself. Ha ha ha! You're not angry, gentlemen? You'll forgive my impertinence?" he cried, looking at them with a good humor that was almost startling. "It's only Mitya Karamazov, after all, so you can let it slide. It would be unforgivable in a sensible man; but you can forgive it in Mitya. Ha ha!"

Nikolay Parfenovitch listened, and laughed too. Though the prosecutor didn't laugh, he kept his eyes fixed sharply on Mitya, as though anxious not to miss the smallest syllable, the slightest movement, the tiniest twitch of a feature.

"That's exactly how we've treated you from the start," said Nikolay Parfenovitch, still laughing. "We haven't tried to throw you off by asking how you got up in the morning or what you had for breakfast. We began, in fact, with the most important questions."

"I understand. I noticed it and appreciated it, and I appreciate your kindness to me now even more, an unprecedented kindness, worthy of your noble hearts. The three of us here are gentlemen, so let everything proceed on a footing of mutual trust, between educated, well-bred people, bound together by the common ties of noble birth and honor. In any case, allow me to regard you as my best friends at this moment in my life — this moment when my honor is under attack. That's no offense to you, gentlemen, is it?"
"Quite the opposite. You've put that beautifully, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," Nikolay Parfenovitch answered, with dignified approval.
"And enough of those trivial questions, gentlemen, all those tricky little questions!" Mitya cried, enthusiastically. "Or there'll simply be no telling where we'll end up! Isn't that so?"

"I'll follow your sensible advice entirely," the prosecutor put in, addressing Mitya. "I don't withdraw my question, though. It's now vitally important for us to know exactly why you needed that sum — precisely three thousand."
"Why I needed it?... Oh, this and that.... Well, it was to pay off a debt."
"A debt to whom?"

"That I flatly refuse to answer, gentlemen. Not because I couldn't, or wouldn't dare, or because it would harm me, since it's really a paltry, thoroughly trivial matter — but I won't, on principle: that's my private life, and I won't allow anyone to intrude on my private life. That's my principle. Your question has no bearing on the case, and whatever has nothing to do with the case is my own affair. I wanted to pay a debt. A debt of honor. But to whom, I won't say."
"Allow me to note that down," said the prosecutor.
"By all means. Write down that I won't say, that I won't. Write that I'd consider it dishonorable to say. Ech, go ahead and write it; you've got nothing better to do with your time."

"Allow me to caution you, sir, and remind you once more, in case you're unaware," the prosecutor began, with a peculiar, stern weight, "that you have every right not to answer the questions put to you now, and that we, for our part, have no right to force an answer out of you if you decline to give one, for whatever reason. That's entirely your own decision to make. But it is our duty, on the other hand, in cases like this one, to explain and lay before you just how much harm you'll do yourself by refusing to give this or that piece of testimony. After which I'll ask you to continue."
"Gentlemen, I'm not angry ... I ..." Mitya muttered, in a rather flustered tone. "Well, gentlemen, you see, that Samsonov I went to see then ..."

We won't, of course, reproduce his account of what the reader already knows. Mitya was impatiently anxious not to leave out the smallest detail. At the same time, he was in a hurry to get it over with. But since his testimony was being written down as he gave it, they had to keep interrupting him. Mitya disliked this, but put up with it; he grew irritated, though still good-humoredly. He did, it's true, exclaim now and then, "Gentlemen, that's enough to try an angel's patience!" Or, "Gentlemen, it does you no good to irritate me."

But even with these exclamations, he kept up, for a time, his genially expansive mood. So he told them how Samsonov had made a fool of him two days before. (He'd fully realized by now that he'd been fooled.) The lawyers found the sale of his watch for six roubles, to raise money for the trip, entirely new to them. It interested them at once, and, to Mitya's intense indignation, they even thought it necessary to write it down as secondary confirmation that he'd been all but penniless at the time. Little by little Mitya began growing surly. Then, having described his trip to see Lyagavy, the night spent in the stifling hut, and so on, he arrived at his return to town. Here, without being pressed, he began giving a minute account of the agonies of jealousy he'd suffered over Grushenka.

He was heard out in silent attention. They asked particularly about his having a lookout post at Marya Kondratyevna's house, behind Fyodor Pavlovitch's garden, to keep watch on Grushenka, and about Smerdyakov bringing him information. They laid special stress on this point, and noted it down. He spoke of his jealousy warmly and at length, and though inwardly ashamed to be exposing his most intimate feelings to "public disgrace," so to speak, he evidently overcame his shame in order to tell the truth. The cold severity with which the investigating lawyer, and even more the prosecutor, stared intently at him as he told his story eventually left him considerably unsettled.

"That boy, Nikolay Parfenovitch, to whom I was talking nonsense about women only a few days ago, and that sickly prosecutor — they're not worth telling this to," he reflected, mournfully. "It's disgraceful. 'Be patient, be humble, hold thy peace.'" He closed his thoughts with that line. But he pulled himself together and went on. When he got to his visit to Madame Hohlakov, his spirits picked up, and he even tried to tell a little anecdote about the lady that had nothing to do with the case. But the investigating lawyer stopped him, and politely suggested he move on to "more essential matters." At last, when he described his despair, and told them how, on leaving Madame Hohlakov's, he'd thought he'd "get three thousand if he had to kill someone to do it," they stopped him again and noted down that he'd "intended to kill someone." Mitya let them write it without protest. At last he reached the point in his story where he learned that Grushenka had deceived him, and had left Samsonov's the moment he departed, though she'd told him she'd stay there until midnight.

"If I didn't kill Fenya right then, gentlemen, it was only because I didn't have time," burst out of him suddenly, at that point in his story. That, too, was carefully written down. Mitya waited, gloomy, and was starting to tell how he'd run into his father's garden when the investigating lawyer suddenly stopped him, and, opening the large portfolio lying on the sofa beside him, brought out the brass pestle.
"Do you recognize this object?" he asked, showing it to Mitya.
"Oh, yes," he laughed, gloomily. "Of course I recognize it. Let me have a look.... Damn it, never mind!"
"You forgot to mention it," the investigating lawyer observed.
"Hang it all, I wouldn't have hidden it from you. Do you think I could have managed without it? It just slipped my mind."
"Would you be so good as to tell us exactly how you came to arm yourself with it?"
"Certainly I'll be so good, gentlemen."
And Mitya described how he'd grabbed the pestle and run.
"But what was your purpose in arming yourself with such a weapon?"
"Purpose? No purpose at all. I just grabbed it and ran off."
"What for, then, if you had no purpose?"

Mitya's temper flared. He looked hard at "the boy" and smiled, gloomy and malicious. He was growing more and more ashamed of having told "people like this" the story of his jealousy so sincerely, so openly.
"To hell with the pestle!" burst from him suddenly.
"But even so—"
"Oh, to keep off dogs.... Oh, because it was dark.... In case something came up."
"But have you ever, on other occasions, taken a weapon with you when going out, given that you're afraid of the dark?"

"Ugh, damn it all, gentlemen! There's simply no talking to you people!" cried Mitya, pushed past endurance, and, turning to the secretary, crimson with anger, he said quickly, a note of fury in his voice:

"Write down right now ... right now ... 'that I snatched up the pestle to go and kill my father ... Fyodor Pavlovitch ... by striking him on the head with it!' Well, are you satisfied now, gentlemen? Does that put your minds at ease?" he said, glaring defiantly at the two lawyers.

"We understand perfectly well that you made that statement just now out of exasperation at us, and at the questions we've been asking, which you consider trivial, even though they're actually essential," the prosecutor remarked, dryly, in reply.

"Well, upon my word, gentlemen! Yes, I took the pestle.... What does a man pick things up for, at moments like that? I don't know what for. I grabbed it and ran — that's all. As for why, gentlemen, passons — let's drop it, or I swear I won't tell you another word."

He sat with his elbows on the table and his head in his hand. He sat turned sideways to them, staring at the wall, fighting off a wave of nausea. He genuinely felt a terrible urge to stand up and declare that he wouldn't say another word, "not if you hang me for it."

"You see, gentlemen," he said at last, struggling to control himself, "you see. I listen to you, and I'm haunted by a dream.... It's a dream I have sometimes, you know.... I dream it often — always the same one ... that someone is hunting me, someone I'm terribly afraid of ... that he's hunting me in the dark, at night ... tracking me, and I hide somewhere from him, behind a door or a cupboard, hiding in some degrading way, and the worst part is, he always knows exactly where I am, but pretends not to know on purpose, just to drag out my agony, to enjoy my terror.... That's exactly what you're doing right now. It's exactly like that!"
"Is that the kind of thing you dream about?" the prosecutor asked.
"Yes, it is. Don't you want to write it down?" said Mitya, with a twisted smile.
"No, no need to write that down. But you do have some curious dreams, all the same."
"It's not a matter of dreams now, gentlemen — this is realism, this is real life! I'm a wolf, and you're the hunters. Well, hunt him down, then!"
"You're wrong to make such comparisons ..." Nikolay Parfenovitch began, with extraordinary gentleness.

"No, I'm not wrong, not in the least!" Mitya flared up again, though his outburst had clearly eased his heart. He grew more good-humored with every word. "You may not trust a criminal, or a man on trial, worn down by your questions — but an honorable man, the honorable impulses of his heart — I say that boldly! — no, that you have no right to distrust ... but—
Be silent, heart, Be patient, be humble, hold thy peace.
Well, shall I go on?" he broke off, gloomily.
"If you would be so kind," answered Nikolay Parfenovitch.

title: V. The Third Ordeal
paragraphs: Though Mitya spoke sullenly, it was clear he was trying harder than ever not to forget or leave out a single detail of his story. He told them how he'd leapt over the fence into his father's garden, how he'd approached the window, told them everything that had happened beneath it. Clearly, precisely, distinctly, he described the feelings that had tormented him during those minutes in the garden, when he'd longed so desperately to know whether Grushenka was with his father or not. But, strangely enough, both lawyers now listened with a kind of grim reserve, looking at him coldly, asking few questions. Mitya couldn't read anything from their faces.
"They're angry and offended," he thought. "Well, to hell with them!"

When he described how he'd finally decided to give his father the "signal" that Grushenka had arrived, so he'd open the window, the lawyers paid no attention at all to the word "signal," as though they'd entirely missed its meaning in this context — so much so that Mitya noticed it. Coming at last to the moment when, seeing his father peering out the window, his hatred had flared up and he'd pulled the pestle from his pocket, he suddenly, almost deliberately, stopped short. He sat staring at the wall, aware that their eyes were fixed on him.
"Well?" said the investigating lawyer. "You pulled out the weapon and ... and then what happened?"
"Then? Why, then I murdered him ... struck him on the head and cracked his skull.... I suppose that's the story you've got. That's it!"
His eyes suddenly flashed. All his suppressed rage suddenly blazed up in his soul with extraordinary violence.
"Our story?" repeated Nikolay Parfenovitch. "Well — and yours?"
Mitya dropped his eyes and stayed silent a long while.

"My story, gentlemen? Well, it was like this," he began softly. "Whether it was someone's tears, or my mother praying to God, or a good angel kissing me at that instant, I don't know. But the devil was defeated. I rushed away from the window and ran for the fence. My father was startled, and for the first time saw me right then, cried out, and jumped back from the window. I remember that very clearly. I ran across the garden to the fence ... and that's where Grigory caught me, while I was sitting on the fence."
At that point he finally raised his eyes and looked at his listeners. They seemed to be watching him with perfectly unruffled attention. A kind of fit of indignation seized Mitya's soul.
"Why, you're laughing at me right now, gentlemen!" he broke off suddenly.
"What makes you say that?" Nikolay Parfenovitch observed.

"You don't believe a single word — that's why! I understand, of course, that I've reached the crucial point. The old man's lying there now with his skull broken, while I — after dramatically describing how I wanted to kill him and how I snatched up the pestle — suddenly run away from the window. A romance! Poetry! As if anyone could just take a fellow's word for it. Ha ha! You're mockers, gentlemen!"
And he swung round in his chair so hard it creaked.
"And did you notice," the prosecutor asked suddenly, as though not registering Mitya's agitation, "did you notice, when you ran from the window, whether the door into the garden was open?"
"No, it wasn't open."
"It wasn't?"
"It was shut. And who could have opened it? Bah! The door. Wait a moment!" he seemed suddenly struck by a thought, and almost with a start:
"Wait — did you find the door open?"
"Yes, it was open."
"Then who could have opened it, if not one of you?" cried Mitya, greatly astonished.

"The door stood open, and your father's killer undoubtedly went in through that door, and, having committed the crime, went out again the same way," the prosecutor pronounced deliberately, as though chiseling out each word one by one. "That's perfectly clear. The murder was committed inside the room, not through the window — that's beyond doubt from the examination that's been carried out, from the position of the body, from everything. There's no question about that fact."
Mitya was utterly dumbfounded.

"But that's absolutely impossible!" he cried, completely at a loss. "I ... I didn't go in.... I'm telling you positively, definitely, the door was shut the whole time I was in the garden, and when I ran out of the garden too. I only stood at the window and saw him through it. That's all, that's all.... I remember it down to the last minute. And even if I didn't remember, it would still be true. I know it, because no one knew the signals except Smerdyakov, me, and the dead man. And he wouldn't have opened that door to anyone on earth without the signal."

"Signals? What signals?" the prosecutor asked, with a greedy, almost hysterical, curiosity. He instantly dropped every trace of his reserve and dignity. He asked the question with a kind of cringing timidity. He sensed an important fact he'd known nothing about, and was already dreading that Mitya might refuse to disclose it.

"So you didn't know!" Mitya winked at him, with a malicious, mocking smile. "And what if I don't tell you? Who could you possibly find out from? No one knew about the signals except my father, Smerdyakov, and me — that's all. Heaven knew too, but Heaven won't tell you. Still, it's an interesting fact. No telling what you might build on it. Ha ha! Take heart, gentlemen, I'll reveal it. You've got some foolish notion in your hearts. You don't know the man you're dealing with! You're dealing with a prisoner who gives evidence against himself, to his own detriment! Yes, because I'm a man of honor, and you — are not."

The prosecutor swallowed this without a word. He was trembling with impatience to hear the new fact. Minutely, at length, Mitya told them everything about the signals Fyodor Pavlovitch had devised for Smerdyakov. He told them exactly what each tap on the window meant, tapped the signals out on the table, and when Nikolay Parfenovitch asked whether he supposed he, Mitya, had tapped the signal for "Grushenka has come" when he knocked at his father's window, he answered flatly that yes, he had tapped that very signal, "Grushenka has come."
"So now you can build your tower," Mitya broke off, and again turned away from them with contempt.
"So no one knew of the signals besides your late father, you, and the valet Smerdyakov? No one else?" Nikolay Parfenovitch asked once more.
"Yes. The valet Smerdyakov, and Heaven. Write down about Heaven. That might come in useful. Besides, you'll need God yourselves, before this is over."
And they had, of course, already begun writing it down. But as they wrote, the prosecutor suddenly said, as though hitting on a new idea:

"But if Smerdyakov also knew about these signals, and you flatly deny any responsibility for your father's death, isn't it possible he was the one who tapped the agreed signal, got your father to open the door to him, and then ... committed the crime?"
Mitya turned on him a look of deep irony and intense hatred. His silent stare went on so long it made the prosecutor blink.

"You've caught the fox again," Mitya finally remarked; "you've got the beast by the tail. Ha ha! I see right through you, Mr. Prosecutor. You thought, of course, that I'd jump at that, snatch up your prompt, and shout at the top of my lungs, 'Aie, it's Smerdyakov! He's the murderer!' Admit that's what you thought. Admit it, and I'll go on."
But the prosecutor didn't admit it. He held his tongue and waited.
"You're mistaken. I'm not going to shout 'It's Smerdyakov,'" said Mitya.
"And you don't even suspect him?"
"Why, do you suspect him?"
"He's under suspicion too."
Mitya fixed his eyes on the floor.

"Joking aside," he brought out, gloomily. "Listen. From the very start, almost from the moment I ran out to you from behind the curtain, the thought of Smerdyakov has been in my mind. I've been sitting here shouting that I'm innocent, and thinking, the whole time, 'Smerdyakov!' I can't get him out of my head. In fact, I thought of Smerdyakov just now too; but only for a second. Almost right away I thought, 'No, it's not Smerdyakov.' It's not his doing, gentlemen."
"In that case, is there anyone else you suspect?" Nikolay Parfenovitch asked, cautiously.
"I don't know who it could be — whether it's the hand of Heaven or of Satan, but ... not Smerdyakov," Mitya bit off, with decision.
"But what makes you say so, so confidently, so emphatically, that it's not him?"

"From my own conviction — my own impression. Because Smerdyakov is a man of the most abject character, and a coward. He's not just a coward, he's the sum total of all the cowardice in the world walking around on two legs. He has the heart of a chicken. Whenever he talked to me, he was always trembling, afraid I'd kill him, though I never once raised a hand against him. He fell at my feet and blubbered; he's literally kissed these very boots, begging me 'not to frighten him.' Do you hear that? 'Not to frighten him.' What a thing to say! Why, I even offered him money. He's a sniveling chicken — sickly, epileptic, feeble-minded — an eight-year-old child could thrash him. He hasn't got a character worth mentioning. It's not Smerdyakov, gentlemen. He doesn't care for money; he wouldn't even take gifts from me. Besides, what motive would he have to murder the old man? Why, he's very likely his son, you know — his natural son. Did you know that?"
"We've heard that story. But you're your father's son too, you know — and yet you yourself told everyone you meant to murder him."

"That's a low blow! And a nasty, mean one too! But I'm not afraid! Oh, gentlemen, isn't it rather base of you to say that to my face? It's base, because I told you that myself. I not only wanted to murder him, I might have done it. And what's more, I went out of my way to tell you, unprompted, that I very nearly murdered him. But, you see, I didn't murder him; you see, my guardian angel saved me — that's what you haven't taken into account. And that's exactly why it's base of you to say it. Because I didn't kill him, I didn't kill him! Do you hear me — I did not kill him."
He was nearly choking. He hadn't been so moved at any point during the whole interrogation.
"And what has he told you, gentlemen — Smerdyakov, I mean?" he added suddenly, after a pause. "May I ask that?"

"You may ask any question," the prosecutor replied, with cold severity, "any question relating to the facts of the case, and we are, I repeat, obligated to answer every inquiry you make. We found the servant Smerdyakov, whom you're asking about, lying unconscious in his bed, in an epileptic fit of extreme severity, which had apparently recurred perhaps ten times over. The doctor who was with us told us, after examining him, that he may not survive the night."
"Well, if that's so, the devil himself must have killed him," burst suddenly from Mitya, as if until that very moment he'd still been asking himself: "Was it Smerdyakov, or not?"
"We'll come back to this later," Nikolay Parfenovitch decided. "Now, would you care to continue your statement?"

Mitya asked for a rest. His request was politely granted. After resting, he went on with his story. But he was plainly depressed. He was exhausted, humiliated, morally shaken. To make matters worse, the prosecutor seemed to be deliberately needling him with irritating interruptions over "trivial points." Mitya had barely finished describing how, sitting astride the wall, he'd struck Grigory on the head with the pestle while the old man gripped his left leg, and how he'd then jumped down to look at him, when the prosecutor stopped him to ask him to describe exactly how he'd been sitting on the wall. Mitya was taken aback.
"Oh, I was sitting like this, straddling it, one leg on each side of the wall."
"And the pestle?"
"The pestle was in my hand."
"Not in your pocket? Do you remember that precisely? Was it a hard blow you gave him?"
"It must have been a hard one. But why do you ask?"
"Would you mind sitting on the chair the way you sat on the wall then, and showing us exactly how you moved your arm, and in which direction?"
"You're making fun of me, aren't you?" Mitya asked, looking haughtily at the man; but the other didn't flinch.
Mitya turned abruptly, straddled the chair, and swung his arm.
"This is how I struck him! This is how I knocked him down! What more do you want?"
"Thank you. May I trouble you now to explain why you jumped down, for what purpose, and what you intended?"
"Oh, hang it!... I jumped down to look at the man I'd hurt ... I don't know what for!"
"Even though you were so agitated and were running away?"
"Yes, even though I was agitated and running away."
"You wanted to help him?"
"Help!... Yes, maybe I did want to help him.... I don't remember."
"You don't remember? So you weren't quite aware of what you were doing?"
"Not at all. I remember everything — every detail. I jumped down to look at him, and wiped his face with my handkerchief."
"We've seen your handkerchief. Were you hoping to revive him?"
"I don't know whether I hoped that. I simply wanted to be sure whether he was alive or not."
"Ah! You wanted to be sure? Well, and then?"
"I'm no doctor. I couldn't tell. I ran off thinking I'd killed him. And now he's recovered."
"Excellent," the prosecutor remarked. "Thank you. That's all I wanted. Please, go on."

Alas, it never crossed Mitya's mind to tell them — though he remembered it perfectly — that he'd jumped back out of pity, and, standing over the fallen man, had even murmured a few words of regret: "You've come to grief, old man — there's no help for it now. Well, there you must lie."

The prosecutor could draw only one conclusion: that the man had jumped back "at such a moment, in such agitation, for the sole purpose of determining whether the only witness to his crime was dead; that he must therefore have been a man of considerable strength, coolness, decisiveness, and foresight, even in a moment like that" ... and so on. The prosecutor was satisfied: "I've provoked the excitable fellow with 'trivialities,' and he's said more than he meant to."
With visible effort, Mitya went on. But this time Nikolay Parfenovitch cut him off almost immediately.
"How is it you came running to the servant, Fedosya Markovna, with your hands so thoroughly covered in blood, and, it seems, your face too?"
"Why, I didn't notice the blood at all, at the time," Mitya answered.
"That's entirely plausible. It happens sometimes." The prosecutor exchanged glances with Nikolay Parfenovitch.
"I simply didn't notice. You're quite right about that, Prosecutor," Mitya suddenly agreed.

Next came the account of Mitya's sudden resolve to "step aside" and clear the way for their happiness. But he couldn't bring himself to open his heart to them the way he had before, to talk to them about "the queen of his soul." He didn't like speaking of her in front of these cold men "fastening on him like bugs." So, in response to their repeated questions, he answered briefly and curtly:

"Well, I made up my mind to kill myself. What did I have left to live for? That question stared me right in the face. Her first, rightful lover had come back — the man who'd wronged her, but who'd hurried back to offer his love again, after five years, and make up for the wrong by marrying her.... So I knew it was all over for me.... And behind me, disgrace, and that blood — Grigory's.... What did I have to live for? So I went to redeem the pistols I'd pawned, to load them and put a bullet through my brain the next morning."
"And a grand feast the night before?"

"Yes, a grand feast the night before. Damn it all, gentlemen! Do get on and finish it. I meant to shoot myself not far from here, past the village, and I'd planned to do it at five in the morning. And I already had a note in my pocket. I wrote it at Perhotin's, while I loaded my pistols. Here's the letter. Read it! I'm not telling you this for your sake," he added, contemptuously. He pulled it from his waistcoat pocket and tossed it on the table. The lawyers read it with curiosity and, as usual, added it to the papers relating to the case.
"And you never even thought of washing your hands at Perhotin's? You weren't afraid of arousing suspicion?"

"What suspicion? Suspicion or no suspicion, I'd have galloped here just the same, and shot myself at five o'clock, and you wouldn't have gotten here in time to do a thing about it. If it hadn't been for what happened to my father, you'd have known nothing about any of this, and never come here at all. Oh, it's the devil's doing. It was the devil who murdered father, and it was through the devil that you found out so quickly. How did you manage to get here so fast? It's marvelous, like a dream!"

"Mr. Perhotin informed us that when you came to him, you were holding in your hands ... your blood-stained hands ... your money ... a great deal of money ... a bundle of hundred-rouble notes, and that his houseboy saw it too."
"That's true, gentlemen. I remember it was so."

"Now, one small point comes up. Can you tell us," Nikolay Parfenovitch began, with extreme gentleness, "where you got hold of so much money, all at once, when the facts, the timeline, show that you hadn't been home?"
The prosecutor's brows drew together at this question being asked so plainly, but he didn't interrupt Nikolay Parfenovitch.
"No, I didn't go home," Mitya answered, seemingly perfectly composed, but staring at the floor.

"Allow me, then, to repeat my question," Nikolay Parfenovitch went on, as though inching up to the subject. "Where were you able to get such a sum, all at once, when, by your own admission, at five o'clock that same day you were—"

"I needed ten roubles and pawned my pistols with Perhotin, and then went to Madame Hohlakov to borrow three thousand, which she refused, and so on, and all the rest of it," Mitya cut in sharply. "Yes, gentlemen, I needed it badly, and suddenly thousands turned up, eh? Do you know, gentlemen, you're both worried right now, 'What if he won't tell us where he got it?' That's exactly how it is. I'm not going to tell you, gentlemen. You've guessed right. You'll never find out," said Mitya, chipping off each word with extraordinary determination. The lawyers were quiet for a moment.
"You must understand, Mr. Karamazov, that it's of vital importance for us to know," said Nikolay Parfenovitch, softly, smoothly.
"I understand; but I still won't tell you."

The prosecutor stepped in as well, again reminding the prisoner that he was free to refuse to answer questions, if he judged it in his own interest, and so on. But given the harm he might do himself by his silence, especially in a case of such importance as—

"And so on, gentlemen, and so on. Enough! I've heard that speech before," Mitya broke in again. "I can see perfectly well how important it is, and that this is the crux of the matter, and still I won't say."
"What is it to us? It's not our concern, it's yours. You're the one doing yourself harm," Nikolay Parfenovitch observed, nervously.

"You see, gentlemen, joking aside" — Mitya raised his eyes and looked steadily at both of them — "I had a feeling from the very start we'd butt heads at this exact point. But at first, when I began giving my evidence, it was all still far off, misty; it was all still drifting, and I was simple enough to start out on the assumption that there was mutual trust between us. Now I can see for myself that such trust is out of the question, because either way we were bound to hit this cursed stumbling block. And now we've hit it! It's impossible, and that's the end of it! But I don't blame you. You can't just take it all on my word alone. I understand that, of course."
He lapsed into gloomy silence.

"Without giving up your resolve to stay silent on the main point, could you at least give us some small hint as to the nature of the motives strong enough to make you refuse to answer, at a moment so full of danger for you?"
Mitya smiled mournfully, almost dreamily.

"I'm a good deal more good-natured than you think, gentlemen. I'll tell you why, and give you that hint, even though you don't deserve it. I won't speak of that, gentlemen, because it would stain my honor. The answer to where I got the money would expose me to far greater disgrace than murdering and robbing my father, if I'd actually murdered and robbed him. That's why I can't tell you. I can't, for fear of the disgrace. What, gentlemen, are you going to write that down too?"
"Yes, we'll write it down," Nikolay Parfenovitch said, with a slight lisp.

"You shouldn't write down that bit about 'disgrace.' I only told you that out of the goodness of my heart. I didn't have to tell you at all. I made you a gift of it, so to speak, and you pounce on it right away. Oh, well, write — write whatever you like," he concluded, with scornful disgust. "I'm not afraid of you, and I can still hold my head up in front of you."
"And can't you tell us the nature of that disgrace?" Nikolay Parfenovitch ventured.
The prosecutor scowled darkly.

"No, no, c'est fini — it's finished, don't trouble yourselves. It's not worth soiling one's hands over. I've soiled myself enough already, thanks to you. You're not worth it — no one is.... Enough, gentlemen. I'm done."
This was said too decisively. Nikolay Parfenovitch didn't press further, but he could see from Ippolit Kirillovitch's eyes that the man hadn't given up hope.
"Can you not at least tell us what sum you had in hand when you walked into Mr. Perhotin's — how many roubles, exactly?"
"I can't tell you that."
"You told Mr. Perhotin, I believe, that you'd received three thousand from Madame Hohlakov."
"Maybe I did. Enough, gentlemen. I won't say how much I had."
"Would you be so good, then, as to tell us how you got here, and what you've done since you arrived?"
"Oh! You could just ask the people here about that. But I'll tell you, if you like."

He went on to do so, but we won't repeat his account. He told it dryly and curtly. Of the raptures of his love he said nothing, but told them he'd abandoned his plan to shoot himself, due to "new developments." He told the story without going into motives or detail. And this time the lawyers didn't press him much. It was clear there was nothing here of essential interest to them.

"We'll verify all of that. We'll return to it during the questioning of the witnesses, which will of course take place in your presence," Nikolay Parfenovitch said, in conclusion. "And now allow me to ask you to place on the table everything in your possession, especially all the money you still have on you."

"My money, gentlemen? Certainly. I understand that's necessary. I'm honestly surprised you hadn't asked about it sooner. True, I couldn't have gone anywhere. I've been sitting right here in plain sight. But here's my money — count it, take it. That's everything, I think."

He turned out all his pockets; even the small change — two twenty-kopeck coins — he pulled from his waistcoat pocket. They counted the money, which came to eight hundred and thirty-six roubles and forty kopecks.
"And that's everything?" the investigating lawyer asked.
"Yes."
"You stated just now in your testimony that you spent three hundred roubles at Plotnikov's. You gave Perhotin ten, your driver twenty, you lost two hundred here, then...."
Nikolay Parfenovitch worked it all out. Mitya helped him along readily. They recalled every last kopeck and worked it into the tally. Nikolay Parfenovitch quickly added up the total.
"With this eight hundred, you must have started out with about fifteen hundred?"
"I suppose so," Mitya snapped.
"How is it that everyone insists there was much more?"
"Let them insist."
"But you said so yourself."
"Yes, I did too."

"We'll compare all this against the testimony of other people not yet questioned. Don't worry about your money. It will be properly looked after and put at your disposal once ... whatever's beginning ... concludes, if it turns out, or is shown, that you have an undisputed right to it. Well, and now...."
Nikolay Parfenovitch suddenly stood up and informed Mitya, firmly, that it was his duty and obligation to carry out a thorough, detailed search "of your clothing, and everything else...."
"By all means, gentlemen. I'll turn out all my pockets, if you like."
And he did, in fact, start emptying his pockets.
"It will be necessary to remove your clothing as well."
"What! Undress? Ugh! Damn it! Can't you just search me as I am? Isn't that possible?"
"That's simply not possible, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You must remove your clothing."
"As you like," Mitya submitted, gloomily. "Only, please, not here — behind the curtains. Who'll be searching them?"
"Behind the curtains, of course."
Nikolay Parfenovitch inclined his head in agreement. His small face wore an air of peculiar solemnity.

title: VI. The Prosecutor Catches Mitya
paragraphs: What followed was something utterly unexpected, astonishing to Mitya. Not even a minute before, he could never have imagined that anyone would treat him, Mitya Karamazov, this way. Worst of all, there was something humiliating in it, and on their side something "superior and scornful." Taking off his coat was nothing, but he was asked to undress further — or rather, not asked, but "ordered," as he understood perfectly well. Out of pride and contempt, he complied without a word. Several peasants had come along with the lawyers and stayed on the same side of the curtain. "In case force is needed," Mitya thought, "and maybe for some other reason too."

"Well, do I have to take off my shirt too?" he asked sharply, but Nikolay Parfenovitch didn't answer. He was busy with the prosecutor, examining the coat, the trousers, the waistcoat, and the cap, and it was clear both of them found the inspection absorbing. "They don't stand on ceremony," thought Mitya, "not even the most basic politeness."
"I'm asking you a second time — do I need to take off my shirt or not?" he said, still more sharply, more irritably.
"Don't trouble yourself. We'll tell you what to do," said Nikolay Parfenovitch, his voice downright peremptory, or so it seemed to Mitya.

Meanwhile a low-voiced consultation was going on between the two lawyers. It turned out there was a huge bloodstain on the coat, especially on the left side at the back — dried, and still stiff. There were bloodstains on the trousers too. Nikolay Parfenovitch, moreover, in front of the peasant witnesses, ran his fingers along the collar, the cuffs, and every seam of the coat and trousers, obviously searching for something — money, of course. He didn't even bother hiding from Mitya his suspicion that he was capable of sewing money into his clothes.

"He's treating me like a thief, not an officer," Mitya muttered to himself. The two of them shared their thoughts with astonishing candor. The secretary, for instance, also behind the curtain, fussing about and listening in, drew Nikolay Parfenovitch's attention to the cap, which they were also examining.

"You remember Gridyenko, the copying clerk," the secretary observed. "Last summer he collected the wages for the whole office, and claimed he'd lost the money while drunk. And where was it found? Why, in the piping of his cap, of all places. The hundred-rouble notes were rolled up small and sewn into the seam."
Both lawyers remembered the Gridyenko case perfectly well, and so set Mitya's cap aside, deciding that all his clothing needed a more thorough examination later.
"Excuse me," cried Nikolay Parfenovitch suddenly, noticing that the right cuff of Mitya's shirt was turned in and covered in blood, "excuse me, what's that, blood?"
"Yes," Mitya bit out.
"That is — whose blood? ... And why is the cuff turned in?"
Mitya told him how he'd gotten the sleeve stained with blood while tending to Grigory, and had turned it inward while washing his hands at Perhotin's.
"You'll need to remove your shirt too. It's important as material evidence."
Mitya flushed and flew into a rage.
"What, am I supposed to sit here naked?" he shouted.
"Don't trouble yourself. We'll arrange something. And in the meantime, take off your socks."
"You're not joking? Is that really necessary?" Mitya's eyes flashed.
"We're in no mood for joking," Nikolay Parfenovitch answered, sternly.

"Well, if I must—" Mitya muttered, and, sitting on the bed, took off his socks. He felt unbearably self-conscious. Everyone else was dressed, while he was bare, and strangely enough, being undressed made him feel somehow guilty in front of them, almost ready to believe himself genuinely inferior to them, that they now had every right to look down on him.

"When everyone's undressed, somehow it's not shameful, but when you're the only one, and everyone's looking, it's degrading," he kept repeating to himself, over and over. "It's like a dream — I've sometimes dreamed of being in a humiliating position like this." Taking off his socks was misery. They were filthy, and so was his underwear, and now everyone could see it. And worse still, he hated his own feet. All his life he'd thought his big toes hideous. He particularly loathed the coarse, flat, crooked nail on the right one, and now they'd all see it. The unbearable shame of it made him, at once and deliberately, rougher. He pulled off his shirt himself.
"Would you care to look anywhere else, if you're not too ashamed?"
"No, there's no need for that, at present."
"Well, am I supposed to just stand here naked, then?" he added, savagely.
"Yes, that can't be helped for now.... Kindly sit here for a while. You can wrap yourself in a quilt from the bed, and I ... I'll see to all this."

All the items were shown to the witnesses. A report of the search was drawn up, and at last Nikolay Parfenovitch went out, the clothes carried out behind him. Ippolit Kirillovitch went out too. Mitya was left alone with the peasants, who stood in silence, never taking their eyes off him. Mitya wrapped himself in the quilt. He felt cold. His bare feet stuck out, and he couldn't pull the quilt far enough to cover them. Nikolay Parfenovitch seemed to be gone a long time, "an unbearably long time." "He thinks of me as a puppy," thought Mitya, grinding his teeth. "That rotten prosecutor's gone too, no doubt full of contempt, disgusted at the sight of me naked!"

Mitya assumed, though, that his clothes would be examined and returned to him. So imagine his outrage when Nikolay Parfenovitch came back carrying entirely different clothes, brought in behind him by a peasant.

"Here's something for you to wear," he remarked, breezily, looking rather pleased with how his errand had gone. "Mr. Kalganov has kindly provided these for this unusual situation, along with a clean shirt. Fortunately he had them all in his trunk. You may keep your own socks and underclothes."
Mitya flew into a rage.
"I won't wear other people's clothes!" he shouted, menacingly. "Give me my own!"
"That's not possible!"
"Give me my own. Damn Kalganov and his clothes too!"

It took a long while before they could talk him round. But somehow they managed to calm him down. They impressed on him that his clothes, being stained with blood, had to be "included among the other material evidence," and that they "didn't even have the right to let him keep them now ... given the possible outcome of the case." Mitya finally understood this. He sank into gloomy silence and hurriedly got dressed. As he put them on, he only remarked that the clothes were much better than his old ones, and that he disliked "coming out ahead" from the exchange. The coat, besides, was "ridiculously tight. Am I meant to be dressed up like a fool ... for your amusement?"

They assured him again that he was exaggerating, that Kalganov was only slightly taller, so it would only be the trousers that might run a little long. But the coat did, in fact, turn out to be tight across the shoulders.
"Damn it all! I can barely button it," Mitya grumbled. "Be so good as to tell Mr. Kalganov, from me, that I didn't ask for his clothes, and it's not my doing that they've dressed me up like a clown."
"He understands that, and he's sorry ... I mean, not sorry to lend you the clothes, but sorry about this whole business," Nikolay Parfenovitch mumbled.
"To hell with his sorry! Well, where now? Am I to keep sitting here?"

He was asked to go back into the "other room." Mitya went in, scowling with anger, trying to avoid anyone's eyes. Dressed in someone else's clothes, he felt disgraced, even in front of the peasants, and of Trifon Borissovitch, whose face appeared for some reason in the doorway, then vanished at once. "He's come to look at me all dressed up," thought Mitya. He sat back down in the same chair as before. He had an absurd, nightmarish feeling, as though he'd lost his mind.

"Well, what now? Are you going to flog me? That's all that's left," he said, clenching his teeth, addressing the prosecutor. He wouldn't turn to Nikolay Parfenovitch, as though he scorned to speak to him.
"He examined my socks a little too closely, and turned them inside out on purpose, so everyone could see how filthy they were — the scoundrel!"
"Well, now we must move on to the questioning of witnesses," Nikolay Parfenovitch observed, as though replying to Mitya's outburst.
"Yes," said the prosecutor, thoughtfully, as though turning something over in his mind.

"We've done everything we could in your interest, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," Nikolay Parfenovitch went on, "but given your uncompromising refusal to explain to us the source of the money found on you, we find ourselves, at this moment—"
"What's that stone in your ring?" Mitya cut in suddenly, as though waking from a daydream. He pointed to one of the three large rings on Nikolay Parfenovitch's right hand.
"Ring?" Nikolay Parfenovitch repeated, surprised.
"Yes, that one ... on your middle finger, with the little veins running through it — what stone is that?" Mitya persisted, like a fretful child.
"That's a smoky topaz," said Nikolay Parfenovitch, smiling. "Would you like to see it? I'll take it off ..."

"No, don't take it off," Mitya cried furiously, suddenly snapping back to himself, angry at his own distraction. "Don't take it off ... there's no need.... Damn it!... Gentlemen, you've sullied my heart! Do you really think I'd hide it from you, if I'd actually killed my father — that I'd dodge, lie, hide myself away? No, that's not Dmitri Karamazov, he couldn't do that, and if I were guilty, I swear to you I wouldn't have waited for you to get here, or for the sunrise as I first planned — I'd have killed myself before now, without waiting for dawn! I know that about myself now. I've learned more about myself in this cursed night than in twenty years!... And would I be like this tonight, at this very moment, sitting here with you — could I talk like this, move like this, look at you, look at the world, like this, if I'd really been my father's murderer, when the mere thought of having accidentally killed Grigory gave me no peace all night — not out of fear, oh, not simply fear of your punishment! The disgrace of it! And you expect me to be open with mockers like you, who see nothing, believe in nothing, blind moles and scoffers, and confess to you some other filthy thing I've done, some other disgrace, even if it would save me from your accusation? No — better Siberia! Whoever opened that door to my father, whoever walked through it — he killed him, he robbed him. Who was it? I'm racking my brains and I can't think who. But I can tell you it wasn't Dmitri Karamazov, and that's all I can tell you, and that's enough, enough — leave me alone.... Send me into exile, punish me, but stop tormenting me. I'll say no more. Call your witnesses!"

Mitya delivered this sudden monologue as though he'd resolved to fall completely silent from here on out. The prosecutor watched him the whole time, and only once he'd stopped speaking did he remark, as though it were the most ordinary thing in the world, in the coldest, most composed tone:

"Oh, speaking of that open door you mentioned just now, we might as well tell you, in passing, about a very interesting piece of testimony, of great importance to both of us, given by Grigory, the old man you wounded. On regaining consciousness, he stated clearly and emphatically, in answer to our questions, that when, having come out onto the steps and heard a noise in the garden, he decided to go in through the little gate that stood open — before he noticed you running, as you've already told us, in the dark from the open window where you saw your father — he, Grigory, glanced to the left, and, while noticing the open window, also noticed, much closer to him, the door standing wide open — that same door you've claimed was shut the entire time you were in the garden. I won't hide from you that Grigory himself states, confidently, and testifies, that you must have run from that door, though, of course, he didn't see you do it with his own eyes, since he first spotted you some distance off in the garden, running toward the fence."
Mitya had leapt from his chair halfway through this speech.
"Nonsense!" he yelled, in a sudden frenzy. "It's a bald-faced lie. He couldn't have seen the door open, because it was shut. He's lying!"
"I consider it my duty to repeat that he's firm in his statement. He doesn't waver. He sticks to it. We've cross-examined him several times."
"Precisely. I have cross-examined him several times myself," Nikolay Parfenovitch confirmed, warmly.

"It's false, false! Either it's an attempt to slander me, or the ravings of a madman," Mitya kept shouting. "He's simply delirious, from loss of blood, from the wound. He must have imagined it, once he came to.... He's delirious."
"Yes, but he noticed the open door not once he'd come to after his injuries, but before that, as soon as he went out into the garden from the lodge."
"But it's false, it's false! It can't be! He's slandering me out of spite.... He couldn't have seen it ... I didn't come from that door," Mitya gasped.
The prosecutor turned to Nikolay Parfenovitch and said, with weight:
"Confront him with it."
"Do you recognize this object?"
Nikolay Parfenovitch laid a large, thick official envelope on the table, its three seals still unbroken. The envelope was empty, slit open at one end. Mitya stared at it, eyes wide.

"It ... it must be that envelope of my father's, the one that held the three thousand roubles ... and if it's inscribed, let me see, 'For my little chick' ... yes — three thousand!" he shouted. "You see, three thousand, do you see?"
"Of course we see. But we didn't find the money inside it. It was empty, lying on the floor by the bed, behind the screen."
For a few seconds Mitya stood as though struck by lightning.

"Gentlemen, it's Smerdyakov!" he shouted suddenly, at the top of his voice. "He's the one who murdered him! He's robbed him! No one else knew where the old man hid the envelope. It's Smerdyakov, it's obvious now!"
"But you knew about the envelope too — that it was under the pillow."

"I never knew that. I've never seen it. This is the first time I've laid eyes on it. I'd only heard of it from Smerdyakov.... He was the only one who knew where the old man kept it hidden, I didn't know ..." Mitya was completely out of breath.
"But you told us yourself that the envelope was under your late father's pillow. You specifically stated it was under the pillow — so you must have known."
"We have it written down," Nikolay Parfenovitch confirmed.

"Nonsense! It's absurd! I had no idea it was under the pillow. And maybe it wasn't under the pillow at all.... It was just a guess, that it might be under the pillow. What does Smerdyakov say? Have you asked him where it was? What does Smerdyakov say — that's the main point.... And I went out of my way to tell lies against myself.... I told you, without thinking, that it was under the pillow, and now you— Oh, you know how a man says the wrong thing without meaning to. No one knew but Smerdyakov, only Smerdyakov, no one else.... He didn't even tell me where it was! But it's his doing, his doing, there's no doubt about it, he murdered him, it's as clear as daylight now," Mitya exclaimed, more and more frantic, repeating himself incoherently, growing more exasperated and worked up by the moment. "You have to understand that, and arrest him at once.... He must have killed him while I was running away and Grigory lay unconscious, that's clear now.... He gave the signal, and father opened the door for him ... because no one but he knew the signal, and without the signal father would never have opened that door...."

"But you're forgetting the circumstance again," the prosecutor observed, still speaking with the same restraint, though with a note of triumph now, "that there was no need to give the signal at all, if the door already stood open while you were there, while you were in the garden...."
"The door, the door," Mitya muttered, and stared speechlessly at the prosecutor. He sank back into his chair, helpless. Everyone fell silent.
"Yes, the door!... It's a nightmare! God is against me!" he exclaimed, staring straight ahead, in complete stupefaction.

"Come now, you see," the prosecutor went on, with dignity, "you can judge for yourself, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. On the one hand, we have the testimony about the open door you ran out through — a fact that overwhelms you, and us. On the other hand, your baffling, persistent, one might say stubborn silence about the source of the money that appeared so suddenly in your hands, when only three hours earlier, by your own account, you were pawning your pistols for the sake of ten roubles! Given all these facts, judge for yourself. What are we to believe, and what can we rely on? And don't accuse us of being 'cold, cynical, mocking men,' incapable of believing in the generous impulses of your heart.... Try to see it from our position ..."
Mitya was agitated beyond description. He turned pale.
"Very well!" he exclaimed, suddenly. "I'll tell you my secret. I'll tell you where I got the money!... I'll expose my own shame, so I don't have to reproach myself, or you, afterward."

"And believe me, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," Nikolay Parfenovitch put in, in a voice of almost touching delight, "that any sincere and complete confession from you at this moment may, later on, weigh enormously in your favor, and may, moreover—"
But the prosecutor gave him a slight nudge under the table, and he caught himself in time. Mitya, it's true, hadn't even heard him.
