title: VII. Mitya’s Great Secret. Received With Hisses
paragraphs: "Gentlemen," he began, still just as agitated, "I want to make a full confession: that money was my own." The lawyers' faces fell. That wasn't at all what they'd expected.
"What do you mean?" Nikolay Parfenovitch faltered, "when at five o'clock that very day, by your own admission—"

"Damn five o'clock that day and my own admission! That has nothing to do with it now! That money was my own, my own — that is, stolen by me ... not mine, I mean, but stolen by me, and it was fifteen hundred roubles, and I had it on me the whole time, the whole time ..."
"But where did you get it?"

"I took it off my neck, gentlemen, off this very neck ... it was here, around my neck, sewn into a rag, and I'd had it round my neck for a long while, a month since I put it there ... to my shame and disgrace!"
"And from whom did you ... appropriate it?"
"You mean 'steal it'? Say it plainly. Yes, I consider that I effectively stole it, but if you prefer, I 'appropriated' it. I consider that I stole it. And last night I stole it once and for all."
"Last night? But you said it's been a month since you ... obtained it?..."

"Yes. But not from my father. Not from my father, don't worry. I didn't steal it from my father, but from her. Let me tell it without interruptions. It's hard enough as it is, you know. You see, a month ago, Katerina Ivanovna, formerly my betrothed, sent for me. Do you know her?"
"Yes, of course."
"I know you know her. She's a noble creature, the noblest of the noble. But she's hated me for a long time now, oh, a long time ... and hated me with good reason, good reason!"
"Katerina Ivanovna!" Nikolay Parfenovitch exclaimed, astonished. The prosecutor stared too.

"Oh, don't take her name in vain! I'm a scoundrel to drag her into this. Yes, I've seen that she's hated me ... for a long time.... From the very start, even that evening at my lodgings ... but enough, enough. You're not even worthy of knowing about that. No need for it at all.... I only need tell you that she sent for me a month ago, gave me three thousand roubles to send to her sister and another relation in Moscow (as though she couldn't have sent it herself!) and I ... it happened to be that fateful moment in my life when I ... well, in fact, when I'd just fallen in love with another woman, with her — she's sitting downstairs right now, Grushenka. I carried her off here to Mokroe then, and burned through half that cursed three thousand here in two days, but I kept the other half on me. Well, I kept that other half, that fifteen hundred, like a locket around my neck, but yesterday I undid it, and spent it. What's left of it, eight hundred roubles, is in your hands right now, Nikolay Parfenovitch. That's the change from the fifteen hundred I had yesterday."
"Excuse me. How's that? Why, when you were here a month ago you spent three thousand, not fifteen hundred — everyone knows that."
"Who knows it? Who counted the money? Did I let anyone count it?"
"Why, you told everyone yourself that you'd spent exactly three thousand."

"That's true, I did. I told the whole town so, and the whole town repeated it. And right here at Mokroe, too, everyone reckoned it was three thousand. And yet I didn't spend three thousand, only fifteen hundred. And the other fifteen hundred I sewed into a little pouch. That's how it was, gentlemen. That's where that money came from yesterday...."
"This is almost miraculous," Nikolay Parfenovitch murmured.
"Allow me to ask," the prosecutor said at last, "have you told absolutely anyone about this before now — that you had fifteen hundred left on you a month ago?"
"I told no one."
"That's strange. You mean, absolutely no one?"
"Absolutely no one. No one at all, nobody."

"What was your reason for this secrecy? What motive did you have for keeping it so hidden? To put it more precisely: you've finally told us your secret, one you yourself called so 'disgraceful,' though in reality — comparatively speaking, of course — this act, the appropriation of three thousand roubles belonging to someone else, and only temporarily, is, in my view at least, an act of great recklessness, but not so disgraceful, given your character.... Even granting it was a highly discreditable act, still, discreditable isn't 'disgraceful.'... Plenty of people have already guessed, over the past month, at Katerina Ivanovna's three thousand that you spent, and I heard the rumor myself, apart from your own confession.... Mihail Makarovitch, for instance, had heard it too, so it was scarcely even a rumor, but the talk of the whole town. There are also indications, unless I'm mistaken, that you confessed this yourself to someone — that the money was Katerina Ivanovna's — and so it strikes me as extremely surprising that until now, up to this very moment, you've made such an extraordinary secret of the fifteen hundred you claim to have set aside, apparently attaching something like sheer dread to that secret.... It's hard to believe it could have cost you such anguish, to confess a secret like that.... You just cried out, a moment ago, that Siberia would be better than confessing it ..."

The prosecutor fell silent. He was irritated. He made no attempt to hide his annoyance, which was close to anger, venting all his pent-up frustration in a disjointed, incoherent rush, without choosing his words.
"It's not the fifteen hundred that's the disgrace, it's that I set it apart from the rest of the three thousand," said Mitya, firmly.

"Why?" the prosecutor smiled, irritably. "What's disgraceful, in your view, about having set aside half the three thousand you'd discreditably — 'disgracefully,' if you prefer — appropriated? Taking the three thousand in the first place matters more than what you did with it afterward. And by the way, why did you do that — why did you set aside that half, to what purpose, for what end did you do it? Can you explain that to us?"

"Oh, gentlemen, the purpose is the whole point!" cried Mitya. "I set it aside because I was vile — that is, because I was calculating, and to be calculating in a situation like that is vile ... and that vileness has been going on a whole month."
"It's incomprehensible."

"I'm amazed at you. But let me make it clearer. Maybe it really is hard to follow. Listen closely to what I say. Suppose I appropriate three thousand entrusted to my honor, spend it on a spree — say I spend it all — and the next morning I go to her and say, 'Katya, I did wrong, I squandered your three thousand.' Well, is that right? No, it's not right — it's dishonest and cowardly, I'm an animal with no more self-control than a beast, that's so, isn't it? But even so, I'm not a thief. Not an out-and-out thief, you'll grant me that! I squandered it, but I didn't steal it. Now here's a second, somewhat better alternative: follow me carefully, or I'll get muddled again — my head's spinning — so, the second alternative: I spend only fifteen hundred of the three thousand here, that is, only half. The next day I go and bring her that other half: 'Katya, take this fifteen hundred from me, I'm a low beast, an untrustworthy scoundrel, because I've squandered half the money, and I'll squander this too, so keep it out of my reach!' Well, what about that? I'd be a beast and a scoundrel, and whatever else you like — but not a thief, not entirely a thief, or I wouldn't have brought back what was left, I'd have kept that too. She'd see at once that, since I'd brought back half, I'd pay back what I'd spent, that I'd never stop trying, that I'd work to earn it and repay it. So in that case I'd be a scoundrel, but not a thief — you can say what you like, but not a thief!"
"I grant there's a certain distinction," said the prosecutor, with a cold smile. "But it's strange that you see such a vital difference there."

"Yes, I do see a vital difference! Any man can be a scoundrel, and maybe every man is a scoundrel, but not everyone can be a thief — it takes an arch-scoundrel for that. Oh, of course, I don't know how to draw these fine distinctions properly ... but a thief is lower than a scoundrel, that's my conviction. Listen — I carry the money on me for a whole month, I may decide to give it back tomorrow, and I'm no longer a scoundrel, but I can't bring myself to do it, you see, even though I resolve to do it every single day, spurring myself on to it every day, and yet for a whole month I can't manage it, you see. Is that right, do you think — is that right?"

"Certainly, that's not right, I can understand that much, and I won't dispute it," the prosecutor answered, reservedly. "And let's drop this discussion of subtleties and distinctions, and, if you'd be so kind, get back to the point. And the point is that you still haven't told us — despite all our asking — why, in the first place, you split the money in two, squandering one half and hiding the other? What exactly did you mean to do with that hidden fifteen hundred? I press this question, Dmitri Fyodorovitch."

"Yes, of course!" cried Mitya, striking himself on the forehead. "Forgive me, I'm wearing you out and not explaining the main point, or you'd understand in a moment, because it's precisely the motive for it that's the disgrace! You see, it all came down to the old man, my late father. He was always pestering Agrafena Alexandrovna, and I was jealous; I thought at the time she was torn between him and me. So I kept thinking, every day, suppose she suddenly made up her mind, suppose she suddenly stopped tormenting me, and said to me one day, 'I love you, not him; take me to the ends of the earth.' And I'd have had only forty kopecks; how could I take her away, what could I do? Why, I'd have been ruined. You see, I didn't know her then, I didn't understand her, I thought she wanted money, and that she wouldn't forgive me my poverty. And so I fiendishly counted out half of that three thousand, and sewed it up, calculating in advance, sewed it up before I'd even gotten drunk, and once I'd sewn it up, went off to get drunk on the rest. Yes, that was low. Do you understand now?"
Both lawyers laughed out loud.
"I'd have called it sensible and even principled on your part, not to have squandered it all," Nikolay Parfenovitch chuckled. "After all, what does it amount to?"

"Why, that I stole it, that's what it amounts to! Oh, God, it horrifies me that you don't understand! Every day I had that fifteen hundred sewn up around my neck, every day, every hour, I said to myself: 'You're a thief! You're a thief!' Yes, that's why I've been so vicious this whole month, that's why I fought in the tavern, that's why I attacked my father — because I felt like a thief. I couldn't bring myself to do anything about it, I didn't even dare tell Alyosha, my own brother, about that fifteen hundred: I felt like such a scoundrel, such a common pickpocket. But, you know, while I carried it, I told myself, at the very same time, every single hour: 'No, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, you may still not be a thief.' Why? Because I might go the next day and pay Katya back that fifteen hundred. And it was only yesterday that I made up my mind to tear the amulet from my neck, on my way from Fenya's to Perhotin's. I hadn't been able to bring myself to it before that moment. And it was only once I'd torn it off that I truly became a thief, outright — a thief and a dishonest man for the rest of my life. Why? Because with that, I also destroyed my dream of going to Katya and saying, 'I'm a scoundrel, but not a thief!' Do you understand now? Do you understand?"
"What made you decide to do it yesterday?" Nikolay Parfenovitch broke in.

"Why? What a strange thing to ask. Because I'd sentenced myself to die at five o'clock this morning, right here, at dawn. I thought it made no difference whether I died a thief or a man of honor. But I see now that it's not so — it turns out it makes all the difference. Believe me, gentlemen, what tormented me most this whole night wasn't the thought that I'd killed the old servant, and was facing Siberia just when my love was finally being rewarded, when Heaven had opened up to me again. Oh, that tormented me too, but not the same way, not nearly as much as the damned awareness that I'd finally torn that cursed money off my chest and spent it, and become an outright thief! Oh, gentlemen, I tell you again, with a bleeding heart, I've learned a great deal this night. I've learned that it's not just impossible to live as a scoundrel — it's impossible to die as one either.... No, gentlemen, a man must die honest...."
Mitya was pale. His face had a haggard, exhausted look, despite his being intensely worked up.

"I'm beginning to understand you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," the prosecutor said slowly, in a soft, almost sympathetic tone. "But all of this, if you'll forgive me saying so, is a matter of nerves, in my opinion ... your overwrought nerves, that's what it is. And why, for instance, couldn't you have spared yourself nearly a month of this torment, simply by going and returning that fifteen hundred to the lady who'd entrusted it to you? And why couldn't you have explained things to her, and, given your situation, which you describe as so dire, why couldn't you have turned to the plan that would so naturally occur to anyone — that is, after honestly confessing your errors to her, why couldn't you have asked her to lend you the sum you needed, which, with her generous heart, she surely wouldn't have refused you in your distress, especially with some guarantee, or even the same kind of security you offered the merchant Samsonov and Madame Hohlakov? I take it you still regard that security as worth something?"
Mitya suddenly flushed crimson.
"Surely you don't take me for that much of an out-and-out scoundrel? You can't be serious?" he said, indignantly, looking the prosecutor straight in the face, seeming unable to believe his own ears.
"I assure you, I'm quite serious.... Why would you think otherwise?" Now it was the prosecutor's turn to be surprised.

"Oh, how vile that would have been! Gentlemen, do you know, you're torturing me! Let me tell you everything, so be it. I'll confess all my infernal wickedness, if only to put you to shame, and you'll be amazed yourselves at just how low a tangle of human passions can sink. You should know I'd already had that very plan myself, the one you just mentioned, Prosecutor! Yes, gentlemen, I too had that thought in my mind this whole past month, so that I very nearly decided to go to Katya — I was low enough for that. But to go to her, to tell her of my betrayal, and, for the sake of that very betrayal, to carry it through, to beg her — Katya — for money to fund it (to beg, do you hear, to beg), and then walk straight from her to run off with the other woman, her rival, who'd hated and insulted her — just think of it! You must be out of your mind, Prosecutor!"

"I'm not out of my mind, but I did speak hastily, without thinking ... about that feminine jealousy ... if jealousy could enter into it, as you claim ... yes, perhaps there's something to that," said the prosecutor, smiling.

"But that would have been so vile!" Mitya slammed his fist down on the table. "That would have been filthy beyond anything! Yes, do you know, she might have given me that money — yes, she would have given it, too; she'd certainly have given it, to get her revenge on me, she'd have given it to satisfy her vengeance, to show her contempt for me, because hers is an infernal nature too, and she's a woman of great wrath. And I'd have taken the money, oh, I would have taken it; I'd have taken it, and then, for the rest of my life ... oh, God! Forgive me, gentlemen, I'm making such a scene because I had that very thought in my mind so recently — just two days ago, that night I was having all that trouble with Lyagavy, and then yesterday, all day yesterday, I remember, right up until that happened ..."
"Until what happened?" Nikolay Parfenovitch put in, curious, but Mitya didn't hear him.

"I've made you a terrible confession," Mitya said, gloomily, in conclusion. "You ought to appreciate it, and more than that, you ought to respect it, because if you don't, if it leaves your souls untouched, then you simply have no respect for me at all, gentlemen, I tell you that, and I'll die of shame at having confessed it to men like you! Oh, I'll shoot myself! Yes, I see it now, I see you don't believe me. What, you want to write that down too?" he cried, dismayed.

"Yes, what you just said," Nikolay Parfenovitch said, looking at him in surprise, "that up until the last hour you were still considering going to Katerina Ivanovna to beg that sum from her.... I assure you, that's a very significant piece of testimony for us, Dmitri Fyodorovitch — for the whole case, I mean ... and especially significant for you."

"Have mercy, gentlemen!" Mitya threw up his hands. "Don't write that down, at least — have some shame. Here I've torn my own heart open in front of you, and you seize the chance and start poking at the wounds on both halves.... Oh, my God!"
In despair, he buried his face in his hands.

"Don't distress yourself so, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," the prosecutor remarked. "Everything written down will be read back to you afterward, and whatever you don't agree with, we'll change to your satisfaction. But now let me ask you one small question a second time. Has absolutely no one, no one at all, heard from you about that money you sewed up? I have to say, that's almost impossible to believe."
"No one, no one, I told you already, or you haven't understood a word of it! Leave me be!"

"Very well, this matter is bound to come to light, and there's ample time for that, but in the meantime, consider — we have perhaps a dozen witnesses that you yourself spread the story around, even shouted it nearly everywhere, about the three thousand you spent here — three thousand, not fifteen hundred. And even now, when you got hold of the money you had yesterday, you gave plenty of people to understand you'd brought three thousand with you."
"You've got not dozens, but hundreds of witnesses, two hundred witnesses, two hundred have heard it, thousands have heard it!" cried Mitya.
"Well, you see, they all testify to it. And the word all means something."
"It means nothing. I talked rubbish, and everyone started repeating it."
"But what need did you have to 'talk rubbish,' as you put it?"

"The devil knows. Bravado, maybe ... at having wasted so much money.... To try to forget the money I had sewn away, maybe ... yes, that was it ... damn it ... how many more times are you going to ask me that? Well, I told a fib, and that was that — once I'd said it, I couldn't be bothered to correct it. What does a man tell lies for, sometimes?"

"That's a very hard thing to determine, Dmitri Fyodorovitch — what makes a man tell lies," the prosecutor observed, weightily. "Tell me, though — was that 'amulet,' as you call it, around your neck, a large thing?"
"No, not large."
"How large, for instance?"
"If you fold a hundred-rouble note in half, that would be about the size."
"You'd better show us the remains of it. You must have them somewhere."
"Damnation, what nonsense! I have no idea where they are."
"But excuse me — where and when did you take it off your neck? By your own testimony, you never went home."
"On my way from Fenya's to Perhotin's, along the way, I tore it off my neck and took out the money."
"In the dark?"
"What would I need a light for? I did it with my fingers, in a minute."
"Without scissors, in the street?"
"In the marketplace, I believe it was. Why would I need scissors? It was an old rag. It tore in a minute."
"Where did you put it afterward?"
"I dropped it there."
"Where, exactly?"
"In the marketplace, in the marketplace! The devil knows exactly where. What do you need to know for?"
"That's extremely important, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. It would be material evidence in your favor. How is it you don't grasp that? Who helped you sew it up, a month ago?"
"No one helped me. I did it myself."
"Can you sew?"
"A soldier has to know how to sew. No special skill was needed for that."
"Where did you get the material — the rag you sewed the money into?"
"Are you making fun of me?"
"Not at all. And we're in no mood for jokes, Dmitri Fyodorovitch."
"I don't know where I got the rag from — somewhere or other, I suppose."
"I'd have thought you couldn't forget a thing like that."
"Upon my word, I don't remember. I might have torn a piece off some linen of mine."
"That's very interesting. We might find, tomorrow, in your lodgings, the shirt or whatever it was you tore the rag from. What sort of rag was it — cloth, or linen?"
"Heaven only knows what it was. Wait a moment.... I don't believe I tore it off anything. It was a scrap of calico.... I think I sewed it up inside a cap belonging to my landlady."
"Your landlady's cap?"
"Yes. I took it from her."
"How did you come by it?"

"You see, I remember once taking a cap to use as a rag, maybe to wipe my pen on. I took it without asking, because it was a worthless scrap. I tore it up, and took the notes and sewed them into it. I believe it was that very rag I sewed them in. An old bit of calico, washed a thousand times."
"And you're certain of that now?"
"I don't know if I'm certain. I think it was the cap. But hang it, what does it matter?"
"In that case, your landlady will remember the thing going missing?"
"No, she won't, she never noticed it was gone. It was an old rag, I tell you, an old rag not worth a kopeck."
"And where did you get the needle and thread?"
"I'll stop now. I won't say another word. Enough of this!" said Mitya, finally losing his temper.
"It's strange that you'd have so completely forgotten where you threw the pieces, in the marketplace."

"Give orders to have the marketplace swept tomorrow, and maybe you'll find it," said Mitya, sneering. "Enough, gentlemen, enough!" he decided, in an exhausted voice. "I see you don't believe me! Not for one moment! It's my fault, not yours. I shouldn't have been so eager to talk. Why, why did I lower myself, confessing my secret to you? It's all a joke to you. I can see it in your eyes. You led me into it, Prosecutor? Sing your hymn of triumph, if you can.... Damn you, you torturers!"

He bowed his head and buried his face in his hands. The lawyers said nothing. A minute later he raised his head and looked at them, almost blankly. His face now showed complete, hopeless despair, and he sat mute and passive, as if barely aware of what was happening. Meanwhile, they had to finish what they'd set out to do. They now had to begin questioning the witnesses without delay. It was already eight in the morning. The lamps had been put out long ago. Mihail Makarovitch and Kalganov, who'd been going in and out of the room continually the whole time the questioning had gone on, had both stepped out again now. The lawyers looked worn out too. It was a wretched morning; the whole sky lay overcast, and rain poured down in sheets. Mitya stared blankly out the window.
"May I look out the window?" he asked Nikolay Parfenovitch, suddenly.
"Oh, as much as you like," the man replied.

Mitya got up and went to the window.... The rain lashed against its small, greenish panes. He could see the muddy road just below the house, and farther off, through the rain and mist, a row of poor, black, dismal huts, looking even blacker and poorer in the downpour. Mitya thought of "Phoebus the golden-haired," and how he'd planned to shoot himself at the first ray of light. "Maybe it would be even better on a morning like this," he thought, with a smile, and suddenly, flinging his hand down, he turned back to his "torturers."

"Gentlemen," he cried, "I see that I'm lost! But her — tell me about her, I beg you. Surely she doesn't have to be ruined along with me? She's innocent, you know, she was out of her mind when she cried out last night, 'It's all my fault!' She's done nothing, nothing! I've been grieving over her all night, the whole time I've been sitting here with you.... Can't you, won't you, tell me what you intend to do with her now?"

"You can set your mind entirely at ease on that score, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," the prosecutor answered at once, with evident readiness. "So far, we have no grounds for taking any action against the lady you're so concerned about. I trust that will remain true as the case develops further.... On the contrary, we'll do everything in our power in that regard. Set your mind entirely at ease."
"Gentlemen, I thank you. I knew you were honest, straightforward people, in spite of everything. You've taken a weight off my heart.... Well, what do we do now? I'm ready."
"Well, we ought to hurry. We need to move on to questioning the witnesses without delay. That must happen in your presence, and so—"
"Shouldn't we have some tea first?" Nikolay Parfenovitch put in. "I think we've earned it!"

They decided that if tea was ready downstairs (Mihail Makarovitch had no doubt gone down to arrange some), they'd have a glass and then "press on and on," putting off a proper breakfast for a more convenient moment. Tea really was ready below, and was soon brought up. Mitya at first refused the glass Nikolay Parfenovitch politely offered him, but then asked for it himself and drank it down greedily. He looked strikingly worn out. Given his herculean strength, one might have assumed that a single night of carousing, even one wrapped in such violent emotion, could hardly touch him. But he felt he could barely hold his head up, and every so often everything around him seemed to heave and swim before his eyes. "A little more and I'll start raving," he told himself.
